Alabama Cannabis & Hemp Research — Parts 0–12 (Audited and Corrected)

Last audited: 28 October 2026. This is an independent audit of the Alabama Parts 0–12 report originally checked 25 October 2026. The auditor did not write the original report. The federal baseline below was used as given and was not re-audited; only the report's statement of it and Alabama's responses to it were checked.

How to read this file. Part A is the audit table (one verdict per claim). Part B lists everything that stays unverified, with the route to confirm it. Part C is the complete corrected rewrite, Parts 0–12, with every correction applied in place. A superseded figure is mentioned in the rewrite only where it is explicitly identified as superseded, erroneous, or removed — it is never presented as current law or a current figure. Where the corrected rewrite and the original Research Notes gap log differ, the corrected rewrite and the Track D disposition prevail.

AUDIT METHOD AND FEDERAL BASELINE

Method. Primary sources only for law facts: the Code of Alabama and bill/Act pages on the Alabama Legislature's official site (legislature.state.al.us / alison.legislature.state.al.us), the Alabama Administrative Code (admincode.legislature.state.al.us), the Alabama Medical Cannabis Commission (amcc.alabama.gov, including meeting minutes, resolutions and award announcements), the Alabama Department of Agriculture and Industries, the Alabama Department of Revenue, the Alabama Department of Public Health, the Alabama Board of Medical Examiners, Attorney General official opinions, court dockets and orders (Montgomery County Circuit Court, Alabama Court of Civil Appeals, Alabama Supreme Court, and federal courts), official tribal government sources, and official county and city sites and codes. News, law-firm blogs, trade press and AI summaries were never used to confirm a law fact; where only a secondary source exists the claim is marked Unverified. Every claim received exactly one verdict: Confirmed, Corrected, Removed, or Unverified.

Federal baseline (as given). Scheduling is split. Under a final rule at 91 FR 22714 (effective 28 April 2026), FDA-approved cannabis products and state-licensed medical marijuana are in Schedule III. All other marijuana, including all adult-use, remains Schedule I. The broader 2024 rescheduling proposal is NOT final. IRS 280E: Treasury has said rescheduling generally removes 280E as a bar for businesses no longer dealing in Schedule I/II substances (guidance forthcoming); adult-use activity remains fully subject to 280E. Hemp: Public Law 119-37 §781 takes legal effect 12 November 2026, but Public Law 119-103 §2019 limits it until 11 December 2026 to only the provisions excluding cannabinoids that are not naturally produced or are synthesized; the full total-THC definition and 0.4 mg per container cap apply after 11 December 2026. USDA has delayed enforcement of the DEA-registered-laboratory hemp testing requirement until 31 December 2026. The federal medical-marijuana appropriations rider is in force through 11 December 2026. No federal cannabis banking law has been enacted.

Application to Alabama (audited position). Alabama is medical-only. Its licensees are operating and selling: the first legal medical dispensary opened 4 June 2026 (AMCC Patients page), with Talladega opening 28 August 2026 and Athens (Bama Bloom) 14 September 2026 — three dispensaries open, three of four dispensary licences issued (8 January 2026), Yellowhammer awarded 11 December 2025 but stayed and not issued, and zero of five integrated-facility licences issued. The baseline's Schedule III / 280E logic therefore applies in principle to those operating state-licensed medical licensees, while any non-medical possession remains Schedule I federally. No Alabama official statement (AMCC or ALDOR) confirming Schedule III flow-through, 280E treatment, or a response to the federal hemp dates was located in this audit — that application is labelled analysis only, [VERIFY] with ALDOR/AMCC, and must not be presented as Alabama-confirmed law. Likewise no Alabama official statement addressing PL 119-37 §781 / PL 119-103 §2019 by number or by the 12 November / 11 December 2026 dates was located — [UNAVAILABLE] in the original, retained here.

Headline corrections that change the original everywhere they appeared

  • First-offering applicants: 94, not 90 — AMCC official page: 12 cultivator, 12 processor, 18 dispensary, 11 secure transporter, 3 testing, 38 integrated. Issued: cultivators 9 of 12, processors 4 of 4, secure transporters 4 (no cap), testing 1 currently licensed (Green Health; Certus expired 29 December 2025), dispensaries 3 of 4 issued 8 January 2026, integrated 0 of 5. Dispensing sites: 3 open, 9 authorised by issued licences, 37 maximum (12 + 25).
  • Cultivation-transfer bill: HB 390 (2024), Act 2024-342, not HB 342. Rep. Danny Crawford; Senate passage 8 May 2024. The original's HB 342 appears to be a tracker mislabel.
  • 2026 bills that died at sine die (not "pending"): SB 1 (2026) and SB 321 (2026) died at the end of the 2026 Regular Session; SB 285 (2026) did not advance and creates no licence type; HB 72 (2026) died — passed House, never passed Senate, never signed. HB 445 signing-date split: 14 May 2025 reported signature vs 27 May 2025 tracker "Enacted" recording — confirm on the Secretary of State enrolled act.
  • Leni's Law signing corrected to 4 May 2016 (Governor's archive; effective 1 June 2016); the original's "4 May 2026" in one place was a typographical error. Carly's Law dates remain "Secondary sources only — Verify."
  • Expungement fee resolved to $500 under current (2024) §15-27-4(a); the $300 figure is the superseded 2014 text and is removed as a current figure. Fentanyl-testing exception resolved to §13A-12-260(f) (Act 2022-154, eff. 1 June 2022). The 5 ng/mL driving proposal is SB 255 (2016), not SB 180 (2017); proposal only, never law; Alabama has no per se THC driving limit (impairment-based).
  • Licence-data corrections: AMCC Annual Report 2025 exists (18 licences + dispensary issuance narrative); dispensary + integrated applicant-summary PDFs do exist (2024/2025 versions, stale for January 2026 issuances). Jemmstone: Court of Civil Appeals opinion released 6 February 2026 (CL-2025-0314/0330/0337); the 12 February 2026 minutes' "6 February 2025" is a typo for 2026. Supreme Court cert. denials cited in the original are cert. denials, not merits rulings.
  • Hemp fees confirmed from primary rules: ADAI $150 application (not stale $200) + $1,000 per site (grower and processor); ABC retailer $50 filing + $1,000 annual + $25,000 bond per location; manufacturer/wholesaler $5,000 (HB 445 engrossed text; current-Code section numbers still unverified). ENDS-retailer eligibility effective 1 October 2026 confirmed (SB 287, Act 2026-504). Alabama runs its own USDA-approved state plan (ADAI, effective 1 January 2022; AMS list updated 17 February 2026), not USDA-direct licensing.
  • Removed as counts: the early-March 2026 "8 ABC retailers" figure (Track C) and the "Alabama cardholder" description of Wilson v. Lynch (plaintiff was a Nevada resident holding a Nevada card). Part 8 headline stands: zero verified cannabis-zoned properties.
  • Largest residual limit (drives most Unverified verdicts): the Legislature Code viewer did not return directly openable section pages in this audit pass, so most statute quotations read on Justia / LawServer / Cornell mirrors remain [VERIFY] against the official Code, even where substance is consistent with AMCC/ADOR pages. Medical sales-tax stacking (9% plus 4% general + local, or 9% only) is likewise unresolved — do not publish a single all-in patient tax rate until ADOR issues a determination or an itemised dispensary receipt is obtained. No official ADOR/AMCC totals for medical-cannabis tax collections, privilege-tax collections, total retail sales, or consumable-hemp excise collections were located.
  • No personal phone or email for any individual licence holder, applicant, or physician is reproduced in this audited file. Official public agency contacts only.

PART C — CORRECTED REWRITE (Parts 0–12)

Complete corrected report, with every audit correction applied in place. Every fact carries a source link next to it. Verify / Unavailable flags are kept only on items still unresolved after the audit.

PART 0 — HEADLINES

0.1 The programme in one paragraph

Alabama is medical-only. There is no adult-use programme, no decriminalisation law, and no home-grow right — including for registered patients. The Darren Wesley 'Ato' Hall Compassion Act (Act 2021-450, signed 17 May 2021) created the Alabama Medical Cannabis Commission (AMCC) and a closed, non-smokable medical programme. After three voided/rescinded award rounds and years of Montgomery County Circuit Court and Court of Civil Appeals litigation, the first dispensary opened 4 June 2026. As of 28 October 2026, three dispensaries are open (Montgomery, Talladega, Athens), nine dispensing-site municipalities are listed by AMCC for licences issued to date, integrated-facility licences are still in administrative hearings, and one dispensary licence is awarded but stayed and not issued. Separately, Alabama now runs a tightly licensed consumable-hemp regime under Title 28, Chapter 12 (HB 445, Act 2025-385): smokable hemp has been banned since 1 July 2025, and from 1 January 2026 consumable hemp may be sold only by ABC-licensed retailers, only to buyers 21+, only in person, at 10 mg total THC per serving / 40 mg per package.

0.2 Federal baseline — how it applies to Alabama (given baseline, not re-researched)

Under the fixed federal baseline, state-licensed medical marijuana and FDA-approved products moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714); all adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I; IRS 280E is generally lifted for Schedule III medical activity while adult-use remains fully subject to it. Alabama's programme is state-licensed medical only, and its licensees are operating and selling (from 4 June 2026, AMCC Patients page), so the baseline's Schedule III / 280E logic applies in principle to those operating licensees, while any non-medical possession remains Schedule I federally. That application has not been confirmed in an Alabama official statement located in this audit — flag as [VERIFY] with ALDOR/AMCC; do not present it as Alabama-confirmed law. Alabama-specific twist, secondary-reported only: Alabama law is reported to adopt a federal reclassification automatically unless the State Committee of Public Health objects within 30 days; the Committee is reported to have objected 21 May 2026, held a public hearing 22 July 2026, then voted in September 2026 to withdraw/drop its objection. The automatic-adoption statute citation is [VERIFY] on the Legislature's official site before stating it as law, and this file does not state that Alabama has rescheduled anything. No Alabama official statement on the federal hemp dates (PL 119-37 §781, 12 Nov 2026; PL 119-103 §2019, to 11 Dec 2026) was located — [UNAVAILABLE]; see Part 1.5. There is no federal cannabis banking law (baseline).

0.3 Latest awards and litigation in brief

11 December 2025: AMCC adopted an Administrative Law Judge's Recommended Order as its final order, awarding dispensary licences, superseding prior award/denial decisions for those applicants. Three licences have issued; one licence awarded 11 December 2025 has been stayed (AMCC Patients page). Integrated-facility administrative hearings are under way; no integrated licence has issued. The licensee names, the 8 January 2026 issuance date, the hearing start date, and the detailed litigation chronology for these awards are in the licence track (Part 4, audited separately) and were not re-confirmed on AMCC minutes pages opened in this audit — [VERIFY — AMCC 11 Dec 2025 minutes]. Do not merge "awarded" with "issued" anywhere in this file.

PART 1 — LAWS

1.1 Legal status: medical only; what is not legal for non-patients

Only a registered qualified patient or registered caregiver, holding a valid AMCC card, may possess or use medical cannabis — and only in the listed non-smokable forms, only purchased from a licensed dispensary (or, for an integrated facility's own sites, its dispensing sites), and only within the 60-dose purchase / 70-dose possession limits (Part 1.4 — limits [VERIFY on official Code]). Everything else is criminal: recreational possession, sale, cultivation and use; home grow (including for patients); smokable flower, vapes and conventional food edibles as medical cannabis; and diversion. There is no reciprocity and no visiting-patient programme: an out-of-state card gives no rights in Alabama, and a dispensary may not dispense to a nonresident, including a patient registered under another jurisdiction's laws (Ala. Admin. Code r. 538-X-8-.02, official site: Rule 538-X-8-.02 — rule text (5)(c) and (5)(h) prohibit dispensing to non-residents and to patients/caregivers registered under another jurisdiction's laws).

There is no weight threshold for simple possession (secondary summary — [VERIFY on official Code]); intent and priors control. Cultivation / home grow: no personal-cultivation defence exists. Cultivation by a non-licensee is manufacture (§§13A-12-217/218 — [VERIFY]). (quotation from a mirror — [VERIFY on official Code]). Public consumption for patients: the Act does not permit possessing or using medical cannabis on any K-12 school property, in any correctional facility, or in a vehicle unless it is in its original sealed package and reasonably inaccessible while the vehicle is moving (§20-2A-8(b)(2) — enacted numbering [VERIFY]). AMCC Ch. 538-X-2 adds: no possession/administration on federal property/buildings or at state/federal correctional detention facilities; no possession/administration outside packaging on a dispensing-site or licensed-facility premises; "No patient shall operate a motor vehicle, watercraft, heavy machinery, or aircraft while under the influence of medical cannabis." No general freestanding public-consumption misdemeanor for patients was located — because the allowed forms are non-smokable, "public smoking" is already excluded by the product definition. Whether "daycare" appears in the enacted §20-2A-8 text or only in a draft/secondary summary is [VERIFY].

Allowed medical forms — §20-2A-3(14) (confirmed in substance on AMCC Patients page):

"MEDICAL CANNABIS. a. A medical grade product in the form of any of the following, as determined by rule by the commission, that contains a derivative of cannabis for medical use by a registered qualified patient pursuant to this chapter: 1. Oral tablet, capsule, or tincture. 2. Non-sugarcoated gelatinous cube, gelatinous rectangular cuboid, or lozenge in a cube or rectangular cuboid shape. 3. Gel, oil, cream, or other topical preparation. 4. Suppository. 5. Transdermal patch. 6. Nebulizer. 7. Liquid or oil for administration using an inhaler. b. The term does not include any of the following: 1. Raw plant material. 2. Any product administered by smoking, combustion, or vaping. 3. A food product that has medical cannabis baked, mixed, or otherwise infused into the product, such as cookies or candies."

AMCC's patient page confirms the same list in plain language: AMCC Patients. Gelatinous cubes are not gummies in Alabama law: the statute requires non-sugar-coated cubes/cuboids/lozenges in cube/rectangular-cuboid shape. Flavour claims (e.g. "peach gel cubes only") are secondary and unverified — do not state a peach-only rule unless an AMCC rule or product list confirms it. Nebulizer vs vape: nebulizers convert liquid/oil to mist without combustion; vaporizers/smoking are expressly excluded, which is why inhaler liquids/oils are allowed while vape carts are not.

Daily dose limits — confirmed, with exact triggers (§20-2A-33(f)(2); r. 540-X-25-.11, official: Rule 540-X-25-.11):

"The maximum daily dosage may not exceed 50 mg of delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol; provided, however, the maximum daily dosage may be increased under either of the following circumstances: a. A registered certifying physician may increase a patient's daily dosage if, after 90 days of continuous care under the physician during which time the patient was using medical cannabis, the physician determines that a higher daily dosage is medically appropriate, provided the maximum daily dosage under this paragraph may not exceed 75 mg of delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol. b. A registered certifying physician may increase a patient's daily dosage if the patient has been diagnosed with a terminal illness, provided, if the recommended daily dosage exceeds 75 mg of delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol, the physician shall notify the patient that the patient's driver's license will be suspended."

Per r. 540-X-25-.11(3), the 75 mg increase also requires a clear articulation in the medical record of the justification. Above 75 mg is terminal-illness only, with the driver's-licence-suspension notice. The suspension mechanism (which agency, automatic vs court-ordered) is [VERIFY] before stating it as automatic. Minor potency cap: a physician may not recommend medical cannabis with potency greater than 3% THC to any minor (§20-2A-33(g)). "Daily dosage" (§20-2A-3(6)) is the total amount of one or more cannabis derivatives that may be ingested by a patient during a 24-hour period, as determined by the certifying physician.

1.4 Medical programme

Qualifying conditions — §20-2A-3(21) (confirmed in substance on AMCC Patients page). "Any of the following conditions or symptoms of conditions, but only after documentation indicates that conventional medical treatment or therapy has failed unless current medical treatment indicates that use of medical cannabis is the standard of care:" (a) Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD); (b) Cancer-related cachexia, nausea or vomiting, weight loss, or chronic pain; (c) Crohn's Disease; (d) Depression; (e) Epilepsy or a condition causing seizures; (f) HIV/AIDS-related nausea or weight loss; (g) Panic disorder; (h) Parkinson's disease; (i) Persistent nausea not significantly responsive to traditional treatment, except nausea related to pregnancy, cannabis-induced cyclical vomiting syndrome, or cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome; (j) Post Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD); (k) Sickle Cell Anemia; (l) Spasticity associated with a motor neuron disease, including ALS; (m) Spasticity associated with Multiple Sclerosis or a spinal cord injury; (n) A terminal illness; (o) Tourette's Syndrome; (p) A condition causing chronic or intractable pain in which conventional therapeutic intervention and opiate therapy is contraindicated or has proved ineffective. Count: 16 lettered categories (a–p). Secondary sources variously say 15, 16 or 17 — use the lettered list, not a bare number. The gatekeeper condition is that conventional treatment must have failed, unless medical cannabis is the standard of care; AMCC's definition rule adds that "failed" is in the certifying physician's sole discretion and need not entail exhaustion of conventional therapies if the physician is reasonably satisfied other approaches are contraindicated/futile (r. 538-X-1-.04 — [VERIFY on official Admin Code]).

Physician registration and certification (§20-2A-31; Ch. 540-X-25). Verbatim core, §20-2A-31(a) (mirror — [VERIFY on official Code]): "(1) Hold an active license to practice medicine under Chapter 24 of Title 34. (2) Complete a four-hour course related to medical cannabis and complete a subsequent examination, both of which shall be offered by a multi-specialty statewide professional organization of physicians in this state that is recognized to accredit intrastate organizations to provide AMA PRA category 1 credits. The course must be administered at least annually and may be offered in a distance learning format, including an electronic online format upon request. The price of the course may not exceed five hundred dollars ($500). Every two years thereafter, in order to requalify, a certifying physician must complete a two-hour refresher course offered by an entity described in this subdivision. (3) Pay an initial registration fee established by the board, not to exceed three hundred dollars ($300). (4) Meet any additional qualifications established by rule by the board." ALBME rules add (mirror — [VERIFY in Ch. 540-X-25]): active unrestricted Alabama medical/osteopathic licence; active unrestricted Alabama Controlled Substances Certificate (ACSC); active unrestricted Alabama-specific DEA registration; current PDMP query registration (ADPH); current/intended AMCC Patient Registry registration; practice-experience test — at least 3 years' active practice, or at least 1 year plus specialty-board certification; $300 initial fee (non-refundable, non-transferable); annual renewal by 31 Dec, $200 renewal cap in statute (§20-2A-31(c)). AMCC confirms the general requirement on its official page (AMCC Patients: recommendation must come from a registered certifying physician approved by ALBME and AMCC; ALBME requires a medical cannabis training course and certification). Certification (§20-2A-33) is valid as determined by the Board but never more than 12 months; the physician sets form and THC content up to the statutory maximum daily dosage; certification is a recommendation, not a prescription (r. 540-X-25-.10 — [VERIFY]). In-person visit and telehealth specifics are [VERIFY — secondary sources conflict on telehealth]. Physician prohibitions reported in law-firm summaries (no remuneration for certifying except customary patient charges; no interest in a licensee / referral to a specific dispensary) are [VERIFY in Ch. 540-X-25].

Patient registry, cards, caregivers, fees, limits (§20-2A-30; Ch. 538-X-2). Adult patient, §20-2A-30(a) verbatim core (mirror — [VERIFY on official Code]): "A resident of this state who is 19 years of age or older is a registered qualified patient if he or she meets all of the following conditions: a. Has been certified by a registered certifying physician as having a qualifying medical condition. b. Is registered with the commission. c. Has been issued a valid medical cannabis card by the commission." Residency, the 19-year threshold, and registry/card requirements are confirmed on AMCC Patients page. Minor patient, §20-2A-30(b): under 19, same certification + registration, plus a qualified designated caregiver who is the parent/legal guardian; a minor "may use medical cannabis but may not purchase or possess medical cannabis." AMCC confirms: a patient under 19 must have a registered qualified caregiver who is the patient's parent or legal guardian. [CONFLICT] AMCC Ch. 538-X-2 extends the caregiver relationship for minors to parent/legal guardian/grandparent/spouse/power-of-attorney holder in one summary — pin the enacted rule before stating who may serve for a minor. Caregiver, §20-2A-30(c): Alabama resident; registered; issued a valid card; at least 21, unless the parent/legal guardian of the patient; must be parent, legal guardian, grandparent, spouse, or holder of health-care power of attorney (adult-caregiver categories confirmed on AMCC Patients page). A caregiver may purchase/possess but "may not use medical cannabis unless he or she is also a registered qualified patient." Whether Ch. 538-X-2 sets a numeric limit on patients per caregiver was not located [VERIFY]. Purchase/possession limits, §20-2A-30(d) verbatim (mirror — [VERIFY on official Code]): "a registered qualified patient or registered caregiver may not purchase more than 60 daily dosages of medical cannabis and may not renew the supply more than 10 days before the 60-day period expires. At no time may a registered qualified patient or registered caregiver possess more than 70 daily dosages of medical cannabis." AMCC implements this as a 60-day purchase period; arrest/prosecution protection applies if possessing no more than 70 daily dosages with a valid card. Card fees — [CONFLICT]: statute (§20-2A-35, enrolled SB 46) caps the application fee at $65; current AMCC practice per a coalition summary of AMCC FAQs is digital card $40, physical (hard) card +$10 (initial and renewal), replacement physical card $25, card valid 1 year from issuance. Publish both, labelled; verify the current figures on the AMCC portal/FAQ on the day of use. Portal instructions: AMCC Portal Instructions — Patients (PDF). Out-of-state patients: no reciprocity, no visiting-patient programme; residency is a statutory element (§20-2A-30(a)) and dispensing to non-residents is prohibited by r. 538-X-8-.02 (official: Rule 538-X-8-.02). Registry opened late April 2026 (secondary, MPP); the exact launch day was not located on an AMCC announcement [VERIFY]. Caregiver counts: none found [UNAVAILABLE].

1.5 Hemp — limits, measurement, psychoactive products, beverages, federal dates

Farm hemp definition and the measurement conflict. Statute, §2-8-381(4) (2017 mirror — [VERIFY on official Code]): "All parts and varieties of the plant Cannabis sativa, cultivated or possessed by a licensed grower, whether growing or not, that contain a delta-9 tetrahydrocannabinol concentration of not more than 0.3 percent on a dry weight basis. Industrial hemp shall be considered an agricultural crop or an agricultural commodity, or both, in all respects under state law. The term excludes marijuana as defined in subdivision (14) of Section 20-2-2." ADAI rule, r. 80-10-21-.02, defines hemp with "total delta-9 tetrahydrocannabinol concentration of not more than 0.3 percent on a dry weight basis" and defines "Percentage of THC on a dry weight basis" as "the percentage of total THC, by weight, in a cannabis item (plant, extract, or other derivative), after excluding moisture from the item." (mirror — [VERIFY]). So the statute says "delta-9"; the ADAI rule says "total delta-9." Whether Alabama's current programme applies a total-THC (THCA-inclusive) test at farm level is [VERIFY] against the current ADAI programme page and current §2-8-381 text; do not state "total THC" as the statutory test without that check. Keep three tests distinct: (i) farm hemp definition, (ii) consumable-hemp serving/package caps, (iii) federal post-11-Dec-2026 total-THC definition.

Consumable hemp (Title 28, Ch. 12) — operative retail regime from 1 January 2026. Age: 21+ only. Permitted forms (in scope, meeting caps/testing/labelling/licensing and not in an excluded category): tablets, capsules, tinctures, gummies/edibles (individually wrapped), beverages, gels/oils/creams/topicals, sublinguals, suppositories. Banned/excluded: (1) smokable hemp — flower, pre-rolls, joints, buds, leaves, ground flower, hemp cigarettes/cigars — banned from 1 July 2025; sale or possession is a Class C felony per AG guidance 11 June 2025 and HB 445 (attribute the felony consequence to the AG's enforcement position; the enrolled-text penalty pinpoint is [VERIFY]); (2) psychoactive cannabinoids created by chemical synthesis, modification or conversion (the commercial delta-8/delta-10 route) — excluded from "consumable hemp product," so sale/possession falls outside the lawful Chapter 12 channel. Consequences by compound (stated as consequences, with caveats): Delta-8 overwhelmingly produced by CBD conversion → effectively unlawful in Alabama retail from 1 Jan 2026 (smokable delta-8 unlawful from 1 July 2025); trace naturally occurring delta-8 vs converted delta-8 distinction [VERIFY — no official guidance located]. Delta-9 (hemp-derived) lawful only as a compliant consumable hemp product (caps, ABC licence, 21+, in person) — not as flower, not by mail, not in a convenience store. THCA: smokable/inhalable THCA banned as smokable hemp; non-smokable THCA that decarboxylates on ingestion is counted in "total THC" for serving/package caps, so a high-THCA edible exceeding 10 mg total THC/serving is non-compliant even if delta-9 alone is ≤0.3%. The THCA-to-total-THC formula (secondary sources cite the standard 0.877 decarboxylation factor) is [VERIFY in §28-12-2 / ABC rule]. HHC, delta-10, THC-O and other converted/synthetic cannabinoids: same synthesis/conversion exclusion as delta-8 → outside the lawful channel. CBD (non-psychoactive): consumable hemp products containing CBD are governed by Chapter 12 from 1 Jan 2026; this file does not state the status of non-consumable hemp/CBD outside Chapter 12's definition — [VERIFY]. FDA-approved Epidiolex remains a prescription drug outside both regimes.

Per-serving / per-package caps (secondary consensus — pinpoint [VERIFY] in enrolled text): edibles and beverages 10 mg total THC per serving; edible carton/package max 40 mg total THC (max four 10 mg individually wrapped servings); topical, sublingual and other non-beverage/non-edible consumables 40 mg total THC per container; beverages one serving per container, max 12 fluid ounces, max 10 mg total THC, carton max four containers.

Retailer/manufacturer/wholesaler permits (summary; full treatment in Part 7). ABC Board licences manufacturers, wholesalers and retailers. Retailer fees confirmed for retailers on the Alison fiscal note for the enacted Act (FN-ARGIKSQ-5): $50 application filing fee + $1,000 licence fee on approval + $25,000 surety bond per location (bond [VERIFY in §§28-12-40 et seq.]); manufacturer/wholesaler $5,000 [VERIFY in §§28-12-40 et seq.]. Applicants (10%+ owners, except publicly traded companies) submit fingerprints, 10-year criminal history, proof of lawful presence, proof of premises, and a municipal/county approval letter — the ABC Board "may not issue a license under this article unless the local governing body of the county or municipality in which the licensee's facility will be located has approved the application for licensure" (secondary quotation — statutory pinpoint [VERIFY in §§28-12-40 et seq.]). Eligible retailer categories (as amended by Act 2026-504): (1) specialty retailers — 21+-only, dedicated entrance, ≥500 sq ft hemp retail area (enrolled SB 287: ≥500 sq ft sales/service area, employee present at all times open, purchase on licensed premises); (2) pharmacies — topical/sublingual only; (3) qualifying retail food stores — beverages only, ≥75% of selling area dedicated to food items AND ≥14,000 sq ft of footprint dedicated to food items, separated signed area; (4) from 1 Oct 2026, qualifying specialty ENDS retailers (Act 2026-504, FN-G3DT7C6-4). Convenience stores generally are NOT eligible — the most misreported point; the ENDS expansion does not change it. Monthly sales reports to the ABC Board; 10% excise tax shown as a separate receipt line (Part 2).

Testing and labelling (Chapter 12). Independent laboratory certificate of analysis (COA) per batch; label must carry: ingredient list in descending predominance order; scannable barcode/QR code linked to the COA; manufacture and expiration dates; batch number; serving size; total mg THC per container and per serving; consumer warnings (not for minors, may impair driving, may cause a failed drug test, pregnancy/breastfeeding warning). Packaging must be child-resistant and tamper-evident; no cartoon imagery, no mimicry of children's snacks, no appeal to minors. Testing panel (potency, pesticides, heavy metals, solvents, mycotoxins, microbials, terpenes) and ISO 17025 accreditation are secondary-reported [VERIFY in the ABC rule, not the statute text extracted here].

THC beverages — specific rules. Beverages are the only consumable hemp form a qualifying grocery store may sell; they must be kept in a separated area (ABC's final approach reported as unlocked plexiglass, separate refrigerator from beer, self-service like beer — [VERIFY against the final ABC rule; the initial proposal required locked glass + employee retrieval]); max 12 fl oz, 10 mg total THC, one serving per container. Beverages may not be sold by gas stations/convenience stores as a general category. No on-premises consumption rule was located — sales are for off-premises consumption only (secondary summary). Online / delivery / vending / drive-through: prohibited (secondary summaries of HB 445 — [VERIFY in enrolled text / ABC rule]). Out-of-state brands may not ship consumable hemp products to Alabama addresses after 1 Jan 2026 even if federally compliant (secondary summary — [VERIFY]).

The vape / "smokable vs inhalable" conflict — open, not settled. The enrolled §28-12-2 text extracted here defines "smokeable hemp product" by combustible plant material (cigarettes, cigars, joints, buds, flowers, leaves, ground flower) and contains no express reference to vaporisation devices, cartridges or e-liquids (enrolled text not re-opened in this audit — [VERIFY]). The Attorney General's enforcement position and most secondary guides treat vapes as banned ("If it burns, you can't stock it or possess it"). At least one detailed industry memorandum argues vaping is not combustion and therefore not within the statutory definition. Present this as an open interpretive conflict with enforcement risk, not as settled law either way. A retailer relying on the "vapes are legal consumables" reading faces Class C felony exposure under the AG's reading.

Litigation (hemp). Hemp businesses sued, including a federal preemption challenge reported as filed 27 June 2025 by Mellow Fellow, and a Montgomery Circuit Court TRO request denied, allowing the 1 July 2025 ban to take effect on schedule, with the court clarifying hemp may still move through Alabama in interstate commerce. Case names/numbers were not pinned to a docket in this audit [VERIFY — do not name a case without a docket]. Secondary consensus is that no injunction has stopped enforcement as of Aug 2026. Pre-HB 445 hemp-psychoactive law: Act 2023-169, §13A-12-214.4 (sale/distribution of psychoactive cannabinoids to minors) — repealed by HB 445. Before HB 445, delta-8/delta-10/THCA flower and vapes were widely sold under the federal hemp definition (secondary market observation).

Alabama response to the new federal hemp definition and its 12 November / 11 December 2026 dates: none located — [UNAVAILABLE]. No ADAI, ABC Board, AMCC or Attorney General statement addressing PL 119-37 §781 or PL 119-103 §2019 by number or by those dates was found. The only built-in federal-conflict mechanism found is enrolled §28-12-1(d): "Any federal law enacted after July 1, 2025, that conflicts with a provision [of] this chapter shall supersede the conflicting provision of this chapter." Whether Alabama treats PL 119-37/119-103 as triggering that clause, and how the 0.4 mg/container federal cap interacts with Alabama's 10 mg/serving / 40 mg/package caps, is [VERIFY]. Note as analysis only (not an official Alabama statement): Alabama's 10 mg-per-serving cap is higher than the federal 0.4 mg-per-container cap that applies after 11 December 2026, so an Alabama-compliant 10 mg serving in a single container would exceed the federal per-container cap; the federal change does not by itself liberalise Alabama retail, and Alabama's own caps, licensing, age and channel rules continue to apply unless Alabama says otherwise. A secondary discrepancy to note: one Alabama Daily News passage states the federal law takes effect 13 Nov 2026, conflicting with the fixed baseline (12 Nov / 11 Dec 2026); this file uses the baseline dates.

1.6 Packaging, labelling, advertising, delivery, zoning and buffers

Medical — packaging/labelling (processor rule 538-X-6-.05, verbatim core — [VERIFY on the live Admin Code site before quoting verbatim]):

"Packaging and containers must be child-resistant. … must be tamper-evident. … must identify the Processor and type of product. … must not be attractive to minors. … must be designed to minimize appeal to children. … must not contain any false statement or statement that advertises health benefits or therapeutic benefits of medical cannabis." — "Labels must … identify the type of product (pills, tinctures, transdermal patches, etc.). … contain lot and batch numbers. … contain the name of and a license identification number for the Cultivator. … contain the name of and a license identification number for the Processor. … identify the cannabinoid content and potency of the product. … identify the amount, number or count of the product in the package … contain the universal state symbol approved by the Commission, printed in color at least one-half inch by one-half inch in size, and placed on the principal display panel … contain the words 'Keep out of reach of children.' … contain a digital image or QR Code for purposes of tracking medical cannabis products and must interface with the Statewide Seed-to-Sale Tracking System." Warning (label or insert): "WARNING: This product may make you drowsy or dizzy. Do not drink alcohol with this product. Use care when operating a vehicle or other machinery. Taking this product with medication may lead to harmful side effects or complications. Consult your physician before taking this product with any medication. Women who are breastfeeding, pregnant, or plan to become pregnant should discuss medical cannabis use with their physicians."

QR coding for transport: batches/containers shipped between licensees must be QR/digitally coded with cultivator/processor, facility, type, processing/packaging date, expiration date (or notation), state-lab testing approval date, and Alabama Poison Control contact info; shipment date/time logged in the seed-to-sale system (rr. 538-X-6-.06, 538-X-8-.05 — [VERIFY]). Universal-symbol appendix dated 26 Jan 2026 — the rule was updated for launch.

Medical — advertising (Ch. 538-X-4, verbatim core, AMCC PDF — [VERIFY against the June 2026 Admin Code text before quoting the 2024 PDF as current]):

"No licensee shall place or maintain, or cause to be placed or maintained, an advertisement of medical cannabis or any related product, in any of the following ways: (a) Within 500 feet of the perimeter of a prohibited facility or any business or organization where, in the opinion of the Commission, the placement of the advertisement targets or is attractive to minors; (b) On a billboard; (c) On a radio or television broadcast, including a system for transmitting visual images and sound that are reproduced on screens, and includes broadcast, cable, on-demand, satellite, cinema, social media, or another internet-based platform; (d) On any handheld or other portable sign; (e) With respect to public places, on a brochure, handbill, pamphlet, leaflet, or flyer directly handed, deposited, fastened, thrown, scattered, cast, or otherwise distributed to any person; (f) Left upon any private property without the consent of the property owners; (g) On or in a vehicle, public transit vehicle, or public transit shelter; or (h) On or in a publicly-owned or operated property."

Content bans include: cartoon characters / persons more than 15% of whose audience is minors; apparel/merchandise; suggesting a relationship to edibles (candy, cookies, brownies, cakes) or beverages; designs targeting minors; implying Commission/State approval or endorsement; advertising inconsistent with medicinal/approved use; encouraging use for a non-qualifying condition; false/misleading statements; non-registered names; depictions of cannabis plants (except inside a dispensing site or on a patients-only website); slang; disparagement; obscenity. External signage: no sign larger than 16 inches high by 18 inches wide (secondary summaries of the rule — pinpoint [VERIFY in Ch. 538-X-4]); no brand names/graphics on building exteriors or vehicles; products/paraphernalia not visible from outside the facility; all names/logos/campaigns submitted to the Commission (21-day review per secondary summaries — [VERIFY]); websites must verify users are not minors and may not facilitate online transactions.

Medical — delivery: PROHIBITED to patients. Dispensary rule 538-X-8-.02 (official: Rule 538-X-8-.02, (5)(e)): a dispensary licence does not permit the dispensary "to … (e) Deliver medical cannabis to anyone, including a registered qualified patient or registered caregiver." Secure transporters move product between licensed facilities only (§20-2A-65: "A license does not authorize transport to a registered qualified patient or registered caregiver" — [VERIFY on official Code]). Patients/caregivers must collect in person at a dispensing site with a valid card.

Medical — zoning / buffers. 1,000-foot buffer: "At Least One Thousand Feet shall mean at least one thousand feet in a straight line from the property line of the dispensing site premises to the property line of the school, daycare or childcare facility, measured at the nearest possible point between the two." "School, Daycare or Childcare Facility" = real property where a public/private K-12 school (excluding a homeschool residence) or a licensed daycare/childcare facility has actively operated within the last six months (Ch. 538-X-8, official: Chapter 538-X-8). Opt-in: "A dispensing site may not operate in the unincorporated area of a county or in a municipality that has not adopted a resolution or ordinance authorizing the operation of dispensing sites under §20-2A-51, Code of Alabama 1975 (as amended)." (rule subsection number [VERIFY — the original cites r. 538-X-8-.05(4) here and r. 538-X-8-.04(4) in Part 3.1 for the same prohibition]; statute §20-2A-51(c) — see Part 3). No statewide buffer for cultivators/processors was located beyond facility security/zoning via local law [VERIFY in Chs. 538-X-5/6]. A 2023 bill (HB 227, introduced only) would have extended the buffer to prisons, detention facilities, federal/state facilities and sports venues — not enacted; do not cite as law.

Hemp-derived products. Packaging/labelling/advertising: see Part 1.5 (child-resistant/tamper-evident, QR-to-COA, no child-appealing packaging, 21+ labelling). Advertising-specific rules for consumable hemp (e.g. whether the 500-foot / billboard / broadcast bans from Ch. 538-X-4 apply to hemp) were not located — Chapter 12's advertising provisions were not extracted in this audit [VERIFY — do not transplant the medical advertising bans onto hemp]. Delivery: prohibited (Part 1.5). Zoning/buffers for hemp retailers: no statewide 1,000-foot buffer was located; local approval is the control (municipal/county approval letter), plus local ordinances may add local rules. The 500 sq ft specialty-retailer area and dedicated-entrance rules are state eligibility rules, not buffers.

1.7 Seed-to-sale tracking

Statute — §20-2A-54(a) (verbatim via mirror — re-check official Code [VERIFY]): "In order to ensure that all medical cannabis sold in the state maintains product quality to protect the health and welfare of state residents, the commission shall establish a statewide seed-to-sale tracking system for use as an integrated cannabis and medical cannabis tracking, inventory, and verification system. The system must allow for interface with third-party inventory and tracking systems as described in Section 20-2A-60 to provide for access by this state, licensees, and law enforcement personnel, to the extent that they need and are authorized to receive or submit the information, to comply with, enforce, or administer this chapter." Vendor: Metrc — AMCC-documented. AMCC Intent to Award, 15 July 2022 (RFP 2022-MCSST-01): "On July 14, 2022, the Alabama Medical Cannabis Commission voted to award Metrc, LLC the Alabama Medical Cannabis Seed-to-Sale Tracking System contract per RFP#: 2022-MCSST-01. The final award of this contract is subject to review by the Legislative Contract Review Committee and signature by the Governor." (AMCC PDF — not re-opened in this audit, [VERIFY]). Metrc Alabama FAQ (vendor material, not an official rate): $40/month per licence; plant tags $0.45, package tags $0.25; licensees see only their own data — [VERIFY]. Licensees must pay for/maintain access to the Patient Registry (§20-2A-35), the Statewide Seed-to-Sale System (§20-2A-54), and any third-party inventory system (§20-2A-60) (AMCC Ch. 3 — [VERIFY]). Hemp seed-to-sale: no statewide hemp seed-to-sale system under Chapter 12 was confirmed in this audit; the 2026 SB 1 proposal would have required ADAI to build one for consumable hemp — as a proposal (now died, see Part 1.9), that confirms none existed under Chapter 12 at filing [VERIFY for Part 7/11 — ADAI hemp production tracking (plot registration, pre-harvest sampling) is a separate farm-level system].

1.8 Employment and drug-testing protections — there are essentially none

Statute — §20-2A-6(a) (verbatim, via mirror — [VERIFY on official Code]): "This chapter does not do any of the following: (1) Require an insurer, organization for managed care, health benefit plan, or any individual or entity providing coverage for a medical or health care service to pay for or to reimburse any other individual or entity for costs associated with the use of medical cannabis. (2) Require any employer to permit, accommodate, or allow the use of medical cannabis, or to modify any job or working conditions of any employee who engages in the use of medical cannabis or for any reason seeks to engage in the use of medical cannabis. (3) Prohibit any employer from refusing to hire, discharging, disciplining, or otherwise taking an adverse employment action against an individual with respect to hiring, discharging, tenure, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment as a result, in whole or in part, of that individual's use of medical cannabis, regardless of the individual's impairment or lack of impairment resulting from the use of medical cannabis. (4) Prohibit or limit the ability of any employer from establishing or enforcing a drug testing policy, including, but not limited to, a policy that prohibits the use of medical cannabis in the workplace or from implementing a drug-free workforce program established in accordance with Article 13, commencing with Section 25-5-330, of Chapter 5 of Title 25. (5) Prohibit or limit any employer from adopting an employment policy requiring its employees to notify the employer if an employee possesses a medical cannabis card. … (7) Permit, authorize, or establish any individual's right to commence or undertake any legal action against an employer for refusing to hire, discharging, disciplining, or otherwise taking an adverse employment action … due to the individual's use of medical cannabis." Unemployment consequence — §20-2A-6(c): "An individual who is discharged from employment because of that individual's use of medical cannabis, or refusal to submit to or cooperate with a drug test, shall be legally conclusively presumed to have been discharged for misconduct if the conditions of paragraph (3)a. of Section 25-4-78 are otherwise met." The one countervailing protection — §20-2A-6(b): "For the purpose of obtaining needed medical care, including organ transplants, a registered qualified patient's authorized use of medical cannabis in accordance with this chapter is considered the equivalent of the authorized use of any other medication used at the direction of a licensed health care professional and may not constitute the use of an illicit substance or otherwise disqualify a registered qualified patient from such needed medical care." Child-welfare exposure — §20-2A-6(d): nothing in the chapter prohibits the Department of Human Resources from considering a parent/caretaker's medical cannabis use as a factor where there is evidence of abuse/neglect, in custody best-interest determinations, or in foster/adoptive/kinship background checks. Bottom line: no employment protection, no drug-testing protection, no right to sue the employer, and a misconduct presumption for unemployment purposes. Federal DOT and other federal employment restrictions are expressly preserved (§20-2A-6(a)(6) — pinpoint [VERIFY]).

PART 2 — TAXES

2.1 Medical cannabis: 9% gross-proceeds tax — verified rate

Ala. Code §20-2A-80(a) (enrolled SB 46, Alison PDF): "Commencing January 1, 2022, there is levied, in addition to all other taxes of every kind now imposed by law, and shall be collected and remitted in accordance with Article 1, commencing with Section 40-23-1, of Chapter 23 of Title 40, a tax on the gross proceeds of the sales of medical cannabis when sold at retail in this state at the rate of nine percent of the gross proceeds of the sales." Origin: Compassion Act, Act 2021-450, signed 17 May 2021. Who pays / remits: the tax is levied on the gross proceeds of retail sales; collection is under Title 40, Chapter 23, Article 1 (the sales-tax collection machinery), i.e. in practice the retail dispensary / integrated-facility dispensing site remits it (audit reading of the collection machinery, not a separate statutory sentence). Do not double-count it: some secondary pages describe "a 9% sales tax AND a 9% excise tax" — that is the same single §20-2A-80 tax counted twice. The second medical levy is the annual privilege tax in §20-2A-80(b) (Part 2.3). Distribution: §20-2A-10(a) puts into the Medical Cannabis Commission Fund: "(1) Tax proceeds collected pursuant to subsections (a) and (b) of Section 2 of the act adding this language, less an amount sufficient to cover the cost of administration of the tax levies … which shall be retained by the Department of Revenue. (2) License fees, civil penalties, and other fees or charges … (3) Any monies appropriated … for the initial operation of the commission." (mirror — [VERIFY — official Code re-check]). Excess-fund distribution from 1 Oct 2025: §20-2A-10(c): "Beginning October 1, 2025, any funds in the Medical Cannabis Commission Fund in excess of actual expenses from the previous fiscal year shall be distributed, less 10 percent, as follows: (1) 60 percent shall be transferred to the General Fund. (2) 30 percent shall be transferred to the Medical Cannabis Research Fund established pursuant to subsection (f) of Section 4." The Department of Examiners of Public Accounts audit summary reads this as the Commission retaining 10% of the balance, transferring 60% to the General Fund and 30% to the Medical Cannabis Research Fund — summing to 100% of the balance. The arithmetic reading ("60% + 30% of what remains after retaining 10%" vs "60% + 30% of the whole balance") is ambiguous in the statutory sentence — flag [VERIFY]; use the Examiners' reading (10/60/30) as the working interpretation.

2.2 Sales-tax treatment of medical cannabis — the key unresolved point

General state sales tax is 4%: Ala. Code §40-23-2(1) levies "four percent of the gross proceeds of sales" on retail tangible personal property, and ADOR confirms "General: 4%" (official: ADOR Sales/Use Tax Rates). Section 20-2A-80(a) says the 9% is "in addition to all other taxes of every kind now imposed by law." On its face that points to stacking: 9% medical tax plus applicable general state and local sales taxes, not a replacement for them. Corroborated by the City of Dothan's official medical-cannabis fact sheet ("Sales and use taxes will be collected by the City of Dothan. Excise taxes will be collected by the State." — fact sheet not re-opened in this audit) and by Alabama Cannabis Coalition president Marty Schelper (2023, secondary) describing "a special 9% sales tax in addition to regular state and local sales taxes that can be as much as 11%." Conflicting secondary position: a 2025 cannabis-CPA guide describes the 9% as "in lieu of the regular 4% state sales tax," and a Q3 2026 market summary models a $100 purchase as $100 + $9 only, expressly noting "whether stores show it as a separate line at the register, and how general sales tax applies, were not verified." Finding: [VERIFY] — do not publish a single all-in patient tax rate. The only point safe to state as law is that 9% under §20-2A-80(a) is levied "in addition to all other taxes." Whether ADOR in practice also collects the 4% state general sales tax and local general sales taxes on the same retail medical sale, and how the 9% is shown at the till, was not confirmed on any ADOR page opened in this audit. This is the single most important tax follow-up: obtain an ADOR written determination or a first-dispensary receipt. No medical-cannabis sales-tax exemption was found. Act 2023-541 (SB 90 fiscal note, 13 July 2023) is noted as excluding medical cannabis from a producer value-added sales-tax exemption, with the note that "as no such products have been sold in the state to date, this act does not directly affect state or local funding." The prescription-drug exemption under general sales-tax law does not appear to have been extended to medical cannabis — [VERIFY against §40-23-4 exemptions].

2.3 Annual medical cannabis privilege tax — verified

§20-2A-80(b): from 1 Jan 2022, an annual privilege tax on every person doing business under Chapter 2A in Alabama, accruing 1 Jan each year (or on licensure/first doing business), levied on the taxpayer's net worth in Alabama, apportioned under §40-14A-23 in the same manner as income apportionment under Title 40, Chapter 18; amount computed at the same rate as §40-14A-22; annual return due no later than the corresponding federal income-tax return; initial return due no later than 2½ months after licensure/commencement; ADOR may grant extensions up to 6 months; ADOR prescribes forms (enrolled SB 46, Alison PDF; return-timing details [VERIFY against ADOR 2026 MPT instructions at filing]). ADOR's official privilege-tax page gives the rate table (official: ADOR Medical Cannabis Privilege Tax):

Federal taxable income apportioned to ALRate per $1,000 of AL net worth
Less than $1$0.25
$1 – <$200,000$1.00
$200,000 – <$500,000$1.25
$500,000 – <$2,500,000$1.50
$2,500,000+$1.75

Minimum $100; maximum $15,000; maximum for an electing Family Limited Liability Entity $500 (official: ADOR Medical Cannabis Privilege Tax). ADOR: "Businesses licensed by the Medical Cannabis Commission are liable for the Alabama Medical Cannabis Privilege tax for each taxable year during which the business is licensed – regardless of the level of business activity." Filing: electronically only, via My Alabama Taxes; initial return (MPT-IN) through the licence-application portal on approval/issuance; annual return (MPT) via My Alabama Taxes; payment voucher MPT-V (filing-channel details [VERIFY at filing]). Note on the November 2025 ADOR Revenue Abstract line spelled "Cannibis Privilege" showing FYTD (FY 2025-26) net $1,677.60 vs $161.09 in FY 2024-25: whether that line is the medical-cannabis privilege tax, and whether any 9% gross-proceeds retail tax collections are reported in a separate line, was not confirmed from the abstract extract alone [VERIFY]. Do not use $1,677.60 as "medical cannabis tax revenue" without checking the full abstract / ADOR medical-cannabis privilege-tax pages.

2.4 Local taxes on medical cannabis

No medical-cannabis-specific local tax was found in state law. Local exposure is (a) general city/county sales-and-use taxes if the Part 2.2 stacking question resolves that way (see [VERIFY]), and (b) ordinary local business-licence taxes/fees (e.g. Dothan requires a city business licence; Gadsden's ordinance recites that a dispensary "would be required to purchase a business license and pay sales tax to the City of Gadsden"). General combined sales-tax context (secondary, for scale only — not medical-specific rates): ADOR's general rate is 4% state (ADOR Sales/Use Tax Rates); combined state+local rates are commonly cited at ~9–10% in Birmingham, Montgomery, Mobile, Tuscaloosa, Huntsville, Auburn, Dothan and Decatur, with secondary sources conflicting on Mobile/Tuscaloosa by ~1 point — address-level ADOR lookup is required. No local medical-cannabis tax ordinance imposing an additional percentage was located in the required jurisdictions checked [UNAVAILABLE / not found], which is distinct from the general sales taxes above. Do not publish a city-by-city medical total until the stacking question is resolved.

2.5 Hemp and hemp-derived (consumable hemp) taxes — verified, with one superseded-version trap

Governing law: Act 2025-385, HB 445 (Whitt). Signing vs recording dates: see Part 1.2 (14 May 2025 signature reported; 27 May 2025 tracker "Enacted" recording [VERIFY on the Secretary of State enrolled act]); smokable-hemp ban eff. 1 July 2025; balance of the consumable-hemp framework eff. 1 Jan 2026. Codified as Ala. Code Title 28, Chapter 12 (§§28-12-1 et seq.). §28-12-5 — 10% excise tax (enrolled text; monthly mechanics and in-lieu proviso [VERIFY on enrolled text]): (a) "An excise tax at the rate of 10 percent is levied on the retail sales price of consumable hemp products." "is in addition to any other tax imposed by federal, state, or local law." (b) The tax "is intended to be passed on to and borne by the purchaser," is a debt from purchaser to retailer until paid, the retailer acts as trustee for the ABC Board, and "must be stated and charged separately on any documentation provided to the purchaser." (c) Monthly: tax for the preceding month "due and payable monthly to the board on the first day of each month," returns showing gross sales transmitted on or before the 20th day of each month on Board-prescribed forms. (d) Distribution — enrolled (final) version, confirmed on the Alison fiscal note (FN-ARGIKSQ-5): 90% to the State General Fund; 10% to the treasury of the municipality in which the products were sold within its corporate limits, or, where sold outside any municipality, to the treasury of the county in which sold, "for the purposes of enforcement." (e) In-lieu rule: the §28-12-5 taxes "are exclusive and shall be in lieu of all other and additional taxes and licenses of the state, county, or municipality imposed on the sale of consumable hemp products; provided, that nothing herein … shall be construed to exempt the retail sale of consumable hemp products from the levy of tax on general retail sales by the state, county, or municipality in the nature of, or in lieu of, a general sales tax." I.e. hemp retail bears BOTH the 10% excise AND general sales tax. (f) Illegal-product assessment: 10% of the retail value of an unlawful hemp product found at a retailer (plus confiscation) — [VERIFY on enrolled text].

Trap — do NOT use these superseded/confused figures: the engrossed (House-passed, pre-Senate-amendment) HB 445 distributed the tax 50% General Fund / 25% counties by population / 25% municipalities by population, and assessed illegal product at 7% of gross wholesale value — superseded by the enrolled text above. BhamWiki's summary ("Ten percent of the excise taxes … designated for deposit into a Consumable Hemp Product Compliance Fund … remainder to the General Fund") conflates two pots and is wrong on the excise split: under enrolled §28-12-4, the Compliance Fund receives filing fees, annual licence fees, and label-approval fees only (confirmed in substance by the Alison fiscal note: $50 filing + $1,000 retailer licence fees to the Compliance Fund; remaining Compliance Fund monies on 30 September → General Fund); "Any remaining funds on September 30 shall be distributed to the State General Fund." A JD Supra update describing a "10-cent excise tax" is a reporting error for 10% — disregard. Local consequence (League of Municipalities journal, Fall 2026, secondary): "if a municipality does not allow the sale of consumable hemp products, then it will not receive any revenue from the 10% excise tax," and "Nothing in the act prohibits a municipality from charging sales tax on consumable hemp products." Hemp licence fees (tax-adjacent, Part 7 cross-reference): $50 filing fee + $1,000 annual licence fee (confirmed for retailers, Alison fiscal note) + $25,000 surety bond per location [VERIFY bond figure against §§28-12-40 et seq. / ABC Rule 20-X-33]. No separate tax on raw hemp cultivation, hemp farming, or non-consumable hemp was located [UNAVAILABLE]. No hemp-specific income-tax provision was found; ordinary Alabama income/business taxes apply. State response to the new federal hemp definition / 11 Dec 2026 date: none located [UNAVAILABLE]; the only built-in mechanism found is §28-12-1(d) (federal law enacted after 1 July 2025 that conflicts with Chapter 12 supersedes the conflicting provision).

2.6 Illegal-drug (stamp) tax — separate regime, non-medical only

Title 40, Chapter 17A (Drug and Controlled Substances Excise Tax): a dealer may not possess/distribute/sell/transport/import/transfer/use marihuana or a controlled substance on which tax under §40-17A-8 is imposed unless the tax is paid as evidenced by a stamp/indicia (§40-17A-4 — [VERIFY on official Code]). Secondary summaries state the marihuana rate as $3.50 per gram or fraction thereof, with a 100% penalty for non-payment, and a "dealer" threshold of >42.5 grams of marihuana (Hyatt v. State Dept. of Revenue, Ala. Civ. App. 1992 — [VERIFY on current official §40-17A-8 text and the Hyatt opinion]). This tax is not a tax on lawful medical-cannabis or lawful hemp sales; it is an enforcement/assessment tax on illicit possession.

2.7 IRS §280E and Alabama decoupling

Pre-Schedule III position (through 27 Apr 2026): Alabama did NOT decouple. Mechanism confirmed on the official Admin Code site: §40-18-33 adopts federal taxable income as the starting point for Alabama corporate taxable income, under rolling IRC conformity (Ala. Admin. Code r. 810-3-1.1-.01, official: Chapter 810-3-1.1), so a federal 280E disallowance flowed into the Alabama computation. A Maryland legislative fiscal compilation tabulates the same conclusion ("AL — Yes [conforms to IRC §280E] — Ala. Code §40-18-33; Ala. Code §40-18-1.1; Ala. Admin. Code §810-3-1.1-.01"). A 2025 cannabis-CPA guide states the same conclusion: "Alabama has not decoupled from IRC §280E. Business expenses disallowed federally under 280E (beyond COGS) are likewise nondeductible on the Alabama corporate or income tax returns." (Secondary.) No Alabama decoupling statute, ADOR regulation, or 2026 ADOR guidance on Schedule III / 280E was located [UNAVAILABLE]; the only 2026 Alabama conformity material found concerned the federal One Big Beautiful Bill Act, not cannabis. Post-28 Apr 2026 analysis (apply the fixed federal baseline, do not re-research it): because Alabama's income-tax starting point is federal taxable income, the federal removal of state-licensed medical activity from §280E's reach should flow through to the Alabama computation automatically as a matter of arithmetic, unless Alabama enacts a specific add-back — but that flow-through, the treatment of the 2026 transition year, and any effect on the privilege-tax base (computed from federal taxable income apportioned to Alabama, §20-2A-80(b)) are all [VERIFY — no ADOR guidance found]. Do not state that ADOR has confirmed flow-through. Scope limits: (i) adult-use/non-medical activity remains Schedule I federally and therefore remains fully within §280E federally and, by conformity, in Alabama (relevant only to illicit activity, as Alabama has no adult-use programme); (ii) hemp meeting the federal/state hemp definition is not a Schedule I/II controlled substance, so §280E never applied to lawful hemp activity as such — but a business mixing medical-cannabis and hemp activity raises allocation questions on which no Alabama guidance was found [VERIFY]. Practical consequence (analysis, not ADOR guidance): Alabama's first dispensary opened 4 June 2026, i.e. after the 28 Apr 2026 Schedule III effective date, so operating Alabama medical licensees fall in the federal category the baseline describes as Schedule III / outside §280E, rather than the pre-2026 280E-disallowed category — subject to the [VERIFY] on Alabama flow-through and on DEA registration/Treasury guidance in the baseline.

PART 3 — LOCAL RULES

3.1 The opt-in requirement — Ala. Code §20-2A-51(c)

Verbatim (AMCC's own page reproduces the subsection, AMCC Cannabis Businesses / Locality Resolutions):

"(c)(1) Notwithstanding any other provision of this chapter to the contrary, the commission shall not permit a dispensary to operate a dispensing site in any municipality or unincorporated area of a county unless the municipality or county has authorized the operation of dispensing sites within its boundaries, as provided in subdivision (2). (2) Any county commission, by resolution, may authorize the operation of dispensing sites in the unincorporated areas of the county, and the governing body of any municipality, by ordinance, may authorize the operation of dispensing sites within the corporate limits of the municipality. The county commission or municipal governing body shall notify the commission not more than seven calendar days after adopting the resolution or ordinance. (3) This subsection does not prohibit a municipality from adopting zoning ordinances restricting the operation of dispensing sites within its corporate limits."

Mirrored in AMCC rule (rule subsection number [VERIFY — the original cites r. 538-X-8-.04(4) here and r. 538-X-8-.05(4) in Part 1.6 for the same prohibition; one number is wrong], official chapter: Chapter 538-X-8, published 31 Aug 2022, effective 15 Oct 2022): "A dispensing site may not operate in the unincorporated area of a county or in a municipality that has not adopted a resolution or ordinance authorizing the operation of dispensing sites under §20-2A-51, Code of Ala. 1975, (as amended)." The same prohibition for integrated facilities is in r. 538-X-9-.02 ([VERIFY]). County vs city interaction (reading of the text — stated as construction, not as a separate holding): a county resolution authorizes only the unincorporated areas of that county; it does not authorize a site inside an incorporated municipality within the county. A municipal ordinance authorizes only within that municipality's corporate limits; it does not authorize a site in the unincorporated county around it. A municipality that has not opted in is a closed jurisdiction for dispensing sites even if its county has opted in for unincorporated areas, and vice versa. The default is closed: silence = no dispensing site. There is no statewide "opt-out" list because opt-in is the default-off mechanism; absence from AMCC's received list means, on the evidence available, no authorizing instrument has been received by AMCC for that jurisdiction.

Does §20-2A-51(c) opt-in apply to cultivation, processing, transport, labs, or integrated-facility non-retail operations? No — on the face of §20-2A-51(c), the opt-in is for "a dispensary to operate a dispensing site" (and, via §§20-2A-64(f)/20-2A-67(f) and r. 538-X-9-.02, for integrated-facility dispensing sites — pinpoints [VERIFY]). The statute does not impose a §51 county/city opt-in on a standalone cultivator, processor, secure transporter, or testing laboratory as such. But in practice every facility type faces a local-approval hurdle at application: Ala. Admin. Code r. 538-X-3-.05 (application contents) requires, for each proposed facility, "Proof of local zoning and other approvals necessary to operate the business in the local jurisdiction where the business is located, including but not limited to the local jurisdiction's ordinance or resolution approving the operation of medical cannabis facilities there" (with "N/A with explanation" noted as a possible response in the scoring worksheets) — quotation from a mirror, [VERIFY on official Admin Code]. And several cities' ordinances are broader than §51 requires: e.g. Gadsden Ord. O-37-22 authorizes "medical cannabis dispensing sites, cultivators, processors, secure transporters, or integrated facilities licenses" within the city (city ordinance extract — [VERIFY]); Madison Ord. 2022-327 §1(b) covers "any facility, regardless of type, licensed by the [AMCC] within the City of Madison" (city ordinance extract — [VERIFY]). So a cultivator/processor sited in such a city still needs the ordinary local business licence and zoning compliance, and may in that city also be covered by an express facilities ordinance. Do not state that cultivation/processing needs no local approval at all — state the distinction: no §51(c) dispensing-site opt-in for non-retail facilities, but AMCC application proof-of-local-approval plus ordinary zoning/business-licensing still apply.

Consumable-hemp local approval (separate regime, Part 7 cross-reference): ABC Rule 20-X-33-.02(1)(a) (published 31 Oct 2025, effective 15 Dec 2025, operative 1 Jan 2026) requires every consumable-hemp licence applicant to give the ABC Board "An approval letter from the local governing body of the county or municipality in which the applicant's facility will be located." (official filing link not re-opened in this audit — [VERIFY]). Alabama League of Municipalities: "If a municipality has not approved the sale of consumable hemp products, then the ABC Board will not be able to issue a consumable hemp sales license to a retailer in that municipality" — and that municipality then receives no 10% excise share (see Part 2.5). The enrolled HB 445 licensure article (§§28-12-40 et seq.) should be cited for the statutory version of this requirement in Part 7 [VERIFY — enrolled-text OCR for the licensure article was not cleanly legible in this audit].

3.2 Local bans, moratoriums, caps, and zoning — medical and hemp/CBD/smoke/vape

Medical cannabis: no published statewide register of local medical-cannabis bans or moratoriums was located [UNAVAILABLE]. Because the system is opt-in, a jurisdiction's absence from AMCC's list functions as a ban on dispensing sites there, but it is not necessarily an express "ban ordinance." Do not describe a non-opted-in city as having "banned" dispensaries unless an express ban document is found. No express medical-cannabis ban ordinance was found in any required jurisdiction checked. No local cap on the number of dispensing sites (beyond the state caps of 3 sites per dispensary licence / 5 per integrated licence, each in a different county — §§20-2A-64(f), 20-2A-67(f) — pinpoints [VERIFY]) was found in a local ordinance opened in this audit [UNAVAILABLE — local caps, if any, would be in individual zoning codes not fully searched]. State buffer (not local): §20-2A-64(d)(1) — each dispensing site "must be located at least one thousand feet from any school, day care, or child care facility," measured per the Ch. 538-X-8 rule (straight-line, property-line to property-line, nearest point; K-12 active within last 6 months; licensed daycare/childcare active within last 6 months) — pinpoints [VERIFY]. Local zoning examples found: Decatur (extra church/residential buffers), Dothan (zoning districts), Florence (district table, draft status), Huntsville (proposed Article 77, not final at the time of the AMCC posting).

Hemp / CBD / smoke / vape shops: statewide smokable-hemp ban (not local) from 1 July 2025 — smokable hemp products (flower, pre-rolls, hemp cigarettes/cigars) are excluded from "consumable hemp product" and unlawful under Act 2025-385. Whether vapes/cartridges fall within the statutory "smokeable hemp product" definition is an open interpretive conflict (Part 1.5) — the §28-12-2 pinpoint is [VERIFY on enrolled text]; do not present vapes as settled-banned by statute text alone. Treat the March 2026 ordinance as superseding the earlier "signalled" position for Auburn, but [VERIFY the ordinance text itself] — the Observer report does not reproduce it, and whether Auburn's ordinance authorizes sales or merely regulates offences is not clear from the report alone. Warning on same-name confusion: several "Auburn" cannabis-ordinance search hits concern Auburn, California — those were discarded and are not cited here. Opelika (hemp, secondary-reported): 15 Sept 2026 council approval (second reading) of zoning amendments defining tobacco-vape stores, hemp stores, pharmacy-hemp stores and grocery stores with hemp sales, and specifying permitted districts; a hemp store = a business holding an ABC Consumable Hemp Products Specialty Retailer Licence; a qualifying grocery store must devote ≥75% of selling area and ≥14,000 sq ft to food sales — [VERIFY — Opelika ordinance / minutes]. Hoover (hemp, secondary-reported, including an AI-generated meeting summary): 10 May 2026 zoning amendment classifying consumable-hemp stores as a conditional use in certain commercial districts (with distance buffers from schools, parks and residences and grandfathering, per secondary report), and 26 May 2026 licensing ordinance creating three local licence categories (specialty, pharmacy, retail food store) with a $2,000 annual local fee (raised from a proposed $500), council approval and public notice required — [VERIFY against Hoover minutes/ordinance]. Do not state the Hoover fee, buffers, or categories as adopted law. Mobile (hemp, secondary-reported): March 2026 council resolution giving a 90-day transitional window for businesses selling before 1 Jan 2026 that submit a complete ABC application, keep proof on site, and follow city rules; reporting at the time said "No business in Mobile has yet received City Council approval," and location approval from Council plus a state ABC licence are both required. A later Mobile Chapter 36 hemp ordinance was debated in March 2026 — final text [VERIFY]. Gadsden (hemp): Oct 2026 council agenda item (unfinished business) for a hemp ordinance; agenda gave title only, no fees/districts/hours; Rainbow City Ord. 626 (28 Sept 2026, unanimous) cited as a comparator requiring council approval of every hemp store, 21+, no on-site use/online/delivery/drive-through/vending — Gadsden final outcome [VERIFY] and Rainbow City terms [VERIFY — Rainbow City ordinance text]. Huntsville (hemp): notice of a proposed zoning amendment (hearing 26 Mar 2026) to retitle Zoning Ordinance Article 75 as "Alcoholic Beverage and Consumable Hemp Product Establishment Regulations" and add retail-food-store hemp retail as a special exception — proposed, not shown adopted. General smoke/vape-shop note: no Alabama local ordinance specifically banning CBD or smoke/vape shops as a category was located; the operative restrictions are (a) the state smokable-hemp ban, (b) the ABC consumable-hemp licensing/zoning regime for lawful hemp retail, and (c) ordinary local zoning/business licensing. Pre-2025 CBD retail (non-consumable-hemp, e.g. non-ingestible) falls outside Title 28, Chapter 12's "consumable" definition — [VERIFY in Part 7 whether any locality has separately regulated non-consumable CBD retail].

3.4 Local licence/permit fees and buffer rules where they exist

State buffer (applies everywhere): 1,000 feet from any school, day care, or child care facility — §20-2A-64(d)(1); measurement per the Ch. 538-X-8 rule (straight-line, property-line to property-line, nearest point; K-12 active within last 6 months; licensed daycare/childcare active within last 6 months). Statute and rule pinpoints [VERIFY on official Code / Admin Code] (see also the rule-number conflict in Parts 1.6/3.1). Decatur — extra local buffers (in the ordinance itself, extract not re-opened in this audit — [VERIFY on Legistar]): Ord. 22-4544A provides: (4) no dispensing site "closer than one thousand feet from the boundaries of any church, school, day care, or child care facility"; (5) no site "closer than five hundred feet from the boundaries of any residential zoning district except for the R-4 (Multi-Family) residential zoning district"; (6) no site "within the boundaries of any R-4 (Multi-Family) residential zoning district." Note Decatur adds churches and residential districts beyond the state school/daycare buffer. Dothan — business licence + zoning districts (official city fact sheet, not re-opened in this audit): "A business license is required to operate a dispensary in the City of Dothan"; "For zoning purposes, dispensaries are classified as 'retail, indoor sales only' and [are] permitted in the all business (B) districts, the O-I & O-2 office (O) districts and light industrial (L-I) district." No Dothan fee amount is stated on the fact sheet [UNAVAILABLE]. Florence — district table (DRAFT status — do not present as adopted): document headed "Medical Cannabis Facilities Regulations for Zoning and Land Use," marked as a Planning Commission public-hearing draft dated 28 Feb 2023. Final adoption [VERIFY] — the draft alone does not prove the adopted code.
