State that as a negative finding, not as proof no fee exists.

3.5 Business concentration — official sources only, no ranking

AMCC's current issued-licence geography (official, opened 2026-10-28): "Based on the dispensary licenses issued to date, dispensing sites will be located in the municipalities listed below: Athens (Limestone County); Attalla (Etowah County); Bessemer (Jefferson County); Birmingham (Jefferson County); Daphne (Baldwin County); Mobile (Mobile County); Montgomery (Montgomery County); Oxford (Calhoun County); Talladega (Talladega County)." Plus AMCC's notes: "Alabama's first medical cannabis dispensary opened on June 4, 2026. The Commission expects other dispensaries to open during summer 2026."; "One Dispensary license awarded … on December 11, 2025, has been stayed. An additional three (3) retail dispensing sites may be added with the issuance of an additional Dispensary license. … The Commission may issue up to five (5) Integrated Facility licenses and each licensee may operate up to five (5) dispensing sites. Therefore, up to 25 additional retail dispensing sites may be added with the issuance of Integrated Facility licenses." Source: AMCC Patients page. What this does and does not show: it shows 9 issued-licence municipalities, with 2 in Jefferson County (Bessemer + Birmingham) and one each in 7 other counties. Do not rank or label any "cluster" — with 9 sites, any clustering claim would be the researcher's own inference, which the brief forbids. Discrepancy to flag: a December 2025 secondary list of the 12 awarded dispensary locations names Athens, Cullman, Owens Cross Roads, Attalla, Birmingham (×2), Talladega, Oxford, Demopolis, Montgomery, Daphne, Mobile. Cullman, Owens Cross Roads and Demopolis are on that awards list but not on AMCC's current issued-licence list (which has Bessemer instead of a second Birmingham, and omits Cullman/Owens Cross Roads/Demopolis). Reconciliation (analysis, labelled as such): AMCC's page is "licenses issued to date" (with one licence stayed), while the 12-location list reflects awards including the stayed licence's 3 sites — that attribution was not confirmed on an AMCC awards document opened in this audit [VERIFY — AMCC award/licence documents]. Use AMCC's 9-municipality issued list as the current operating footprint; describe the 12-location list only as the awards picture, with the stay noted. No AMCC "health service area" map or regional allocation table was located [UNAVAILABLE]. No statute or rule found in this audit allocates dispensing sites by health service area, region, or population quota — the geographic spread is an outcome of licence awards and local opt-ins, not a published regional plan. Do not invent regions. Applicant PDFs are not a location source for operating sites: AMCC applicant/licensee summaries list proposed facilities for applicants (including denied applicants) in many cities (e.g. Tuscaloosa, Dothan, Decatur, Gadsden, Opelika, Huntsville in denied applications). Those proposed sites must not be presented as current or future operating sites. Notable absences on the issued list (stated factually, not as analysis): Huntsville, Tuscaloosa, Dothan, Decatur, Florence, Gadsden, Auburn, Hoover, Madison city and Prattville — all of which (except Hoover, Auburn, Prattville) appear on AMCC's opt-in list — have no issued-licence dispensing site on AMCC's current page (confirmed by direct comparison of the two AMCC pages opened 2026-10-28). That is consistent with opt-in being necessary but not sufficient for a site: a site also requires an issued licence naming that municipality.

End of Parts 0–3 (audited and corrected, 28 October 2026). Parts 4–12 are audited separately and are not included in this file.

PART 4 — LICENCE TYPES

4.1 Governing law and official licence-type page

Statute: Compassion Act, Ala. Code §§20-2A-1 et seq., Article 4 (§§20-2A-50 to 20-2A-68) [VERIFY — official Code text]. Licence-quantity and dispensing-site rules are in §20-2A-51; individual licence sections are §§20-2A-62 (cultivator), 20-2A-63 (processor), 20-2A-64 (dispensary), 20-2A-65 (secure transporter), 20-2A-66 (state testing laboratory), 20-2A-67 (integrated facility); §20-2A-68 makes a licence a revocable privilege, not a property right. Rules: Ala. Admin. Code Title 538-X, esp. Ch. 538-X-3 (applications/licensing generally), Ch. 538-X-5 (cultivators), Ch. 538-X-6 (processors), Ch. 538-X-7 (secure transporters), Ch. 538-X-10 (testing). Ch. 538-X-3 was republished/revised 2/12/24 and again with history “Published April 30, 2026; effective June 14, 2026” for the 2026 amendments — re-check the June 2026 text before quoting any rule verbatim [VERIFY], because the 2022/2024 PDFs and the 2026 filings differ. Official licence-type summary page (AMCC, short-form only — full detail is in the statute/rules, not on this page): AMCC Licence Types. It states: testing — “No license limits”; secure transporter — “No license limits”; dispensary — “No more than 4 Licenses to be awarded. May operate up to 3 dispensing sites”; processor — “No more than 4 Licenses to be awarded”; cultivator — “No more than 12 licenses to be awarded”; integrated facility — “No more than 5 licenses to be awarded. Each licensee may operate up to 5 dispensing sites.” AMCC's award notice confirms the same caps in prose: “the Commission, per the statute, could award up to twelve (12) cultivator licenses, four (4) processor licenses, four (4) dispensary licenses, five (5) integrated facility licenses and an unspecified number of secure transport and state testing laboratory licenses.” Source: AMCC award notice. One-applicant/one-category rule: Ala. Admin. Code r. 538-X-3-.03: “No person or entity may apply for more than one category of license at a time; an applicant who withdraws an application may reapply, so long as the application is timely.” [VERIFY exact rule text against the current Ch. 538-X-3 filing]. No separate wholesale, delivery, microbusiness or retail-only licence type exists in the statute. Cultivators/processors/integrated facilities supply dispensaries; transport is only via a secure transporter (or, for an integrated facility, its own transport between its facilities). Delivery to patients is not a licence category — [VERIFY against §§20-2A-62–67 full text].

Total possible dispensing sites if every capped licence issued: 4 dispensaries × 3 = 12, plus 5 integrated × 5 = 25, = 37 maximum under the current caps. AMCC's patient FAQ uses exactly this arithmetic: “An additional three (3) retail dispensing sites may be added with the issuance of an additional Dispensary license” (Yellowhammer) and “up to 25 additional retail dispensing sites may be added with the issuance of Integrated Facility licenses.” Source: AMCC Patients.

Other fee rules: awardees have 14 days from notice of award to pay the licence fee (AMCC award notices repeat this in every round; r. 538-X-3-.16). Dispensary licences awarded Dec. 11, 2025: fee within 14 days, then licences issue 28 days from the meeting (i.e. Jan. 8, 2026) unless stayed by the Commission or a court (Dec. 11, 2025 minutes). Licences expire one year from issuance. Application-fee history note: a secondary summary (Butler Snow) says application fees were “set at a minimum of $10,000” in the original Act discussion. That is not the fee AMCC actually charged ($2,500) and must not be quoted as the current application fee.

4.4 Requirements — Alabama ownership/residency, experience, background, finance

  • 15-year Alabama residency — ALL applicants: “Records indicating that a majority of ownership in the Applicant is attributable to an individual or individuals with proof of residence in this state for a continuous period of no less than 15 years preceding the application date” — §20-2A-55(a)(10), implemented in r. 538-X-3-.05; failure to provide those records = ineligibility (r. 538-X-3-.14(5) in the 2/12/24 chapter). Sources: AMCC Chapter 538-X-3 (PDF); Chapter 538-X-3 (official). Note: this is a majority-ownership test, not a requirement that every owner be a 15-year resident, and not a requirement that the entity itself be 15 years old. Secondary summaries that shorten it to “majority ownership by 15+ year residents” for cultivators/integrated only are incomplete — the rule text applies it to all applicants.
  • 15-year horticulture/agronomic experience — cultivator and integrated-facility applicants only: majority ownership attributable to individuals/entities “with cumulative business experience in the field of commercial horticulture or agronomic production for a period of at least 15 years” — §20-2A-55(a)(11); same rule chapter.
  • No economic interest in any other licence/applicant: an applicant may not hold an economic interest in any other applicant/licensee under the Act (pass/fail exhibit item; r. 538-X-3). [VERIFY exact current subsection number — check the 2026 Ch. 3 filing].
  • Background checks: every owner, shareholder, director, board member and individual with an economic interest, plus officers/employees/contractors and others with access to cannabis/facilities, must submit to state (ALEA, SBI Form 46) and national (FBI) checks at the applicant's expense, with verified written consent. Ineligibility: a felony, or a controlled-substance-related misdemeanour, pleaded guilty to / convicted of / released from incarceration within the past 10 years (excluding convictions overturned on appeal or charges expunged under Title 15, Ch. 27). Cultivator employees specifically: no controlled-substance felony/misdemeanour conviction within 10 years — §20-2A-62(d)(3). [VERIFY pinpoint subsections and SBI Form 46 detail against official text].
  • Integrated-facility-only finance tests (§20-2A-67(d)–(e)): (1) letter of commitment/acknowledgement of ability to secure a $2,000,000 performance bond from a Commission-approved surety; (2) proof of ≥$250,000 in liquid assets; (3) proof of financial ability to maintain operations for ≥2 years after application. At issuance the Commission must ensure the $2,000,000 bond is actually secured. Source: LawServer §20-2A-67 — mirror.
  • Cultivator-only operational tests (§20-2A-62(c)–(d)): ability to secure/maintain cultivation facilities; ability to obtain/use the §20-2A-60 inventory/tracking system; ability to commence cultivation within 60 days of application-approval notification; ability to destroy unused/waste cannabis per Commission rules; financial stability to provide proper testing of individual lots/batches; facilities protected by monitored alarm, enclosed and locked at all times; entry/exit monitored by video surveillance and keypad/card entry. [VERIFY — official §20-2A-62 text].
  • Local authorisation: a dispensing site may not operate in a municipality or unincorporated county area that has not adopted an ordinance (municipality) / resolution (county commission) authorising dispensing sites — §20-2A-51(c); §20-2A-67(f) last sentence. Facility business-presence approval (local business licence + resolution/ordinance) is also an application exhibit. This is Part 3's subject; it is a licence-issuance condition, not just a zoning matter.
  • Public notice/comment: 30-day public notice-and-comment period on applications, with hearings if necessary (secondary summary of §§20-2A-55–56; [VERIFY against current §§20-2A-55/56 text]).
  • Cultivator regulator shift — CONFIRMED: Act 2024-342 (HB 342, 2024) deleted the provisions of the original Act envisioning Department (ADAI) participation in cultivator and integrated-facility licensure decisions; AMCC now licenses cultivators under §20-2A-62. Source: Jemmstone opinion (2026), footnote comparing Act 2021-450 with Act 2024-342.
  • Licence as privilege: §20-2A-68; r. 538-X-3-.04(2): “deemed to be a revocable privilege… no vested rights… nondelegable and nontransferable except with the express permission of the Commission” (transfer fees in Part 4.3 above) [VERIFY — official text].

4.5 Social equity / minority-ownership / small-business provisions

Statutory minority share — CONFIRMED, and it is two different fractions, not a single “1/4”: §20-2A-51(b), as restated in r. 538-X-3 and in the Dec. 1, 2023 minutes: “at least one-fourth of all licenses” in the categories considered at that meeting (cultivator, processor, dispensary, secure transporter, testing) must be awarded to minority applicants, and for integrated facilities the floor is one-fifth. Rule text (opened): “the Commission shall ensure that at least one fifth of all integrated facility licenses in Alabama, and at least one fourth of licenses in all other categories, are awarded to business entities at least 51% of which are owned by members of a minority group, or, in the case of corporations, at least 51% of the shares… are owned by members of a minority group, and are managed and controlled by members of a minority group in its daily operations.” “Minority group” = individuals of African American, Native American, Asian, or Hispanic descent — §20-2A-51(b). If deaths/resignations/etc. push a category below the floor, the Commission must at the next award opportunity prioritise a qualified 51%-minority-owned applicant — same rule text. Practical arithmetic: 1/5 of 5 integrated licences = at least 1 integrated licence; 1/4 of 12 cultivators = 3; 1/4 of 4 processors = 1; 1/4 of 4 dispensaries = 1. Sources: AMCC Chapter 538-X-3 (2022 PDF); Dec. 1, 2023 minutes (PDF). Whether the floor was actually met in each awarded slate: [VERIFY]. AMCC's Jan. 2, 2026 applicant/licensee summary PDFs include a “Minority (§20-2A-51(b)): Yes/No” field per applicant (e.g. Certus Laboratories: “No”), so compliance is auditable applicant-by-applicant, but no AMCC summary total (“X of Y licences are minority-owned”) was located in this audit. Do not assert the floor was met overall. No other social-equity programme found: no fee waiver, no reduced fee, no priority scoring, no expungement-linked licensing, and no small-business/micro-licence category was located in the statute, rules or fee schedule in this audit. AMCC has no diversity rule beyond §20-2A-51(b) that could be verified. State this as [UNAVAILABLE — no provision located; absence is not proof it does not exist in a rule chapter not opened (esp. Ch. 538-X-4)]. No residency-based preference beyond the 15-year majority rule in Part 4.4, and no Alabama-ownership percentage beyond “majority” was located.

4.6 Licence rounds in full

Round 0 — application window (2022)

Application process began September 1, 2022. AMCC accepted requests for applications until October 14, 2022; application forms were sent to requestors October 24, 2022; applications were received October 24 – December 30, 2022 (AMCC's own “Begins Application Process” notice — AMCC Sept 2022 notice). Applicant count: 94. AMCC's official “Receives 94 Applications” notice states the Commission received ninety-four (94) applications, by type: 38 integrated + 18 dispensary + 12 cultivator + 12 processor + 11 secure transporter + 3 testing = 94. Source: AMCC Receives 94 Applications. The University of South Alabama (USA) coordinated review using 66 evaluators across 8 scoring categories (financial ability; business/management; operations; facility suitability/infrastructure; security; personnel; quality control/testing; marketing/advertising).

Round 1 — June 12, 2023 awards, stayed June 16, 2023 (VOIDED / abandoned)

June 12, 2023: AMCC voted to award licences in every category. June 12, 2023 minutes record: Integrated: Flowerwood Medical Cannabis, LLC; Southeast Cannabis Company, LLC; Sustainable Alabama, LLC; TheraTrue Alabama, LLC; Verano Alabama, LLC. Secure transport: Alabama Secure Transport, LLC; International Communication, LLC; Tyler Van Lines, LLC. Testing: Certus Laboratories. (Cultivator/processor/dispensary names in the June minutes were only partly captured in the search extract; the Cannabis Law Report summary of the same meeting lists 21 companies total: integrated as above; cultivators Blackberry Farms, Gulf Shore Remedies, Pure by Sirmon Farms, Twisted Herb Cultivation; processors 1819 Labs, Enchanted Green, Jasper Development Group, Organic Harvest Lab; dispensaries CCS of Alabama, RJK Holdings AL, Statewide Property Holdings AL, Yellowhammer Medical Dispensaries. Treat the June cultivator/processor/dispensary sub-lists as secondary-sourced [VERIFY against the full June 12 minutes PDF].) Sources: June 12, 2023 minutes (PDF). Why voided: “due to the discovery of potential inconsistencies in the tabulation of scoring data, the Commission voted on June 16, 2023, to stay all proceedings.” USA then had two senior internal accountants (not involved in the original tabulations) independently recalculate all scores, and KPMG validated the recalculation; KPMG and both internal recalculations identified the same variances (secondary summary of AMCC's explanation, consistent with AMCC's notice — do not present KPMG validation as a minute quote). AMCC's own words: “individual sections were scored correctly… but… there were math errors when calculating cumulative scores for some applicants.” At the same June 12 meeting AMCC announced it “will open a second offering of licenses for cultivators, secure transporters, and state testing laboratories” — see Part 4.7. The Commission had planned to issue licences July 10, 2023; that issuance never happened for any category in Round 1.

August 10, 2023: AMCC “nominated applicants and voted to award” (AMCC award notice): Integrated (5): Insa Alabama, LLC; Flowerwood Medical Cannabis, LLC; Southeast Cannabis Company, LLC; Sustainable Alabama, LLC; TheraTrue Alabama, LLC. (Verano — a Round 1 winner and, per secondary reporting, still the highest scorer after retabulation — was left out. That scorer claim is secondary only.) Cultivator (7): Gulf Shore Remedies, LLC; Pure by Sirmon Farms, LLC; Blackberry Farms, LLC; Twisted Herb Cultivation, LLC; I AM FARMS; Greenway Botanicals, LLC; CRC of Alabama, LLC. Processor (4): Enchanted Green, LLC; 1819 Labs, LLC; Organic Harvest Lab, LLC; Jasper Development Group Inc. Dispensary (4): Yellowhammer Medical Dispensaries, LLC; CCS of Alabama, LLC; RJK Holdings AL, LLC; Statewide Property Holdings AL, LLC. Secure transport (3): Tyler Van Lines, LLC; International Communication, LLC; XLCR, Inc. Testing (1): Certus Laboratories. Source: AMCC Aug 2023 award notice — [VERIFY the Aug 2023 notice URL slug on amcc.alabama.gov before republication; the Dec 2023 notice is at amcc.alabama.gov/2654/…]. Why rescinded: litigation by unsuccessful applicants, including (a) Verano's suit alleging AMCC could not “void” awarded licences without following the Legislature's and its own rules, and (b) Open Meetings Act challenges to the award process. A Montgomery Circuit Court TRO barred AMCC from acting on the August awards. AMCC then adopted an “emergency” rule (Oct. 12, 2023, r. 538-X-3-.20(ER)) to restart review, and on October 26, 2023 voted to rescind the August 10 awards and restart the process. Appellate vindication of the rescission power (2024–2025): the Court of Civil Appeals later held AMCC did have “limited inherent power to rescind a nonfinal administrative order to avoid a procedural legal error” and “properly exercised that limited power when it rescinded the August 10, 2023, license awards,” affirming summary judgment for AMCC on the rescission claims of Southeast Cannabis, Yellowhammer and TheraTrue. See case table in Part 4.9.

The stay / injunction phase (2024)

January 3, 2024: the Montgomery County Circuit Court entered a temporary restraining order in the master case (CV-23-231) purporting to enjoin AMCC from taking any action in furtherance of the December 12, 2023 integrated-facility awards, including issuance. Source: Jemmstone opinion (2026) (Judge Anderson attribution for this TRO remains secondary — the opinion extract does not name Anderson). A further TRO in 2024 kept TROs previously entered as to dispensary and integrated facility licenses in place, pending further order. AMCC's own stay: April 11, 2024 AMCC stay on issuance, clarified July 11, 2024 — under its terms, December 1, 2023 dispensary licences “would not issue until such time that a final order had been entered following contested case hearings in the dispensary license category” [VERIFY against AMCC stay notices]. That stay self-expired only on entry of the Dec. 11, 2025 dispensary final order (Dec. 11, 2025 minutes). What was NOT stayed: cultivator, processor, secure-transporter and testing licences. AMCC's 2024 Annual Report states: “Since December 2023, the AMCC has issued nine cultivator licenses, four processor licenses, four secure transporter licenses and one state testing laboratory license… several cultivator licensees are growing and harvesting cannabis in their facilities.” Source: AMCC Annual Report 2024 (PDF), corroborated by AMCC Annual Report 2025 (PDF) (“issued a total of 18 licenses to cultivators (9), secure transporters (4), processors (4), and a state testing laboratory (1)”). August 8, 2024 — additional cultivators via hearings: AMCC awarded additional cultivator licences to Pure by Sirmon Farms, LLC and Blackberry Farms, LLC “following the completion of investigative hearings,” consistent with ALJ recommended orders; it also denied two other cultivator applicants and one secure-transporter applicant on ALJ recommendations. This is how the cultivator count reached 9 (7 Dec. 2023 + 2 Aug. 2024). Source: AMCC Aug 2024 additional cultivator notice. 2025 — appellate clearing, testing-lab reopening, dispensary hearings

March 2025 (Court of Civil Appeals): TROs/injunctions stalling the programme were vacated or ordered vacated for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction in the Alabama Always line of cases (see Part 4.9, CL-2024-0588/0616, released Mar. 7, 2025), and the Southeast rescission appeals were dismissed in part / affirmed in part (CL-2024-0300/0312). Source: Jemmstone opinion (2026). The Court of Civil Appeals stayed that order pending review. That order targeted the integrated category and the emergency-rule process; it did not void the already-issued non-integrated licences, and AMCC proceeded with dispensary hearings. Testing laboratory reopening (2025): AMCC opened a one-month window in February 2025 for requests for state-testing-laboratory applications after Certus Laboratories chose not to renew (see Part 4.8). Of 5 requests, only Green Health Laboratories (Foley) completed an application; 30-day public comment closed June 15, 2025 with no comments; AMCC voted to award Green Health a testing licence in June 2025 (presentation June 12, 2025; vote reported June 17, 2025 — secondary, MMJDaily/Alabama Reflector, not an AMCC minute opened). Green Health is the only testing lab until AMCC reopens applications; there is no cap on testing licences. Consolidated dispensary hearings were held September 8–9, 2025; ALJ Recommended Order issued November 13, 2025; complete record provided to Commissioners November 25, 2025 (Dec. 11, 2025 minutes). Announced June 12, 2023 for cultivators, secure transporters and state testing laboratories only — never for processors, dispensaries or integrated facilities (which were already at/near their caps in the first offering). Cultivator: no separate new-application window was located; the 2 additional cultivator licences came from investigative hearings on the original applicants (Aug. 2024), not a new offering. Secure transporter: no second offering window located; the count stayed at 4. [UNAVAILABLE — no AMCC notice of a secure-transporter second offering was found; do not assert one opened]. That confirms consideration was on the agenda; it does not confirm a vote to reopen. [VERIFY the June/July 2026 minutes for the vote/outcome before asserting a June 2026 reopening].

4.10 Hemp-derived product licences (brief; full treatment is Part 7)

These are not AMCC licences. Do not merge them into the AMCC counts above. ADAI industrial hemp (grower / processor-handler / university): see Part 5.6. Fees (ADAI official pre-application sheet, 2022 upload — [VERIFY against a current 2025/2026 ADAI sheet before Part 7 use]): application $150 + 4.5% convenience fee (one application per individual/entity per type); site fee $1,000 per site + 4.5% (everywhere hemp is, even briefly, including propagation sheds, greenhouses, barns, drying/storage structures). Minimums: outdoor ≥1 acre / ≥1,000 plants per planting; indoor ≥1,500 sq ft / ≥500 plants, unless ADAI prior approval. Applicants must be Alabama residents or live within 50 miles of the AL grow site; sites ≥1,000 ft from schools/recreational areas where children congregate, ≥300 ft from residential structures unless approved, not in/adjacent to a residential structure. Sources: ADAI pre-application information (PDF). [CONFLICT on processor application fee: a commercial compliance summary lists a hemp processor application fee of $200 + $1,000/location, vs. ADAI's $150 sheet covering grower/handler/processor/university. Adopt ADAI's $150 sheet; list $200 as unverified secondary.] ABC Board consumable-hemp retailer licences (HB 445, Act 2025; Title 28, Ch. 12; Ala. Admin. Code Ch. 20-X-33, published Oct. 31, 2025, effective Dec. 15, 2025, operative Jan. 1, 2026): from January 1, 2026 consumable hemp products may only be sold by ABC-licensed retailers, in three types only: (1) Consumable Hemp Products Retail Food Store Licence; (2) Consumable Hemp Products Pharmacy Licence; (3) Consumable Hemp Products Specialty Retailer Licence. Application requires a local-governing-body approval letter, plus (for ≥10% owners, except public corporations) name/DOB/place of birth/address/phone/driver's licence/SSN — the categories of information required, not any individual's data, which is not reproduced here. ABC's page gives a contact mailbox but no public licensee list was located on that page. Source: ABC Board hemp page; Ch. 20-X-33 filing (official). [VERIFY fees/bond from primary text before Part 7:] secondary summaries state retailer $1,000/year + $50 application, manufacturer/wholesaler $5,000/year, $25,000 surety bond, 21+, local approval, background checks. Those figures were not confirmed on an opened ABC or Title 28 page in this audit and must be flagged as secondary in Part 7. Manufacturer/distributor under HB 445: HB 445's framework is described in secondary sources as licensing manufacturers and distributors/wholesalers through the ABC Board as well, but the ABC page opened lists only the three retailer types, and Ch. 20-X-33 as filed is titled “Licensure of Consumable Hemp Products” with retailer types in §20-X-33-.01. Whether a distinct ABC manufacturer/distributor licence type exists, and its fee, is [VERIFY against Title 28, Ch. 12 full text] — do not list an ABC manufacturer licence as confirmed in Part 7 until checked. 4.11 Estimated startup costs — NON-OFFICIAL ESTIMATES ONLY

AMCC publishes no startup-cost estimate. The figures below are commercial/consulting estimates, not AMCC, ADAI or legislative figures, and must be labelled as such:

  • Dispensary (single site, non-official, alabamacannabis.org): $400,000–$1,000,000+ all-in, broken down in that source as: application $2,500; annual licence $40,000 (dispensary) / $50,000 (integrated); “proof of fund — at least $250,000 in liquid assets” (that $250,000 is actually the integrated-facility statutory test, misapplied to dispensaries in that source — flag it); lease $50,000–$120,000/year; security/software/hardware ~$50,000/year; salaries ~$250,000/year; marketing ~$50,000; inventory “average $1,500 per pound” (a wholesale-price assumption, not an AMCC figure). Source (non-official): alabamacannabis.org — Business.
  • General medical-cannabis business (non-official, CannDelta): $250,000 to $1,000,000+ “from the start of the project, to the day operations begin,” plus $2,500 application fee and $30,000–$40,000 annual licence fees (that range omits the $50,000 integrated fee — flag it as incomplete). Source (non-official): CannDelta — Alabama.
  • Green Rush Consulting (non-official): application $2,500; “additional licensing and development costs $35,000–$75,000”; “capital investments… $400,000 to over $1,000,000.” Its fee range “$10,000–$50,000” is stale/wrong against the current schedule ($30,000–$50,000 annual; $2,500 application) — do not quote it. Source (non-official): Green Rush Consulting.

Statutory/official cost floors that ARE citable (not estimates): integrated facility $2,000,000 bond + $250,000 liquid assets + 2-year operating ability (§20-2A-67(d)); application $2,500 + annual fee $30,000–$50,000 + $80 background check + pre-issuance inspection/build-out (cost not set by AMCC). Any “total startup cost” beyond those floors is an estimate and must be labelled so.

4.12 Adult-use licence types — PROPOSED ONLY (none exists)

There is no adult-use licence type in Alabama law. No adult-use cultivator, processor, dispensary or any other adult-use licence has been enacted, and AMCC has no authority to issue one. Proposed decriminalisation (not adult-use licensing): SB 285 (2026), Sen. Bobby Singleton — first read 10 February 2026 and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee (Alison first-readings record: “Relating to crimes and offenses; to amend Sections 13A-12-213 and 13A-12-214, Code of Alabama 1975, to provide further for the crimes of unlawful possession of marijuana in the first and second degrees; to revise the criminal penalties; and to provide for expungement of a charge, finding, or conviction, under certain conditions” — Alison Senate First Readings; introduced text: SB 285 introduced (PDF)). Secondary (MPP) summary of the proposal: decriminalise possession of up to 1 oz for a first offence (Class C misdemeanour, no jail, fine ≤$250; second offence within 5 years Class C misdemeanour ≤$500; third/subsequent Class D felony, fine $750, no jail), plus an expungement-petition mechanism after 5 years without further conviction. Status: NOT ENACTED — it creates no licence type and must not be listed as one. The detailed penalty ladder and any hearing record are secondary only — [VERIFY final disposition/hearing record on Alison]. Source (secondary summary): MPP Alabama. No 2026 bill expanding the medical programme was verified (MPP: “There were no bills introduced in the 2026 session that would have expanded the nation's most restrictive medical cannabis program”; AMCC Feb. 12, 2026 minutes: “no pending legislation… that directly concerns medical cannabis or the AMCC”). [VERIFY on the Legislature's official site for the final Part 1 pending-legislation table beyond February 2026]. HB 72 (2026) (mandatory-reporter/cannabis-smell bill discussed in secondary coverage) did not become law (secondary: passed House, never passed Senate, died at end of 2026 session — [VERIFY on Alison]) and is not a licence bill — included here only to prevent it being mis-cited as enacted law.

5.10 USDA hemp records for Alabama

USDA AMS, “List of USDA-approved Hemp Plans,” updated February 17, 2026, lists “Alabama — AL Approved Plan (pdf)”. Alabama therefore operates under its own USDA-approved state plan via ADAI, not under a USDA direct producer licence. USDA direct licences apply only to states/territories listed as “USDA Hemp Producer License” (Alabama is not one). Source: USDA AMS — State and Tribal Plan Review. Licensee data: USDA's plan-review page publishes plan documents, not Alabama licensee names/counts. Alabama licensee data sits with ADAI (Part 5.6) and with USDA Farm Service Agency (FSA) acreage/site reports (growers must register sites with their local FSA office and report acreage — secondary ADAI-process summary [VERIFY]). No public USDA Alabama licensee CSV was located. [UNAVAILABLE — do not claim USDA publishes an AL grower list]. Relevance note for Part 7: because Alabama has an approved plan, the federal-baseline USDA lab-testing delay (to Dec. 31, 2026) operates through ADAI's plan implementation — Part 7 must confirm ADAI's lab/testing rule, not USDA's direct-licence rule, for Alabama growers.

5.11 Local (county/city) permit / business-licence records

No statewide local-permit database was located. There is no AMCC, ADAI or ABC page aggregating city/county opt-in ordinances, local business licences or local cannabis permit lists. What exists locally (examples only, not an inventory): city zoning/ordinance texts that reproduce AMCC licence definitions (e.g. Huntsville proposed medical-cannabis facility regulations, filed as an AMCC exhibit — Huntsville Proposed Facility Regulations (PDF) — proposed, not proof of an adopted ordinance; Florence Code of Ordinances Ch. 10, Health — via Municode Library [VERIFY Florence text]). AMCC does publish a list of jurisdictions whose opt-in resolutions/ordinances it has received (jurisdiction names only, not full texts): AMCC Cannabis Businesses — Resolutions/Ordinances Received (including Athens, Attalla, Bessemer, Birmingham, Daphne, Mobile, Montgomery, Oxford, Talladega, and Owens Cross Roads, among others — all Alabama jurisdictions; same-name places elsewhere are not in this list). Municode Library is the practical route for adopted city codes; individual city clerks / county commissions hold the actual opt-in ordinances and business-licence records, generally as PDFs or in-person records, with no uniform search or download. For Part 3, the local-check list must therefore be built city-by-city from Municode + clerk sites, not from a single source — and the absence of a central list must be stated as [UNAVAILABLE], not filled by inference from dispensary-site municipalities. Note: a municipality appearing in AMCC's 9-site list (e.g. Athens, Talladega) necessarily authorised dispensing sites, but that does not prove the full text/date of its ordinance — obtain each ordinance separately.

PART 6 — MARKET DATA

Headline for Part 6: Alabama had no legal medical cannabis sales at all before June 2026. Sales began in June 2026 at one store, with two more stores by 14 September 2026. There is no official full-year, quarterly or state-dashboard sales total, no official price list, and no official post-June 2026 patient total located. All later totals are secondary or [UNAVAILABLE].

6.1 Medical sales — if any

No sales before June 2026; first sale June 2026. Alabama's first medical cannabis dispensary opened 4 June 2026 — Callie's Apothecary, 5232 Atlanta Highway, Montgomery, AL 36109 (official: AMCC Patients). Next openings on the same official page: 28 August 2026 — Callie's Apothecary, 309 Battle Street W, Talladega, AL 35160; 14 September 2026 — Bama Bloom, 809 U.S. Highway 72 W, Suites A&B, Athens, AL 35611. Secondary reporting of the AMCC's own first-week briefing gives the soft-opening detail: soft opening 3 June 2026, formal opening 4 June 2026 (secondary, reporting AMCC General Counsel Justin Aday: Marijuana Moment, June 2026). One secondary site (cannabisal.org) states the first sale was 4 May 2026. That conflicts with AMCC's own 4 June 2026 opening announcement and with the Alabama Reflector / Marijuana Moment first-week report. Adopt AMCC's 4 June 2026 date; treat the May date as erroneous.

First-week sales — the only quantified sales figure found, secondary-reported (not an AMCC publication): about $14,600 in pre-tax sales; 102 patients; 111 transactions; average transaction $131.56 — first week at the single Montgomery store, as reported by AMCC General Counsel Justin Aday on 12 June 2026 (secondary, reporting AMCC: Marijuana Moment; corroborated in CannBus Q3 2026, data as of 30 Sept 2026; rounded version “nearly $15,000” also appears in the 12 June 2026 AMCC-meeting report: MMJDaily, June 2026). The dispensary owner said early purchases were initially rationed/limited so more patients could obtain product, then rationing was lifted so patients could buy their full 60-day allotment (secondary). Later cumulative sales — secondary only, Montgomery only: Montgomery store only, to late August 2026: over 800 patients and nearly 1,300 transactions (cumulative) (secondary synthesis: CannBus Q3 2026). No separate sales total for Talladega or Athens, and no statewide sales total for June–October 2026, was found — [UNAVAILABLE]. No state-published sales dashboard was found. CannBus Q3 2026 states expressly: “AMCC has not published sales dashboards” and “no collections figure found” for tax revenue. Calendar 2025 sales: none — sales had not started.

MPP on 24 February 2026 had said the registry would open “in the next few weeks” and would issue state identification cards to patients and caregivers (MPP blog, 24 Feb 2026). [VERIFY]: no dated AMCC announcement of the exact registry launch day was located. Do not invent a day in April 2026. Cards are issued: AMCC's patients page describes the registration process and card requirement, and the June 2026 AMCC briefing gives cards approved. Patients choose a virtual or physical card per secondary guidance — that card-format detail is secondary only and should be flagged [VERIFY] against AMCC portal instructions if used in Parts 1/4.

6.3 Licence and dispensing-site counts (official, with secondary corroboration kept distinct)

Official AMCC position on open / planned sites: open (official, AMCC patients page, checked 25 Oct 2026): 3 dispensaries — Montgomery (4 June 2026), Talladega (28 Aug 2026), Athens (14 Sep 2026) (official: AMCC Patients). Planned sites from licences issued to date (official, AMCC FAQ): Athens (Limestone), Attalla (Etowah), Bessemer (Jefferson), Birmingham (Jefferson), Daphne (Baldwin), Mobile (Mobile), Montgomery (Montgomery), Oxford (Calhoun), Talladega (Talladega) — 9 municipalities (official: AMCC FAQ — Where are dispensaries located?). AMCC note on the same page: one dispensary licence awarded 11 Dec 2025 has been stayed (3 further sites if issued); administrative hearings continue in the Integrated Facility category; up to 5 integrated licences × up to 5 sites = up to 25 further sites. AMCC licence-type caps (official): cultivator no more than 12; processor no more than 4; dispensary no more than 4 (each up to 3 sites = 12 first-round sites); integrated facility no more than 5 (each up to 5 sites); secure transporter and state testing laboratory no cap stated (official: AMCC Licence Types).

Licence counts — AMCC Annual Reports and AMCC Patients/FAQ (CannBus Q3 2026 is corroboration, not the source): 9 cultivators licensed; 4 processors licensed; 4 secure transporters licensed; 3 dispensary licences issued (4th, Yellowhammer, stayed); 3 dispensaries open; 1 state testing laboratory licensed (Green Health Laboratories, Foley); 0 integrated facility licences issued (AMCC Annual Reports 2024 and 2025; AMCC Patients/FAQ; secondary corroboration: CannBus Q3 2026). Corroboration for the pre-dispensary position: AMCC Annual Report 2024 states that as of its reporting there were 9 licensed cultivators, 4 licensed processors, 4 licensed transporters and 1 licensed testing laboratory — consistent with the 2026 counts above. Testing-lab offering, June 2026: the AMCC June 11, 2026 draft agenda listed “Consider Opening State Testing Laboratory License Offering” as a decision item (June 11, 2026 agenda (PDF)); a vote to reopen in June 2026 is [VERIFY against the June/July 2026 minutes] and must not be asserted without them. The “single application from the prior February 2025 opening” that was approved refers to Green Health (June 2025), not to a June 2026 approval. Operating status of cultivators/processors (how many are actually producing) is not published by AMCC — [UNAVAILABLE]. “Licensed” must not be rewritten as “operating” for any individual licensee.

6.4 Official price data

None found — [UNAVAILABLE]. AMCC publishes no price list, price dashboard or average-price figure, and CannBus Q3 2026 lists flower price/potency trends as N/A because flower is not sold. Secondary price evidence only (June 2026, first store): $42 to $52 per item at Callie's Apothecary, per its patient menu as reported by the Alabama Reflector (via Marijuana Moment); $131.56 average transaction (first week, 111 transactions) — see Part 6.1. That is an average basket, not a product price. No price data for Talladega or Athens stores, and no later (July–October 2026) price update, was found — [UNAVAILABLE].

7.1 ADAI industrial hemp — grower, processor / handler, university

Framework. Alabama Industrial Hemp Research Program Act, Title 2, Chapter 8, Article 11, §§2-8-380 et seq. (Act 2016-293 — Act number [VERIFY] on Alison); ADAI rules at Ala. Admin. Code Chapter 80-10-21; programme pages at ADAI Hemp Program Overview and ADAI Hemp — About. Accessed 2026-10-28 for the re-check.

Fees — the $200 application fee is stale. Grower — Ala. Admin. Code r. 80-10-21-.43: application $150, plus any established online convenience fee, per application; annual grower participation $1,000 for each growing location; secondary pre-harvest sample $250 per sample; post-harvest retest $250 per sample; site modification $1,000 for each GPS coordinate location change after the agreement is executed. History: new rule published 31 Aug 2020, effective 15 Oct 2020, operative 1 Nov 2020; amended published 31 Aug 2023, effective 15 Oct 2023; authority §2-8-383 (r. 80-10-21-.43). Processor / Handler — r. 80-10-21-.44: application $150 plus convenience fee; annual participation $1,000 each for grain, fibre, floral material (such as CBD), and handler (such as seed cleaner or laboratory); GPS site change $1,000; same 2020 / 2023 history (r. 80-10-21-.44). University — r. 80-10-21-.45: application $150 plus convenience fee; annual participation $500 for the initial growing location and $200 for each additional growing location; GPS site change $500; sampling and THC testing $200 for each sample (r. 80-10-21-.45). The ADAI pre-application sheet (Aug 2022, still linked from the overview page) states the application fee as "$150 plus 4.5% convenience fee" and the site fee as "$1,000 per site plus 4.5% convenience fee", with no refunds once paid (ADAI pre-application sheet). The current rules say "any established online convenience fee" without a percentage, so the current percentage is [VERIFY] — do not state 4.5% as current. Harbor Compliance still shows $200 for grower and processor, and a 2018 ADAI rule compilation also showed $200; both are superseded by the 2023-amended rules. Adopt $150.

What each ADAI licence allows. Grower / Handler: grow, produce, cultivate, handle and store hemp. Processor / Handler: process, handle and store hemp. University: university research / production under the university licence type; university-to-university and grower-to-university transfers require a Seed / Propagule Acquisition Request vetted through the ADAI lab, with source licence documents and certificate-of-analysis documentation (ADAI seed acquisition procedures). Boundary notes from the ADAI pre-application sheet: growers who will handle or store harvested hemp materials will also need the Processor / Handler licence; once hemp materials are harvested and transformed into end products (e.g. cosmetics, lotions), they are no longer under ADAI purview; industrial hemp is an agricultural commodity, not intended for individual / personal grows, and not a replacement for medical or recreational marijuana.

Grower requirements (pre-application sheet + r. 80-10-21-.06) — [VERIFY] against current ADAI instructions before citing as current rule text. Applicant must be a resident of Alabama or live within 50 miles of the Alabama grow site. No hemp site in, or adjacent to, a residential structure; sites in neighbourhood settings are deemed unsuitable and will not be approved. Site must be 1,000 feet or more from schools and recreational areas where children congregate, and 300 feet or more from residential structure(s) unless prior approval is obtained (approval may not be forthcoming depending on circumstances). Hemp sites used for public venues (mazes, trails, weddings, etc.) will not be approved. All sites must be ready to plant / use at application (acreage cleared / prepared; structures assembled / constructed; processing facilities established). Applicants leasing or renting land or structures must provide a signed lease / agreement; a Property Owner Affirmation form from the actual property owner is required. GPS coordinates from the centre of each intended site; detailed aerial / satellite photo(s) with notations on structures, a GPS marker at the centre, and an outline around the intended outdoor grow site; ground-level photos of all sides if an aerial photo is outdated and does not show a structure. Entity applicants must apply with the Alabama Secretary of State and provide Articles of Incorporation / formation documents.

Background checks. Key members of an entity must submit a criminal background report run from fingerprints, statewide (not city- or county-wide), not based on name or SSN alone; for key members residing outside Alabama, the report must be completed by a state law enforcement agency rather than a local sheriff or police department, also fingerprint-based. Applicant must submit a copy of the current driver's licence at application. Applications are submitted online via the Kelly Registration System (KRS) at hemppermits.agi.alabama.gov. The federal 10-year controlled-substance felony bar (7 U.S.C. §1639p) applies through the approved plan; the ADAI sheet's own disqualifier wording was not re-pinned in this pass — [VERIFY] against the current application instructions before stating an ADAI-specific felony window. Hemp questions: 334-240-3713 and ALHemp@agi.alabama.gov, confirmed on the ADAI overview page 2026-10-28 (ADAI Hemp Program Overview).

Minimums (pre-application sheet) — [VERIFY] against current ADAI instructions. Outdoor — no less than 1 acre to plant no less than 1,000 plants each time the acre is planted, unless prior ADAI approval; indoor — no less than 1,500 square feet to plant no less than 500 plants each time the site is planted, unless prior ADAI approval; planting less than the minimum without prior approval causes an immediate out-of-compliance issue resulting in enforcement actions; processing / handling site structures / facilities no less than 1,500 square feet; wherever hemp is, even briefly, it must be registered as a site (propagation sheds, greenhouses, indoor growing structures, hoop houses, barns, all structures used for drying / storing / handling).

Grower licensing agreement (r. 80-10-21-.06). An applicant is not a programme participant until the conditionally approved applicant completes ADAI's mandatory orientation session and executes a grower licensing agreement with ADAI; each licensed grower / producer is assigned a department licence number in the form prescribed by USDA. Agreement terms include, at minimum: licensed growers act as agents of the department and comply with department and law-enforcement instructions; pay the licensing fee in the administrative rules; consent to entry and inspection of all premises where hemp or other cannabis plants / materials are located or licensed to be located, with or without cause and with or without advance notice; consent to forfeiture and destruction, without compensation, of (1) material with measured total delta-9-THC over 0.3% on a dry-weight basis, (2) plants in an area not licensed by the department, (3) plants not accounted for in required reporting; apply for registration of all growing, handling and storage locations including GPS coordinates and receive department approval before having hemp on those premises; submit Site Modification Request Forms and appropriate fees and obtain prior written approval before changing licensed sites; hemp must not be grown, handled or stored anywhere other than the location listed in the agreement; no interplanting hemp with any other crop without express written department permission; pesticide applicators must apply pesticides per the administrative regulation; comply with department restrictions on movement of hemp plants and plant parts; financial or other loss risk is borne solely by the licensed grower; a copy of the grower licensing agreement must be available for inspection while hemp is in transit and immediately on request from the department or law enforcement; submit Hemp Grow Plan Reports, Harvest / Destruction Forms, Post-Harvest Reports, Production Reports, and any other reports required by the department or USDA by the deadlines in the regulation; scout and monitor unregistered fields for volunteer cannabis plants and destroy those volunteer plants for 3 years past the last date of planting reported to the department; must not employ or rent land to cultivate hemp from any person terminated or denied admission for failure to obtain an acceptable criminal background check or failure to comply with a department representative's order, and land used for cultivation or storage must not be owned by or leased from such a person; notify the department of any law-enforcement interaction immediately by phone and follow up in writing within 3 calendar days; notify the department of any theft of cannabis materials (theft / vandalism must also be reported to local law enforcement as soon as discovered, and ADAI notified within 3 calendar days — ADAI overview page); department, law enforcement or other authorised entities may conduct annual inspections of licensed growers, at random; failure to agree or comply is grounds for departmental action up to and including termination of the agreement and expulsion from the programme, and a person expelled is not eligible to reapply for 5 years from expulsion; failure to agree and sign terminates conditional approval; the department may deny or revoke any licence for good cause shown. Rule history: new rule filed 15 Nov 2018, effective 30 Dec 2018; repealed and new rule published 31 Aug 2020, effective 15 Oct 2020, operative 1 Nov 2020; amended published 30 Nov 2021, effective 14 Jan 2022; amended published 31 May 2022, effective 15 July 2022; authority §2-8-383 (r. 80-10-21-.06). Theft reporting (overview page): report theft / vandalism to local law enforcement as soon as discovered; ALEA Agriculture & Rural Crimes Unit 1-855-75-CRIME (27463); ADAI must be notified of any theft within 3 calendar days; law-enforcement interaction must be notified to ADAI immediately by phone (334-240-3713) and in writing (ALHemp@agi.alabama.gov) within 3 calendar days (ADAI Hemp Program Overview).

Term / renewal — partly established. The 2018 rule text stated all licences valid for 1 year from issuance; the 2023 programme timeline shows a different cycle (application period 10 Oct 2022–30 Nov 2022; site fee within 14 days of approval; licence documents issued after 1 Jan 2023; licence valid 1 Mar 2023–28 Feb 2024). Whether the current cycle is still a March-to-February licence year, or has moved to the January–February window described in secondary sources for 2026, is [VERIFY] — do not assert a current licence-year start / end date. Secondary renewal summary (Harbor Compliance, not primary): processor renewal $1,000 per location, due annually by the date of initial registration; planting report within 14 days after each outdoor planting, and within 14 days of initial planting plus quarterly thereafter for greenhouse growing; post-harvest report annually by 31 Dec — all [VERIFY] against current ADAI forms / rules.

7.2 USDA-approved state plan vs USDA direct programme

Alabama runs its own USDA-approved state plan; growers apply to ADAI, not to USDA for a direct producer licence. ADAI: "Alabama's Industrial Hemp plan was created, submitted, and accepted by the USDA and went into effect on January 1, 2022" (ADAI Hemp — About). USDA AMS plan list (page updated 17 Feb 2026): Alabama is listed as "AL Approved Plan (pdf)*", where "*" means approved under the final rule which took effect 22 Mar 2021. The page states that once approved, a plan remains in effect unless withdrawn by the state / tribal government or revoked by USDA under Final Rule procedures, and that substantive revisions must be re-submitted for USDA approval (USDA AMS State and Tribal Plan Review). Plan document link: AlabamaHempPlan.pdf (AMS-hosted plan document). The plan PDF's own approval / signature date, as distinct from the 1 Jan 2022 effective date, was not extracted in this pass — [VERIFY] from the PDF itself before stating a USDA acceptance date. Note: the AMS list page publishes plan documents, not Alabama licensee names or counts.

Pilot-to-permanent transition (state carefully). Alabama Industrial Hemp Research Program Act, Act 2016-293 (SB 347, 2016 — pairing [VERIFY] on Alison), under the 2014 Farm Bill pilot authority (Section 7606). First pilot season 2019 counts (152 growers, 59 processors, 5 universities) are secondary-only (Hemp Gazette quoting Commissioner Rick Pate) — [VERIFY] against ADAI programme history before citing them as ADAI figures. The 2018 Farm Bill declassified hemp as a Schedule I drug and classified it as an agricultural commodity; the USDA-approved plan effective 1 Jan 2022 is the permanent-programme instrument. The exact USDA acceptance / submission date is [VERIFY] as above. Consequence for the federal baseline, stated carefully: Alabama growers are under the ADAI approved plan, not USDA direct licences, so any implementation of the USDA DEA-registered-lab testing delay to 31 Dec 2026 for Alabama growers would come through ADAI; no Alabama statement on that implementation was located — [UNAVAILABLE] — so do not present ADAI implementation as confirmed.

7.3 ABC consumable-hemp licences — retailers, ENDS route, manufacturer / wholesaler

ABC Board hemp page (re-opened 2026-10-28). Effective 1 Jan 2026, consumable hemp products may only be sold in Alabama by consumable hemp product retailers licensed by the Alabama ABC Board, per Code of Alabama 1975 Title 28 Chapter 12. Three distinct consumable hemp licence types are listed: (1) Consumable Hemp Products Retail Food Store Licence; (2) Consumable Hemp Products Pharmacy Licence; (3) Consumable Hemp Products Specialty Retailer Licence. The page directs readers to §28-12-45 for retail-establishment guidelines and gives the contact consumablehemp@abc.alabama.gov. No licensee list, count, search or download appears on the page as opened (ABC Board — Hemp).

Retailer licence — §28-12-40. Effective 1 Jan 2026, consumable hemp products may only be sold by retailers licensed by the board under this article, to adults 21 years of age or older. The board may not issue a licence unless the local governing body of the county or municipality where the licensee's facility will be located has approved the application for licensure. Every applicant for an original retailer licence must file a written application in the form and with the information the board prescribes by rule, accompanied by a non-refundable initial filing fee of $50. "Applicant" includes every individual with any proprietary or financial interest of 10% or more in the business seeking a licence, excluding any public corporation whose shares are traded on a recognised stock exchange. Each applicant must be legally present in the United States and provide a valid US-issued driver licence, valid military identification card, or other valid identification card as determined by the board. Applicant must submit a sworn form providing written consent for release of criminal history background information, including name, date of birth, and Social Security number. Applicant must provide two complete functional sets of fingerprints, physical or electronic, properly executed by a criminal justice agency or an individual properly trained in fingerprinting techniques; fingerprints and form are submitted by the board to the State Bureau of Investigation for criminal background checks, and SBI forwards prints to the FBI for a national check; the applicant pays all background-check costs. The board must keep information received under this subsection confidential, except information received and relied on in denying a licence may be disclosed as necessary to support the denial or when subpoenaed by a court. The board must not issue a licence to any applicant convicted of a disqualifying offence within 10 years of the application date. Any person applying for an initial licence must purchase and maintain a surety bond, payable to the board, for each licensed location, executed by the applicant as principal and by a corporate surety company qualified to do business in Alabama as surety, in the amount of $25,000. The board may file a claim against the surety bond of any licensee that fails to timely collect and remit taxes under the chapter or fails to timely pay any outstanding penalty imposed by the board. If the board finds the applicant meets the qualifications and applicable board rules, upon payment of an annual licence fee of $1,000, the board shall issue a retailer licence. Unless revoked or suspended, retailer licences are valid for the licence year beginning 1 Oct each year; licences may be issued at any time during the year, but annual licence fees are not prorated. Citation in the text: Act 2025-385, §1 (Alison §28-12-40). Audit note: the Alison §28-12-40 page fetch timed out on 2026-10-28; re-check it in a live browser at republication. The $50 / $1,000 / $25,000 figures are corroborated by the ABC framework and the enrolled HB 445 text.

Retail-establishment eligibility — §28-12-45. Other than pharmacies selling topical or sublingual products under subsection (b) and retail food stores selling beverage products under subsection (c), all retailer establishments must be restricted so only individuals 21+ may enter, and the establishment must have its own dedicated public entrance. Except as provided in (b) and (c), the board may only issue retailer licences to persons: (1) with a valid retail liquor licence from the board authorising off-premises consumption only; (2) with a valid permit from the board to operate as a specialty retailer of electronic nicotine delivery systems (ENDS) under §28-11-7.1; or (3) that only sell consumable hemp products. Pharmacy: topical and sublingual products may be sold in a pharmacy licensed by the Alabama State Board of Pharmacy, provided the pharmacy obtains an ABC consumable hemp product retailer licence and complies with the chapter and board rules; any topical product sold in a pharmacy must be sold by a licensed pharmacist or by a pharmacy technician / employee under the direct supervision and control of a licensed pharmacist; this does not prohibit a subsection (a) retailer from selling topical / sublingual products in its licensed premises. Retail food store beverages: beverages may be sold in a retail food store provided it obtains an ABC retailer licence and complies with the chapter and board rules; beverages must be kept in an area that is (i) separated from non-alcoholic beverages or beverages intended for children, (ii) behind glass, (iii) demarcated by a sign indicating the beverages contain hemp-derived compounds; a subsection (a) retailer is not prohibited from selling beverages in its licensed premises. "Retail food store" means a store commonly known as a supermarket, food store, or grocery store, primarily engaged in retail sale of a variety of canned goods, frozen foods, non-alcoholic beverages, dry goods (packaged or in bulk), and fresh produce or meats, and which dedicates (i) a minimum of 75% of its selling area to the sale of the listed food items and (ii) at least 14,000 square feet of its footprint to the sale of the listed food items. A subsection (a) retailer must maintain at its licensed premises a minimum of 500 square feet of sales and service area; areas not open to customers or not used for sales / displaying consumable hemp products, such as office space or storage, may not be included. A retailer must have an employee present in the sales and service area at all times the premises is open to customers. Purchase of all consumable hemp products must take place in the licensed premises. A retailer must display the retailer licence in the licensed premises in a conspicuous manner. Citation: Act 2025-385, §1; Act 2026-504, §3 (Alison §28-12-45). Nuance: the current §28-12-45 text already contains the ENDS clause (item (2) above) because it was amended by Act 2026-504. The ABC Board hemp page as opened still lists only the original three licence-type names and does not separately name an ENDS specialty retailer licence. HB 445 engrossed, Article 2 (Licensure), §28-12-20: "The board shall issue and renew licenses to manufacturers, wholesale distributors, and retailers of consumable hemp products as provided in this chapter"; every applicant for an original licence shall file a written application in the form and with the information the board prescribes by rule, accompanied by a non-refundable initial filing fee of fifty dollars ($50) and the appropriate license fee; the board may not issue a licence unless the local governing body has approved the application; licences are valid for the licence year beginning 1 Oct each year, may be issued at any time during the year, but licence fees shall not be prorated; the board may suspend or revoke a licence in accordance with §28-3A-24 or §28-3A-26, and may suspend without a hearing in situations of imminent danger to the public or for protecting public welfare, peace, safety, and health. HB 445 engrossed §28-12-25: annual licence fees — (1) Manufacturer license, $5,000; (2) Wholesaler license, $5,000; (3) Retailer license, $1,000 — payable before a licence is issued or renewed. HB 445 engrossed §28-12-26 (renewal): renewed annually on filing of an application and payment of the applicable fee; renewal application, as prescribed by the board by rule, by 1 Aug annually; renewal without penalty between 1 Oct and 20 Oct of the following fiscal year; after 20 Oct by payment of appropriate state and county licensing and filing fees plus a penalty of 50% of the annual licence fee; if not renewed before midnight 30 Sept of the succeeding licence year, the licence terminates with no privilege of renewal (HB 445 engrossed text). ABC Rule 20-X-33-.02 (application items). Every applicant for an ABC Board licence, in addition to Title 28 information, must also give the board: (a) an approval letter from the local governing body; (b) name, date of birth, place of birth, address, telephone number, driver's licence number, and Social Security number of every person with a 10% or greater proprietary or profit interest, except public corporations traded on a recognised stock exchange; (c) under §28-12-40(d)(2) and §31-13-7, proof that every such person is lawfully present in the United States and otherwise qualified; (d) the true, correct, and complete criminal court record of all arrests and subsequent dispositions for the past 10 years for the applicant and any other 10%+ person, and for corporations / clubs / associations, each officer and / or board member — minor vehicular offences may be omitted, but DUI and reckless driving must be disclosed, with court name(s) and disposition; ABC may require additional information on offences over 10 years old as it deems necessary; (e) proof of a $25,000 surety bond, documented each year at renewal. 7.6 Grower plot registration, pre-harvest sampling / testing (licence-side rules only; detail belongs to Part 11)

Plot / site registration. Every location where hemp is present, even briefly, must be registered as a site with GPS coordinates and department approval before hemp is on the premises (r. 80-10-21-.06; ADAI pre-application sheet). Changes require a Site Modification Request Form, appropriate fees, and prior written department approval; GPS coordinate changes carry the $1,000 surcharge (grower / processor) or $500 (university) in rules .43 / .44 / .45.

Seed / propagule acquisition. Growers must obtain ADAI written approval of source and variety before purchasing seeds / propagules; invoices and shipping / receiving documents must be uploaded in KRS after approval and as received (2023 timeline). ADAI lab reviews COA documentation; COA must show no more than 0.3% THC for material grown from the seeds / propagules. [VERIFY] against current ADAI acquisition procedures.

Planting / production reporting. Secondary Harbor summary states planting report within 14 days after each outdoor planting, and within 14 days of initial planting plus quarterly thereafter for greenhouse growing; post-harvest report annually by 31 Dec. The 2023 ADAI timeline states production / planting reports (outdoor) within 14 days of each planting, and (indoor) within 14 days of each planting. Whether the current rule still uses the 14-day / quarterly pattern is [VERIFY] against current ADAI forms.

Pre-harvest sampling and testing — licence-side rules from ADAI procedures (2019 kick-off deck and seed-acquisition procedures, so confirm currency). All growing sites will be inspected and sampled prior to harvest or destruction by ADAI inspectors — this includes licensed Nursery Growers; samples will be taken of each plot and variety / strain; growers must notify ADAI 14 days before each harvest to allow inspectors time to schedule sampling; the grower's up-to-30-day window to harvest begins the day ADAI samples; growers must take plants as whole plants to a licensed drying / storage site; growers may NOT sell or move harvested material to a processor until after receiving the Release / Movement form and the final lab analysis results from ADAI; THC test results may take up to 6 weeks (ADAI tries to keep this within 8 days — allow for 6 weeks); the grower or a knowledgeable representative must be present for site visits, inspections, and sampling, and ADAI must be notified of all representatives prior to inspection times; additional pre-harvest sampling fees will be assessed for each sample, each variety, invoiced by email with 30 days to pay. For destruction: growers must notify ADAI 14 days before any destruction to allow inspectors time to schedule a day to sample / witness the materials to be destroyed; ADAI must witness the destruction (composting rogue males, skips, etc. is allowed with documented losses). The 14-day notice / 30-day window mechanics come from ADAI's 2019 kick-off materials; whether the current procedures retain them verbatim is [VERIFY] against the current ADAI sampling protocol — do not present them as confirmed current rule text without that check.

Federal framework overlay (for Part 11 cross-reference, not Alabama-specific). 7 CFR §990.3(a)(2) requires samples collected within 30 days prior to the anticipated harvest, for total delta-9-THC testing, collected by a sampling agent; producers may not collect samples from their own growing facilities. USDA FAQ: licensed producers must have a sampling agent collect samples no more than 30 days prior to anticipated harvest; testing uses post-decarboxylation or similarly reliable methods to determine total THC on a dry-weight basis; for state-plan producers, sampling / lab requirements differ by programme and producers should verify with their licensing body. Alabama's specific sampler (ADAI inspector, per ADAI procedures above), lab (ADAI Food & Drug Lab vs DEA-registered lab), measurement-of-uncertainty treatment, and any current sampling fee beyond the $250 secondary sample / $250 retest / $200 university sample in rules .43 / .45 are [VERIFY] / Part 11 detail — do not state a current Alabama pre-harvest window, lab list, or testing fee beyond what is pinned above.

7.7 What happens if hemp tests hot (>0.3%) — negligence vs violation, destruction

Established from primary rule text (r. 80-10-21-.06). Licensed growers consent to forfeiture and destruction, without compensation, of material with measured total delta-9-THC content in excess of 0.3% on a dry-weight basis, as well as plants in unlicensed areas and plants not accounted for in required reporting. Failure to comply can lead to termination of the agreement and expulsion, with a 5-year bar on reapplication after expulsion (r. 80-10-21-.06).

Older violation rule — do NOT present as current without checking. A 2018 ADAI rule compilation (Fox Rothschild PDF of the 2018 rules) states that a sample test result greater than 0.3% THC is conclusive evidence of non-compliance; upon receipt of such a result, the Commissioner may summarily suspend and revoke the registration of the licensee; the Commissioner shall furnish to the licensee a portion of the violative sample if the licensee requests it within 30 days of notification. The same 2018 compilation lists as violations, punishable by civil penalties up to $500 and disciplinary sanctions including revocation: refusal / failure to cooperate with inspection; failure to provide required / requested information; providing false / misleading / incorrect cultivation information; failure to submit any required report; growing industrial hemp that when tested is shown to have THC concentration greater than 0.3% on a dry-mass basis; failure to pay inspection / laboratory analysis fees; cultivating / handling / processing / marketing living hemp plants or viable seeds, leaf, or floral material without a licence. Growers were also required to retain records for no less than 5 years, including application records, use / disposition records, storage / processing records, and destruction records including affidavits, notifications, and electronic records. Status flag: that compilation is dated to the 2018 rules (filed 15 Nov 2018, effective 30 Dec 2018). Whether the $500 civil-penalty figure, the 5-year record rule, and the violation list survive in the current Chapter 80-10-21 text is [VERIFY]. In particular, the current USDA Final Rule framework distinguishes negligent violations (corrective action plan) from culpable violations, and Alabama's current plan may contain a corrective-action / remediation provision that the 2018 text does not.

Federal negligence / violation framework that an approved state plan must implement (for context; Alabama-specific application [VERIFY]). Under 7 U.S.C. §1639p and 7 CFR §990.6, a producer that negligently violates a state plan must comply with a corrective action plan established by the state department of agriculture, including a reasonable date to correct the violation and periodic reporting for not less than the next 2 calendar years; a negligent violation alone is not subject to criminal enforcement by federal, state, tribal, or local government; a producer that negligently violates a plan 3 times in a 5-year period is ineligible to produce hemp for 5 years from the third violation; if the state determines a producer violated the plan with a culpable mental state greater than negligence, the state must immediately report the producer to the Attorney General and the chief law enforcement officer of the state, and the corrective-action paragraph does not apply; a person convicted of a felony relating to a controlled substance is ineligible during the 10-year period following conviction (with a pre-20 Dec 2018 pilot-programme exception). A secondary summary states the federal 1.0% THC negligence threshold (crops above 0.3% but not exceeding 1.0% total THC are subject to remediation or disposal but are NOT a negligent violation; above 1.0% is a negligent violation) — that threshold is secondary only and Alabama's own statement of it is [VERIFY] from the Alabama plan PDF.

Destruction method, who destroys, who pays, and remediation (e.g. stripping / remediation vs whole-crop destruction). [UNAVAILABLE] in this pass, except for the licence-side points pinned above: the Harvest / Destruction Form is a required report under r. 80-10-21-.06; ADAI must witness destruction (ADAI procedures); harvested material may not move to a processor until the Release / Movement form and final lab results are received; and under the Hurricane Helene emergency protocol, if a post-harvest analytical result shows THC above 0.3%, a second post-harvest sample will be collected and tested (ADAI Hurricane Helene emergency harvest protocol). Do not state a current Alabama remediation option or destruction method until the current plan and current violation / corrective-action rules are opened.

For consumable hemp (separate from farm hemp — do not conflate). Unlawful product at a retailer is subject to confiscation and, under §28-12-5(f) as reported in the complete dossier, a 10% assessment on retail value — [VERIFY] §28-12-5(f) on Alison before quoting. That is a retailer-side consequence, not a farm hot-crop consequence.

7.9 Alabama response to federal PL 119-37 §781 / PL 119-103 §2019

Re-check result, Oct 2026 searches (re-confirmed 2026-10-28): No formal Alabama official statement from ADAI, the ABC Board, AMCC, or the Attorney General addressing PL 119-37 §781 or PL 119-103 §2019 by number, or the 12 Nov / 11 Dec 2026 dates, the total-THC definition, or the 0.4 mg / container cap, was located. This is [UNAVAILABLE]; it does not change the earlier finding. Only partial items found (secondary only): ADAI via Alabama Daily News (Nov 2025): "Nothing is expected to change in its [hemp grower / processor] program under the federal ban," as told to Alabama Daily News. This is a programme-continuity comment, not a statement addressing the 12 Nov / 11 Dec dates, the total-THC definition, or the 0.4 mg cap. MPP, 7 Oct 2026 (secondary): "It is undecided as to what will happen to the state's limited consumable hemp market when federal regulations change in December 2026." Secondary analysis only, DrugPolicyWatch (Alabama page, accessed 2026-10-25): Alabama is "among the least exposed" because HB 445 already bans smokable / inhalable hemp, caps consumable THC, and routes remaining products through ABC licensing, testing, and enforcement effective in stages through 1 Jan 2026; the federal change therefore "reinforces existing Alabama law rather than upending an unregulated market", but many ABC-permitted edibles and beverages capped at 10 mg per serving may still exceed the federal 0.3% total-THC standard and the separate 0.4 mg per container cap. This is secondary analysis, not Alabama's position, and must be labelled as such. The generic federal-supersession clause in enrolled §28-12-1(d): "Any federal law enacted after July 1, 2025, that conflicts with a provision [of] this chapter shall supersede the conflicting provision of this chapter." Whether Alabama treats PL 119-37 / 119-103 as triggering that clause remains [VERIFY] on the current Code text. Practical implication to state carefully (analysis, not official Alabama guidance): a 10 mg Alabama serving exceeds 0.4 mg per container, so Alabama-compliant consumable products are not automatically federally compliant after 11 Dec 2026 under the given baseline. That tension must be presented as an implication of the two regimes, not as an Alabama agency statement. A secondary discrepancy to note: one Alabama Daily News passage states the federal law takes effect 13 Nov 2026, conflicting with the fixed baseline (12 Nov / 11 Dec 2026); this file uses the baseline dates.

Hemp land-use rule (context for any future hemp property, not a listing): ADAI Rule 80-10-21-.18 — a licensed hemp processor / handler shall not process / store leaf or floral material in a residential structure, shall not process in a site within 1,000 feet of a school or public recreational area without department approval, shall not process / handle / store on property not owned or completely controlled by the applicant / licensee, and shall not process / handle / store on property owned by, leased from, or previously submitted in an application by any person ineligible or terminated / denied admission for failure to obtain an acceptable criminal background check or failure to comply with a department representative's order (r. 80-10-21-.18).

9.3 Ballot history

Alabama has NO statewide citizen initiative or referendum. The Alabama Constitution, Article XVIII ("Mode of Amending the Constitution"), §§284–287 (with §286.02 added by Amendment 951, ratified 2020, Act 2019-271, authorising recompilation), provides the exclusive means of amending the Constitution, and only the Legislature may initiate amendments. The Alabama Law Institute Election Handbook, Chapter 22, states: Article XVIII §§284, 284.01, 285, 286, 286.01, 286.02 and 287 "provide the exclusive means by which the Alabama Constitution may be changed"; "Only the Legislature may initiate amendments to the Alabama Constitution"; "There is no process for citizen-initiated constitutional amendments or conventions." The Initiative & Referendum Institute (USC) states identically: "Alabama does not have either the initiative or referendum, although voters must approve constitutional amendments proposed by the legislature." Cite Article XVIII itself; the handbook is secondary explanation, not the Constitution (Alabama Law Institute Election Handbook, Ch. 22; Initiative & Referendum Institute — Alabama). Note: the Constitution is now the Constitution of Alabama of 2022 (recompiled); check any 1901 numbering against the 2022 recompilation at republication.

Proposed initiative bills — PROPOSED ONLY, not law. HB 561 (2025), "Referendum measures; authorize general laws and constitutional amendments to be initiated through public petition process": introduced 10 April 2025, referred to House Constitution, Campaigns and Elections 10 April 2025, and died at sine die at the end of the 2025 session (last recorded action 10 April 2025, pending committee — not a distinct 14 May 2025 action). Proposed thresholds (preliminary petition 1,000 voters + $1,000 fee; final petition 7% of last gubernatorial vote for general laws, 10% for constitutional amendments, with per-district minimums) are proposal details only; the per-district percentages remain [VERIFY] against the introduced text (HB 561 introduced text). Earlier similar proposals (HB 201, 2010; HB 209, 2014) likewise did not create an initiative process — [VERIFY] on Alison.

Local ballot questions on cannabis: NONE VERIFIED. Alabama's opt-in system works by city ordinance / county resolution (§20-2A-51(c)), not by ballot. No local cannabis ballot question with official results was found in the sources checked. The Alabama Secretary of State's Local Ballot Measures page currently states: "There are no local ballot measures to display at this time" — that is a current-display statement, not a historical search, so the final wording should be: "No local cannabis ballot question with official results was located in the sources checked (Secretary of State local-ballot-measures page; opt-in city ordinance records are the operative mechanism)" rather than an absolute historical "none ever existed" unless a full SOS archive check is run (Alabama Secretary of State — Local Ballot Measures).
