PART 10 — TRIBAL AND INTERSTATE

10.1 Poarch Band of Creek Indians — federally recognised, Atmore, Escambia County

Identity and federal recognition. The Poarch Band of Creek Indians is the only federally recognised tribe in Alabama. Its own site states it is "the only federally recognized Indian Tribe in Alabama, operating as a sovereign nation with its own government" (Poarch Band of Creek Indians). The Encyclopedia of Alabama's AIAC article states the same: "Of this group, only the Poarch Band of Creeks is officially recognized by the federal government" (Encyclopedia of Alabama — Alabama Indian Affairs Commission). The BIA resolved-petitions list records Poarch Band of Creeks (Petition 013) as Acknowledged (BIA — Petitions Resolved).

Recognition date — June 1984, not 1983. The Eleventh Circuit's account of the acknowledgment record states: "On June 4, 1984, the Secretary of Indian Affairs recognized and 'acknowledge[d] that the Poarch Band of Creeks … exists as an Indian tribe within the meaning of Federal law,'" citing "Final Determination for the Fed. Acknowledgment of the Poarch Band of Creeks, 49 Fed. Reg. 24,083-01 (June 11, 1984)" (Eleventh Circuit — Poarch acknowledgment record). Any source giving "1983" for federal recognition should not be used for the acknowledgment date. The same Eleventh Circuit account states the United States took 229.54 acres in Escambia County into trust as a reservation for the Poarch Band (50 Fed. Reg. 15,502, 18 April 1985), with additional land conveyed into trust in 1992 and 1995. A 2026 Senate testimony report gives a later figure of "roughly 333 acres of trust land" (Indian Gaming — Poarch Parity Act testimony, secondary; the growth from 229.54 acres is consistent with later trust acquisitions, but the 333-acre figure itself is secondary and should be cited as such). The Tribe's reservation is described on its own contact page as "located eight miles northwest of Atmore, AL, in rural Escambia County," with a tribal community of "more than 2,900 citizens" (Poarch — Contact).

Cannabis or hemp operations, ordinances, licences, dispensaries, farms — NONE FOUND. No Poarch cannabis dispensary, cultivation licence, hemp farm, cannabis ordinance, hemp ordinance, AMCC licence, or ADAI licence for Poarch was found in the searches run for this Part. Searches run (2026-10-25): site-restricted search of pci-nsn.gov for cannabis / marijuana / hemp — returned the Tribe's press kit, gaming / economic-development material, and contact page, but no cannabis or hemp programme; general searches for "Poarch Band cannabis / hemp / dispensary / marijuana" — returned only the 2015 Florida episode below, gaming material, and unrelated state guides; USDA AMS State and Tribal Plan Review page — Poarch does not appear in either the tribal "Approved Plan" list or the tribal "USDA Hemp Producer License" list; AMCC and ADAI licence material checked in Run 1 contained no Poarch entry. This is a negative finding from the sources checked, not proof that no internal tribal discussion ever occurred. No complete Poarch Tribal Code or constitution was opened in this pass, so a code-level statement must be marked [VERIFY] until the code is obtained directly from the Tribe or the National Indian Law Library.

The only Poarch-specific cannabis statement found — 2015, Florida, "no plans" (secondary). NorthEscambia.com, March 2015, reprinted from FloridaPolitics.com, quoting the Tribal Chair: "We have been advised that the answer to that question is 'yes' because we are a federally recognized tribe, the same legal status that entitles us to negotiate a gaming compact with Florida. Let me clarify, though: While it appears that we are legally entitled to do so, we have no plans to grow marijuana on our land" (NorthEscambia.com, March 2015). Context matters and must be preserved: the statement concerned a proposed facility / warehouse on Poarch-owned land in Nokomis, Florida (near Pensacola), and a request for Florida Governor Rick Scott to negotiate a gaming compact. A contemporaneous secondary piece framed the same episode as Poarch using cannabis as leverage in Florida gaming negotiations (GGb Magazine, secondary framing; do not present it as the Tribe's stated position). Do not present the 2015 statement as a current Alabama cannabis policy or as an Alabama operation. No current (2024–2026) Poarch cannabis or hemp statement, ordinance, or operation was found.

USDA tribal hemp plan — checked on the live AMS page: NO Poarch plan listed. USDA Agricultural Marketing Service, "List of USDA-approved Hemp Plans," page updated 17 February 2026: Alabama appears under States as "AL Approved Plan (pdf)*" (USDA AMS State and Tribal Plan Review). The same page's Tribes table lists dozens of tribal plans but contains no entry for the Poarch Band of Creek Indians in either the "Approved Plan" or the "USDA Hemp Producer License" column. Consequence: there is no USDA-recognised Poarch hemp production route shown on the current AMS page. Whether an individual Poarch producer could apply for a USDA producer licence outside a tribal plan is [VERIFY] — the AMS table alone does not answer it, and it must not be assumed either way. Re-check the tribal table at republication.

Tribal-state legal framework. Public Law 280 — secondary analysis only. The Tribal Institute jurisdictional analysis (Goldberg, UCLA, updated 2010) places Alabama in Group 1 — "No State Jurisdiction" — with the entry: "Alabama – (1) Legislation: No Public Law 280 or similar legislation. Case Law: Sheffield v. Tullis, 1998 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 14110 (S.D. Ala. 1998). Tribes: Poarch Band of Creek Indians" (Tribal Institute — Jurisdiction Analysis). This is a secondary analysis, not a primary source, and is labelled as such. Practical consequence, stated carefully: PL 280 does not itself grant Alabama criminal or civil jurisdiction over Poarch Indian country. That does not by itself resolve whether federal controlled-substances law, Alabama law off tribal land, or tribal law on tribal land governs a particular cannabis or hemp act. Jurisdiction depends on land status (trust vs fee), actor (tribal member vs non-member), and the specific federal / state / tribal law. Those applications are [VERIFY] for any concrete scenario and must not be generalised.

Whether tribal land is subject to AMCC / ADAI licensing — [UNAVAILABLE]. No Alabama statute, AMCC rule, ADAI rule, or Poarch ordinance was found stating that Poarch trust land is subject to AMCC or ADAI licensing, or that it is exempt from it for cannabis / hemp. The general framework points in two directions that must both be preserved: on trust land, state regulation of a tribe is generally barred absent congressional authorisation — illustrated (for taxation, not cannabis) by the Alabama Attorney General's 1986 position quoted in the Eleventh Circuit case: "Absent cession of jurisdiction or other federal statutes permitting it, there is no authority for state taxation of Indian reservation lands or Indian income from activities carried on within the boundaries of the reservation"; on fee land held by the Tribe outside trust status, the Tribe holds it "in fee simple like any owner of private property," as the Eleventh Circuit put it in the Hickory Ground litigation. That principle suggests Alabama law would apply to a fee-land operation as it would to any owner, but no cannabis / hemp-specific application of that principle to Poarch fee land was located — [VERIFY] before stating it as a cannabis rule. Federal law is a separate layer: the federal Controlled Substances Act applies in Indian country, and no current federal tribal-cannabis policy replaces it (see §10.5 on the rescinded Wilkinson memorandum).

Gaming compact context — relevant only to show what a compact is and is not. Poarch operates three Wind Creek casinos in Alabama (Atmore, Wetumpka, Montgomery) offering Class II gaming under the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act (IGRA), including electronic bingo. Alabama prohibits Class III gaming, so under IGRA the State is not required to negotiate a Class III compact. Gaming-compact proposals are NOT enacted compacts and must not be presented as law. A January 2026 secondary report described a Poarch proposal for exclusivity, two new northern Alabama resorts, Class III at existing casinos, $225 million for exclusivity, and 25% revenue sharing (secondary, proposal only). An older secondary report described a different $1 billion plan ($725 million in licensing / compact fees, $350 million projected tax sharing, 6,500 jobs). These are different proposals at different dates; do not merge them. A Poarch tribal gaming ordinance (secondary reproduction, dated 2 August 1993) defines Class I, Class II, and Class III gaming. It is a gaming ordinance only; no cannabis provision was shown in that extract. Separately, 2026 Senate testimony concerned S. 1750, the Poarch Band of Creek Indians Parity Act, on trust-land status and the Carcieri v. Salazar issue (secondary). It is a trust-land bill, not a cannabis bill, and must not be presented as cannabis legislation.

10.2 State-recognised tribes in Alabama

The working list — nine names. The Encyclopedia of Alabama AIAC article (published 2017, updated 19 November 2025) states: "The state government recognizes nine Native American tribes in Alabama: the Poarch Band of Creek Indians, the Echota Cherokee Tribe of Alabama, the Cherokee Tribe of Northeast Alabama, the Ma-Chis Lower Creek Indian Tribe of Alabama, the Star Clan of Muscogee Creeks, the Cher-O-Creek Intra Tribal Indians, the MOWA Band of Choctaw Indians, the Piqua Shawnee Tribe, and the United Cherokee Ani-Yun-Wiya Nation. Of this group, only the Poarch Band of Creeks is officially recognized by the federal government" (Encyclopedia of Alabama — AIAC). The same article's history section states AIAC was created in 1984, initially represented six tribes (Poarch Band, MOWA Choctaw, Star Clan of Muscogee Creeks, Echota Creeks, Jackson County Cherokees, and Cherokees of Southeast Alabama), and "over time, the commission expanded to include nine state-recognized tribes".

Naming conflict — explained, not smoothed over. Ala. Code §41-9-708(b), as reproduced in statute mirrors, names seven geographically identified groups and states they "shall be state recognized upon passage of this article": Poarch Band of Creeks of Escambia County; Mowa Band of Choctaws of southwest Alabama; Star Clan of Muscogee Creeks of Pike County; Echota Cherokees of Alabama; Cherokees of northeast Alabama; Cherokees of southeast Alabama; and Ma-Chis Lower Creek Indian Tribe. It also gives the Commission power to recognise additional tribes by adopted procedure (§41-9-708(b) mirror reproduction — mirror, not the Legislature's official Code viewer — re-check required). The nine-name AIAC list includes Cher-O-Creek Intra Tribal Indians, Piqua Shawnee Tribe, and United Cherokee Ani-Yun-Wiya Nation, which are not among the seven named in §41-9-708(b) — consistent with later Commission recognitions under that power. A third list (500 Nations) lists nine state-recognised groups plus Poarch as federally recognised: Cher-O-Creek Intra Tribal Indians, Cherokee Tribe of Northeast Alabama, Cherokees of Southeast Alabama, Echota Cherokee Tribe of Alabama, Ma-Chis Lower Creek Indian Tribe of Alabama, MOWA Band of Choctaw Indians, Piqua Shawnee Tribe, Star Clan of Muscogee Creeks, and United Cherokee Ani-Yun-Wiya Nation (500 Nations — Tribes by State). Audit correction: that apparent tenth entry is explained by a state-recognised-tribes compilation that lists "Cher-O-Creek Intertribal Indians (Cherokees of SE Alabama)" — i.e. the same population under a different name — so the total remains nine on the AIAC list, not ten. The current official AIAC list is still marked [VERIFY] against aiac.alabama.gov, because a site-restricted search for aiac.alabama.gov returned no official list page to open; do not cite aiac.alabama.gov as having been opened.

MOWA Band — the most documented state-recognised tribe (secondary history). First state-recognised tribe in Alabama in 1979; located in south Washington County and north Mobile County near Citronelle, Mount Vernon, and McIntosh; name from Mobile + Washington counties (Encyclopedia of Alabama — MOWA Band, secondary encyclopedia). Federal recognition denied by BIA in 1997; a 1999 Interior Solicitor letter was reported as stating there was no evidence of Choctaw or other Indian ancestry for 99% of MOWA membership; a 2008 federal court ruling (Chief U.S. District Judge Ginny Granade) held the tribe waited too long to challenge the denial. A 2013 seizure of 50 electronic bingo machines from a MOWA gambling hall in North Mobile County was reported, with MOWA's attorney arguing state recognition made it sovereign despite lack of federal designation, and opponents arguing state recognition has no validity in the federal acknowledgement process. All of this is secondary-reported history; no BIA decision, court opinion or seizure record was opened in this audit. That gaming dispute is not a cannabis / hemp precedent and must not be presented as one. Legal point for all state-recognised tribes: state recognition alone does not confer federal tribal sovereignty, Indian country jurisdiction, IGRA gaming rights, or a USDA tribal hemp plan. State-recognised groups without federal recognition are, for cannabis / hemp licensing purposes, subject to Alabama state law on non-trust land unless a specific Alabama law says otherwise. No Alabama cannabis / hemp law carving out state-recognised tribes was located in this pass, so a definitive statement of that application is [VERIFY] if a definitive statement is needed.

10.3 Interstate issues

10.3.1 Hemp shipments THROUGH vs INTO Alabama — the central distinction

Federal rule — 2018 Farm Bill §10114 (7 U.S.C. §1639o note). "No State or Indian Tribe shall prohibit the transportation or shipment of hemp or hemp products produced in accordance with subtitle G of the Agricultural Marketing Act of 1946 (as added by section 10113) through the State or the territory of the Indian Tribe, as applicable." "Nothing in this title or an amendment made by this title prohibits the interstate commerce of hemp or hemp products." A USDA Office of the General Counsel memorandum, 28 May 2019, is reported in secondary legal analyses as concluding that after USDA published hemp-production regulations, states and Indian tribes may not prohibit interstate transportation / shipment of hemp lawfully produced under a state or tribal plan or under a USDA-issued licence (secondary legal analyses quoting §10114: Arnold & Porter — USDA hemp guidance; CannaBusiness Law — Interstate transport). The memorandum text itself was not opened in this audit — [VERIFY] before quoting its conclusion as official guidance. Limitation noted in secondary analysis: §10114 protection applies only to hemp produced in accordance with AMA subtitle G. Hemp produced outside that authority is still subject to potential seizure. A Tenth Circuit case (Serna) is reported in a secondary law-firm alert, not a court opinion text, as holding §10114 creates no private right of action for a hemp farmer whose plants were seized, because the provision regulates states rather than creating a protected class of farmers — [VERIFY] against the Tenth Circuit opinion before citing the holding.

Through vs into — apply this distinction strictly. A compliant hemp / hemp-product shipment merely passing through Alabama to a lawful destination elsewhere is protected by §10114 from a state prohibition on transportation through Alabama. That protection does not require Alabama to allow retail sale of the same product to Alabama residents, and does not override Alabama's destination-state retail rules. A product can be lawful to ship "through" Alabama yet unlawful to sell "into" Alabama. Alabama's Chapter 12 direct-to-consumer ban (no mail, online, or direct shipment of consumable hemp products to Alabama consumers after 1 January 2026, even if federally compliant) is therefore in tension with, but not identical to, the §10114 through-shipment protection. Secondary industry analysis frames this as a serious interstate-commerce / federal-preemption question that "remains to be seen" and may become litigation (Nothing But Canna — Alabama HB 445, secondary). Penalties for Chapter 12 violations as reported in that secondary analysis — selling without a licence up to $10,000 + Class C felony; selling to minors up to $20,000, licence revoked for 3 years; shipping DTC to Alabama residents misdemeanor (1st offence), felony (2nd offence); possessing / selling banned products immediate seizure + possible felony charges; noncompliant hemp products deemed contraband subject to warrantless seizure — are [VERIFY] against Title 28, Chapter 12 text. Do not present these penalty figures as verified statute text until checked. Business-to-business shipment into Alabama for further lawful Alabama processing / retail (e.g. to an ABC-licensed manufacturer / wholesaler / retailer, if such a licence type is confirmed in Part 7) is a separate question from DTC shipment and is [VERIFY] against Title 28, Chapter 12 and ABC rules — do not assume B2B shipment is either permitted or prohibited without that text.

Alabama-specific seizure cases — NOT verified; secondary only. StateRegsToday cross-border article (secondary, undated in extract): StateRegsToday — Cross-border issues in Alabama. It claims: (a) February 2019, a truck carrying nearly $800,000 worth of marijuana stopped by Alabama state troopers near the Florida border; driver said he purchased it legally in Colorado for medical use in Florida; driver arrested and charged with drug trafficking under Alabama law — a marijuana trafficking allegation, not a hemp case, with no case number, court, or disposition given; (b) January 2019, a man from Kentucky arrested in Alabama while transporting over 1,300 pounds of hemp from Tennessee where he had legally purchased it; despite paperwork proving legality, arrested and charged with first-degree possession of marijuana under Alabama law — no name, case number, court, or disposition given. Both claims are [VERIFY] / [UNAVAILABLE] as Alabama hemp seizure precedent. This report must not present either as a decided Alabama hemp-transport case without a docket, court record, or contemporaneous news report with a named defendant. No Alabama hemp-transport case with a verified docket was found in the searches run. The hemp-seizure cases returned in search (Pawhuska, Oklahoma, 17,000 pounds; Madison County, Illinois, Alkhulaqi litigation; Denver / Serna) are not Alabama cases and must not be presented as Alabama precedent. They are relevant only as illustrations of the national field-test / THC-testing problem. A practical enforcement risk supported by secondary legal commentary (not Alabama-specific): a roadside field test and a drug dog cannot distinguish hemp from marijuana, and a certificate of analysis does not guarantee a shipment will not be detained. That risk applies to Alabama transit as a practical matter, but no Alabama-specific detention figure was found.

10.3.2 Florida medical — NO reciprocity; seasonal residency is the only route in, and it creates no Alabama right

Florida does not accept out-of-state medical marijuana cards. Fla. Stat. §381.986 (official Florida Legislature text) defines "seasonal resident" as "any person who temporarily resides in this state for a period of at least 31 consecutive days in each calendar year, maintains a temporary residence in this state, returns to the state or jurisdiction of his or her residence at least one time during each calendar year, and is registered to vote or pays income tax in another state or jurisdiction" (Fla. Stat. §381.986). The statute's qualified-patient framework requires Florida residency (permanent or seasonal), a qualified Florida physician certification, and registration in the Florida Medical Marijuana Use Registry (MMUR); only MMUR patients may purchase from a licensed Florida Medical Marijuana Treatment Center (MMTC). Secondary sources are consistent with the statute: "Florida does not accept out-of-state medical marijuana cards. If you hold a card from another state, you cannot use it to buy cannabis at a Florida dispensary. Florida limits its medical marijuana program to permanent and seasonal residents who register through the state's Office of Medical Marijuana Use (OMMU) and obtain a Florida-issued card" (LegalClarity — Florida card use, secondary). The OMMU's own "no reciprocity" wording was reported second-hand in these sources; the OMMU official page itself was not opened as a list page in this pass, so an OMMU-wording citation is [VERIFY] — but the statutory residency point above is primary. Consequence for Alabama residents, stated plainly: (1) An Alabama resident cannot lawfully purchase Florida medical cannabis on an Alabama card alone. (2) A Florida card requires Florida residency (permanent or seasonal as defined above) plus a Florida physician certification — it is a new Florida registration, not recognition of the Alabama card. (3) Bringing Florida-purchased medical cannabis back into Alabama is unlawful: Alabama recognises only Alabama-dispensary product for Alabama patients, Alabama has no reciprocity, and transport of marijuana across state lines is also a federal offence. A Florida card — even one lawfully obtained as a seasonal resident — confers no Alabama possession, purchase, or transport right. Florida possession penalties noted in secondary sources (context only, not Alabama law): possession of 20 grams or less is a first-degree misdemeanor under Fla. Stat. §893.13; more than 20 grams is a third-degree felony. Local civil-citation programmes do not override state law.

10.3.3 Mississippi medical — NO direct card acceptance, but a temporary nonresident card exists (now confirmed)

Mississippi does not honour an out-of-state card for direct dispensary purchase. Instead, Mississippi issues a temporary nonresident registry identification card to a visitor who has a qualifying condition and holds an active home-state card. Confirmed terms, from Mississippi official sources: apply up to 30 days before arriving in Mississippi; card valid for a maximum of two separate 15-day periods in a 365-day year (first period = initial approval, second = renewal); purchase limits for nonresident cardholders of no more than 6 Mississippi Medical Cannabis Equivalency Units (MMCEUs) in a week and no more than 12 MMCEUs in a consecutive 15-day period; possession limit for nonresident cardholders of 14 MMCEUs; nonresident identification card nonrefundable fee of $75.00. Sources: Mississippi Medical Cannabis Program (MMCP) FAQ confirms the 14 MMCEU nonresident possession limit, citing Miss. Code Ann. §41-137-39 (MMCP FAQ); MSDH Medical Cannabis Program Administrative Rules, Title 15, Part 22, Rules 2.4.2–2.4.4 (30-day application, 2×15-day periods, 6/12 MMCEU purchase limits, 14 MMCEU possession, $75 fee) (MMCP Administrative Rules). The [VERIFY] flags for the $75 fee and the 14 MMCEU possession limit are removed by this audit. One secondary source (LegalClarity) incorrectly lists Mississippi among states with "zero recognition" — that shorthand is removed: state the precise distinction: no direct card acceptance, but a Mississippi-issued temporary nonresident card is available. Do not repeat the "zero recognition" shorthand without that qualification. Consequence for Alabama residents: an Alabama patient who obtains a Mississippi nonresident card may lawfully purchase in Mississippi during the card's validity, but bringing that Mississippi product back into Alabama is still unlawful under Alabama law (Alabama recognises only Alabama-dispensary product; Alabama has no reciprocity; the reverse transport is not authorised by Mississippi law either). The Mississippi card does not create Alabama possession rights.

10.3.4 Georgia low-THC oil / medical cannabis — 45-day possession-only rule in Georgia; NO Alabama import right; and the pre-July 2026 premise is now stale

Old framework (pre-July 2026) — verified in statute reproduction. 2022 Code, O.C.G.A. §16-12-191 (via Justia): it was lawful to possess, purchase, or have under control 20 fluid ounces or less of low-THC oil in a pharmaceutical container labelled by the manufacturer with THC percentage, if the person was registered with the Georgia Department of Public Health (DPH) under §31-2A-18 and held a DPH registration card, or held a registration card issued by another state that allows the same possession of low-THC oil as Georgia law provides — provided that card "shall not be lawful authority when such person has been present in this state for 45 days or more" (O.C.G.A. §16-12-191 (2022, via Justia)). Low-THC oil in the old framework: oil containing cannabidiol with no more than 5% THC by weight, no visible plant material, CBD content equal to or greater than THC content (secondary summaries; verify against §16-12-190). Georgia does not accept out-of-state cards for purchase at Georgia dispensaries; the 45-day provision is possession-only, and only for oil meeting Georgia's terms. Flower, edibles not in oil form, and vaporised concentrates were illegal even for registered patients under the old framework.

Transition — SB 220, effective 1 July 2026 (secondary in this pass; [VERIFY] against Georgia DPH / Georgia Access to Medical Cannabis Commission official pages before stating as settled law). Signed 12 May 2026 by Governor Brian Kemp, per secondary sources. Reported changes: Low THC Oil Registry renamed Medical Cannabis Patient Registry; 5% THC cap and CBD-balance rule eliminated; possession limit changed from 20 fluid ounces to 12,000 mg cumulative THC across products (1,200 mg maximum per individual package); allowable forms expanded to oils, tinctures, capsules, patches, lotions at full potency, with vaporisation for patients 21+ phasing in (state ingestion rules due 1 January 2027); smoking / combustion remains prohibited; edible food products (gummies, cookies, candies) remain prohibited in most summaries, while one summary says ingestibles / edibles are allowed; out-of-state cards still honoured for possession for 45 days only. Conflict note: secondary sources differ on details that must not be silently resolved — e.g. vaporisation age is given as 21+ in most summaries but 22+ in one, and one summary says ingestibles / edibles are allowed while others say candy / cookie products remain prohibited. Both details are [VERIFY] against the Georgia DPH / GMCC rules. The pre-July 2026 premise ("Georgia low-THC oil ≤5% THC") is therefore correct for the pre-July 2026 framework but stale for October 2026 if SB 220 is in effect. This report presents both layers with dates and flags SB 220 implementation status as [VERIFY].

Consequence for Alabama — stated explicitly. Georgia's 45-day possession rule is a Georgia rule. It does not create an Alabama right. An Alabama resident cannot lawfully bring Georgia low-THC oil (old 5% oil or new SB 220 product) into Alabama unless all three hold: (a) the person is an Alabama registered qualified patient / caregiver, and (b) the product is an Alabama-authorised medical form, and (c) the product was purchased / acquired from an Alabama licensed dispensary (§20-2A-3(16)). Georgia oil fails (c) in every case, and in most cases also fails (b), because Alabama's authorised forms do not include Georgia oil as such, and Alabama's daily-dose and 60 / 70-dose limits apply. A non-patient in Alabama has no lawful possession of Georgia oil at all; possession is unlawful under Title 13A. Georgia purchase for Alabama residents in Georgia: an Alabama card does not authorise purchase at a Georgia dispensary / pharmacy; purchase requires Georgia DPH registration as a Georgia registrant. That is a separate point from the 45-day possession rule. Do not suggest that Georgia registration, or the fact that Georgia oil is "low-THC," makes it lawful in Alabama.

10.3.5 Tennessee hemp products — in-person, licensed, 21+ in Tennessee; NO shipment into Alabama consumers (secondary in this pass)

Tennessee framework from web search, 2026-10-25 (secondary in this pass; [VERIFY] against Tennessee General Assembly / TABC official text): 2023: Public Chapter 526 set first hemp-derived cannabinoid product (HDCP) rules, including a 21+ age limit, under the Tennessee Department of Agriculture. HB 1376, signed 21 May 2025 by Governor Bill Lee (secondary sources differ on whether the operative chapter is HB 1376 or Public Chapter 526 as amended — flag the citation as [VERIFY] against the Tennessee General Assembly official text), moved oversight of HDCPs to the Tennessee Alcoholic Beverage Commission (TABC) and Department of Revenue, effective 1 January 2026. From 1 January 2026, per secondary summaries: suppliers, wholesalers, and retailers need a TABC licence; HDCPs must be sold face-to-face in person at a licensed store to adults 21+ with ID; shipping or delivering HDCPs to consumers is prohibited; self-checkout and vending-machine sales are prohibited; all suppliers, in-state or out-of-state, must be licensed for Tennessee distribution. THCA: products containing THCA at 0.3% or higher (total THC basis, per secondary summaries) are banned in Tennessee from 1 July 2026; THCA is classified as "the precursor of Delta-9 THC" rather than a hemp-derived product. Low-THCA lotions / gummies and beverages containing up to 15 mg per serving were reported as remaining legal in some secondary summaries, while other summaries state only edibles / gummies / beverages containing 0.3% or less delta-9 remain legal for in-state purchase. That beverage / serving detail is conflicting and secondary — mark [VERIFY] against TABC rules. A further reported cap — 15 mg THC per serving, 300 mg per non-beverage package — is likewise secondary-only [VERIFY]. Cannabinoids listed as remaining legal under the concentration limit in some secondary summaries: delta-8 THC, delta-10 THC, hexahydrocannabinol (HHC), tetrahydrocannabivarin (THCV). Synthetic cannabinoids and THC-P are reported as banned. These lists are secondary; one secondary source instead says HB 1376 "classifies Delta 8 as a synthetic cannabinoid and restricts its retail sale" — that direct conflict means delta-8's post-July 2026 Tennessee status must be [VERIFY] against the statute / rules, not asserted from either summary.

Consequence for Alabama. Tennessee legality does not make a product lawful in Alabama, and Tennessee's own in-person rule means Tennessee HDCPs cannot lawfully be shipped by a Tennessee retailer to an Alabama consumer in the first place. After 1 January 2026, a Tennessee hemp product may enter Alabama lawfully only if it independently satisfies Alabama law: farm hemp / raw hemp material — only if it meets Alabama's farm hemp definition and is handled under an approved plan (ADAI or USDA); consumable hemp product for retail sale in Alabama — only if it meets Title 28, Chapter 12 caps, testing, labelling, and ABC licensing, and is sold in person by an ABC-licensed Alabama retailer to a buyer 21+. A Tennessee TABC licence is not an Alabama ABC licence. Smokable hemp, synthetically converted psychoactive cannabinoids (the commercial delta-8 / delta-10 route), and any product exceeding Alabama's 10 mg / serving / 40 mg / package caps are unlawful in Alabama even if lawful in Tennessee. A Tennessee product that is lawful in Tennessee but is a smokable, vape, or converted-cannabinoid product, or that exceeds Alabama caps, must not be described as "legal hemp" for Alabama purposes.

10.3.6 Interstate laws, compacts, or agreements — NONE LOCATED

No Alabama interstate cannabis / hemp compact or agreement was found in searches on 2026-10-25. No Alabama–Florida, Alabama–Mississippi, Alabama–Georgia, or Alabama–Tennessee cannabis compact, reciprocity agreement, or hemp agreement was located. Supporting context: Alabama's own medical programme is by legislative design a "wholly intrastate system for the cultivation, processing, and distribution of medical cannabis" — Ala. Code §20-2A-2(10) (§20-2A-2 (via Justia)). A secondary reciprocity analysis likewise states that no serious interstate cannabis compact effort had emerged as of May 2026 and that the April 2026 Schedule III order "does not impose any cross-state recognition requirement" (secondary). State this as [UNAVAILABLE — none located in sources checked], listing AMCC, ADAI, ABC Board, Alabama Legislature, and AG opinions as checked as far as searched — not as a proven universal negative. Note the distinction: Alabama does participate in unrelated interstate compacts (e.g. professional-licence compacts under Title 34), but none for cannabis or hemp was located, and those unrelated compacts must not be cited as cannabis authority.

10.4 What can legally be brought into Alabama

ActorLawful to bring into AlabamaNOT lawful
Alabama patient / caregiverAlabama-dispensary product, Alabama-authorised form, within dose limitsFL, MS, GA, or TN product; any out-of-state product, however lawful where bought
Non-patientCompliant farm hemp; Chapter 12-compliant consumable hemp via ABC-licensed in-person retailAny marijuana; smokable hemp; over-cap or converted-cannabinoid products; DTC-shipped consumable hemp
Hemp businessThrough-shipment of subtitle-G-compliant hemp to a lawful destination elsewhere; Alabama retail only via ABC-licensed in-person channelDTC shipment of consumable hemp to Alabama consumers; sale of a product that fails Chapter 12 caps / testing / labelling

By an Alabama registered qualified patient or registered caregiver. Only medical cannabis in an Alabama-authorised form, purchased / acquired from an Alabama licensed dispensary (or integrated-facility dispensing site), within the 60-dose purchase / 70-dose possession limits and the physician's daily-dose limit. Florida medical cannabis, Mississippi medical cannabis (even if purchased on a Mississippi nonresident card), Georgia low-THC oil / SB 220 product, and Tennessee hemp products are not Alabama-dispensary product and therefore do not become lawful Alabama patient possession merely because they were lawful where purchased. Out-of-state cards, Georgia 45-day possession cards, and Mississippi nonresident cards confer no Alabama possession, purchase, or transport rights. A tribal-licensed product from another tribe's programme likewise confers no Alabama patient right: Alabama recognises only Alabama-dispensary product, and no Alabama–tribal cannabis agreement was located (see §10.3.6).

By a non-patient. No marijuana in any form, from any state, is lawful in Alabama. This includes Florida medical flower, Mississippi medical flower, Georgia oil, and any adult-use product from any state. Lawful hemp only: (a) farm hemp meeting Alabama's §2-8-381 definition (≤0.3% delta-9 dry weight; ADAI rule says total delta-9 — conflict flagged) and handled under an approved plan; and (b) consumable hemp products that independently satisfy Title 28, Chapter 12 (caps, testing, labelling, ABC-licensed in-person retail sale to a buyer 21+). A product that is "hemp" federally but is smokable, synthetically converted, or over Alabama caps is not lawful hemp for Alabama retail / possession purposes. A non-patient carrying a Georgia registration card, a Florida seasonal-resident card, or a Mississippi nonresident card has no Alabama possession right by virtue of any of those cards.

By a hemp business. Interstate commerce in hemp / hemp products through Alabama is protected by Farm Bill §10114 if the hemp was produced in accordance with AMA subtitle G (approved state / tribal plan or USDA licence) — see §10.3.1. Interstate shipment into Alabama for retail sale to Alabama consumers is a different act: consumable hemp products may not be shipped direct-to-consumer to Alabama addresses after 1 January 2026; lawful Alabama retail requires an ABC-licensed Alabama retailer and in-person sale. Business-to-business shipment into Alabama for further lawful Alabama processing / retail is [VERIFY] as a distinct question from DTC shipment (see §10.3.1). Tribal hemp: a tribal hemp plan, if approved by USDA, governs production on that tribe's territory under that plan. No Poarch tribal hemp plan was found (§10.1). A tribal hemp product from another tribe's approved plan does not automatically satisfy Alabama Chapter 12 for Alabama retail sale.

10.5 Federal Schedule III effect on tribal licences — [VERIFY], with the rule text now checked

The fixed federal baseline: state-licensed medical marijuana and FDA-approved products moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714). The rule text as published (govinfo) states the rule applies to marijuana "subject to a state-issued license to manufacture, distribute, and/or dispense marijuana or products containing marijuana for medical purposes ('state medical marijuana license')" and creates "an expedited review process under which applicants holding state medical marijuana licenses may submit their existing state credentials" (91 FR 22714). A full-text search of 91 FR 22714 for "tribal" returns only: a disposal reference to "all other applicable federal, state, local, and tribal laws"; the Executive Order 13175 statement that "This action does not have tribal implications warranting the [consultation requirements]"; and a federalism cost discussion mentioning tribal governments in the aggregate. The rule text contains no provision addressing tribal licences, no definition including tribal licences in "state medical marijuana license," and no tribal registration pathway. Secondary commentary on exactly this gap argues the omission may have been an oversight rather than an intentional exclusion, and asks "how will this exclusion from the Order impact Tribal cannabis programs moving forward?" (secondary law-firm analysis, not a DEA / DOJ statement). Therefore: [VERIFY] — do not state that tribal licences are, or are not, Schedule III licences under 91 FR 22714 until DEA / DOJ guidance or a rule amendment addresses tribal licences. The text as written says "state-issued," and a tribal licence is issued by a tribal government, not a state — but silence in the rule is not the same as an express exclusion, and the secondary "oversight" theory is unconfirmed. Related point, stated firmly: even if a tribal product were Schedule III federally, that would not by itself make it lawful in Alabama. Alabama law governs possession in Alabama outside Indian country, and Alabama recognises only Alabama-dispensary product for Alabama patients. Tribal Schedule III status, if established, would be a federal classification point, not an Alabama import right.

DOJ tribal marijuana policy history — Wilkinson memorandum rescinded, not current law (secondary corroboration; DOJ text still to be opened for primary confirmation). The 2014 Wilkinson Memorandum ("Policy Statement Regarding Marijuana Issues in Indian Country," 28 October 2014) extended Cole-memo-style enforcement discretion to Indian country. On 4 January 2018, Attorney General Sessions rescinded it along with the Cole memoranda, and the Sessions memorandum "does not replace the rescinded memoranda with any new guidance" (summaries of the Sessions memorandum listing the Wilkinson memorandum among the rescinded documents, e.g. Hobbs Straus General Memorandum 18-001). Do not cite the Wilkinson memorandum as current law. The DOJ memorandum text itself was not opened in this audit, so keep [VERIFY] against the DOJ text for primary confirmation. No post-2018 replacement tribal-cannabis guidance was located in this pass [VERIFY] if a post-2018 DOJ statement is needed].

PART 11 — OPERATIONS RULES

Given separately for (A) medical licensees and (B) hemp / hemp-derived businesses. All facts dated Accessed 2026-10-28 unless a source itself gives a different date. [VERIFY] = uncertain, conflicting, or not confirmed against an official text opened in this research. [UNAVAILABLE] = no rule / text located in this research; do not treat as "no rule exists". Secondary sources are labelled as such and must not be upgraded to official law.

A. MEDICAL LICENSEES

A.11.1 Testing

Governing chapter: Ala. Admin. Code ch. 538-X-10, Regulation of State Testing Laboratories (Chapter 538-X-10). Required tests — Rule 538-X-10-.04(6): tests must follow Commission minimum standards published on the Commission website, including: cannabinoid content and potency — total THC (THC + THCA), total CBD (CBD + CBDA), THC / CBD ratio if applicable, percent THC relative to original plant material (w / w); terpene profiles; heavy metals; chemical contamination such as residual solvents; microbials including pathogenic microbials; mycotoxins; residual pesticides (insecticides, fungicides, herbicides, growth inhibitors / regulators); residual solvents; and any other protocols in the current minimum standards / Appendix A to Chapter 538-X-10.

Pesticide rule — no numeric list in the rule text itself: no pesticide or growth regulator appearing on any Commission-maintained / published prohibited-pesticides list may be used in cultivation or production. For non-prohibited pesticides, the laboratory must analyse for residue and determine whether the product is "reasonably free" of residue. If a non-prohibited pesticide is detected above the level specified by the Commission, or a Commission-prohibited pesticide is detected in any positively verified amount, the pesticide residue analysis is failed and the product must be recalled. The numeric pesticide limits themselves were not captured — they sit in Commission minimum standards / Appendix A cross-references, not in the rule paragraph opened. [VERIFY] before quoting any numeric pesticide limit.

Appendix A numeric limits found (in-process medical cannabis and crude / resins as received): Moisture content: <15%; Potency and terpene analysis: no numeric limit stated in the extracted table; Foreign matter: none detected; Mycotoxins: <20 µg / kg total aflatoxins B1, B2, G1, G2 combined; <20 µg / kg ochratoxin A; Heavy metals: arsenic <2 ppm; cadmium <0.82 ppm; lead <1.2 ppm; mercury <0.4 ppm; Total yeast and mold: <10,000 CFU / g; Total Enterobacteriaceae: <1,000 CFU / g; Salmonella: none detected per gram; Pathogenic E. coli: none detected per gram; Aspergillus fumigatus, flavus, terreus, niger: none detected per gram; Total coliform: <1,000 CFU / g; Pesticide / herbicide / growth-regulator screening in the table refers back to Rule 538-X-10-.04 (see above).

Laboratory standards — Rules 538-X-10-.04(1)–(2), .05: Must adopt minimum good laboratory practices satisfying at least the OECD Series on Principles of Good Laboratory Practice (GLP) and Compliance Monitoring. Must become certified by an accreditation body, such as the American Association for Laboratory Accreditation, that certifies effective implementation of ISO standards, and agree to have accreditation inspections / reports made available to the Commission. Must be shown to have met and maintained ISO / IEC 17025, and must provide self-certification of operating to standards sufficient to meet ISO / IEC 17025 before commencing testing for licensees. Must follow, where applicable: the American Herbal Pharmacopoeia Cannabis Inflorescence monograph; American Herbal Products Association "Recommendations for Regulators — Cannabis Operations"; and AOAC International "Guidelines for Laboratories Performing Microbiological and Chemical Analyses of Food, Dietary Supplements, and Pharmaceuticals" (2015). Must use validated test methods (AOAC, FDA Bacteriological Analytical Manual, ISO, USP, USDA-FSIS Microbiology Laboratory Guidebook, or a Commission-approved equivalent / third-party validation; otherwise a laboratory-developed method only on demonstrated validity and Commission approval). Must retain / employ at least one scientific director with a relevant advanced degree in a medical or laboratory science from an accredited institution. If the scientific director leaves, the laboratory must not conduct testing until a new scientific director is appointed and the Commission inspects the laboratory.

Proficiency testing — Rule 538-X-10-.06: participation in the Commission proficiency programme is mandatory; samples analysed not less frequently than once each 12 months, using the same procedures, replicates, standards, analysts and equipment as product testing; the laboratory must authorise the proficiency provider to submit results to the Commission. Successful participation = positive identification of 80% of target analytes reported with quantitative results where applicable; any false positive or false negative is an unsatisfactory score. Unsuccessful participation may result in limitation, suspension, revocation, or non-renewal.

Sampling rules. A State Testing Laboratory may, without a Secure Transporter, collect a random sample at a cultivator, processor, dispensary, or integrated facility. The laboratory that performs the test must collect the samples itself. If a lot / batch was segregated into smaller batches, the laboratory must sample and test each batch. Cannabis sample: at least 10 grams and no more than 30 grams. Production-run medical cannabis sample: the lesser of 1% of total product weight or 10 units. All samples must be homogenised before testing. A cultivator or integrated facility must not submit cannabis (as opposed to medical cannabis) for testing unless it is destined for extraction and weighed within 2 hours after harvest. From homogenisation for sample testing through eventual packaging / sale, the source facility must segregate and withhold the entire lot / production run, except samples removed by the laboratory, in a secure, cool, dry location. At transport, the laboratory must use tamper-resistant products and record licensee / facility name, batch / lot / production-run number, and sample weight or quantity. Samples must be sealed in a locked tamper-evident container not accessible to the laboratory transporter during transit. A single employee may transport samples to / from a laboratory; those employees and vehicles are otherwise subject to Chapter 538-X-7 Secure Transporter rules. Seed-to-sale entries per sample must include at minimum: licensee identity; where / how obtained; size / count / weight; date / time obtained; transporter identity including personnel and vehicle; date / time of arrival at the laboratory; tag / lot / batch number and QR / digital-code information; storage conditions on arrival; date / time testing commenced and concluded; types of tests and amount of sample used per test; results; steps to be taken as a result; disposal / return steps; and, if returned, date / time of departure from the laboratory. Official test results are reported to the Commission and are dispositive for clearing batches for further production and ultimate patient use. A licensee must not sell or transfer sampled cannabis / medical cannabis until the laboratory clears it in writing. A licensee must not use more than one State Testing Laboratory for official testing of the same batch / sample, except as expressly provided in Rule 538-X-10-.08. A laboratory may subcontract testing only to another State Testing Laboratory, with direct laboratory-to-laboratory sample transfer. A laboratory must not test for patients or caregivers except at the Commission's request, and must not test for individuals / entities other than Alabama licensees, including out-of-state licensees. Laboratory applicants and any investors in a laboratory applicant are prohibited from having any interest in a cultivator, secure transporter, processor, dispensary, integrated facility, qualified recommending physician, or another State Testing Laboratory.

Failed tests, retesting, remediation, recalls. "Remediation" = methods by which cannabis / medical cannabis that failed an official test may be further processed to remove dangerous substances / contaminants or otherwise bring it within testing ranges. It includes formal remediation changing form / chemical makeup, and decontamination not changing form / makeup. It may be done at the failing licensee's facility or by another licensee at the failing licensee's request. A licensee may do its own tests and remediation before official testing. A licensee requesting a retest, challenge, or new testing after remediation bears all testing costs. If a sample fails the same official test on retesting, barring contrary retest / challenge results under the rule, the licensee must destroy and dispose of the entire batch from which the sample was taken and document destruction / disposal in the Statewide Seed-to-Sale Tracking System. Destroyed material must not be recognisable as cannabis / medical cannabis and must not be usable for any legal or illegal purpose. If a sample passes the same official test on retesting and tie-break testing by a separate State Testing Laboratory, the licensee need not destroy the batch; the laboratory clears it by certificate and a seed-to-sale notation. Licensees must maintain and review at least annually a written contamination and recall plan covering employee / public safety, notification of proper authorities, possible retesting / remediation, proper disposal, preservation of product, and reasonable efforts to maintain patient access. Dispensary applicants must provide a detailed recall plan covering: notification of the originating processor / integrated facility and others in the chain of custody; recall factors and potential retesting / remediation; responsible persons; notification protocols to other licensees and the Commission through seed-to-sale; return, remediation and approval as safe, or destruction; reporting to the Commission and other regulators; avoiding further contamination and preserving uncontaminated product; ensuring patient access; and investigation / protocol changes to avoid recurrence. State Testing Laboratory applicants must provide a detailed recall, return, and remediation plan covering failed-test notification, recall factors, liaison persons, seed-to-sale notification protocols, return / remediation / destruction, regulator reporting, contamination avoidance, patient-access preservation, investigation assistance, and licensee advisories. Processors' recall plans (Rule 538-X-6-.06, secondary extract of official rule) follow the same pattern: adverse-event notification, recall factors and retesting / remediation potential, responsible individuals, seed-to-sale notification to other licensees and the Commission, return / remediation (approved as safe) or destruction, regulator reporting, contamination avoidance, patient-access preservation, and investigation / protocol change.

State Testing Laboratory licensees. Green Health Laboratories, Foley — reported as awarded a State Testing Laboratory licence by unanimous AMCC vote on 17 June 2025, after presentation on 12 June 2025. AMCC had opened a one-month request window in February 2025; of five requests, only Green Health completed an application. The 30-day public-comment period closed 15 June 2025 with no public comments. Reported as the only medical cannabis testing lab in Alabama until AMCC reopens applications, with no statutory cap on testing licences. [VERIFY] all of the above against AMCC June 2025 minutes / testing summary PDF — no AMCC minutes or award document was opened in this audit. Certus Laboratories chose not to renew because of the annual fee and litigation uncertainty, according to AMCC Director John McMillan as reported by Alabama Reflector / Marijuana Moment (secondary). Green Health's own / secondary description calls it a fully licensed and ISO / IEC 17025:2017 accredited laboratory for cannabis and hemp testing. That accreditation claim is company / secondary material, not confirmed from an accreditation body or AMCC rule in this research — the rule requires ISO / IEC 17025 compliance and accreditation-body certification (above), but Green Health's individual certificate was not opened. [VERIFY]. A secondary Bama Buzz item described a $3.4 million Green Health facility on Section Avenue in Foley expected to begin operations in Q1 2025. That pre-award timeline is secondary and must not be presented as the licence date. Certus Laboratories expiry 29 December 2025 is retained from the Run 1 baseline; no new official confirmation was opened in this run.

A.11.2 Licence rules — medical

Governing chapter: Ala. Admin. Code ch. 538-X-4 (Chapter 538-X-4). Transfer / ownership change: Except on express written Commission permission in response to a written application, including a non-refundable application fee, given with no less than 60 days' notice before the proposed date, a licensee must not transfer, sell, lease, assign, merge, cede, gift, delegate, convert, or otherwise turn over its licence to another person / entity. Within any 36-month period, a licensee must not effect or allow owners to transfer, sell, lease, assign, merge, cede, gift, delegate, convert, or otherwise turn over more than 35% of its stock (voting or non-voting), ownership, or controlling interest without that permission. An attempt to avoid Commission approval under the rule and §20-2A-58 is grounds for peremptory suspension or revocation or other appropriate sanction. The Commission may require a licensee seeking transfer / ownership change to resubmit its licence application, including an additional application fee. If approved, before issuance of the transfer licence, the transferee must pay a transfer licence fee equal to one year's licence fee. Category chapters cross-reference Chapter 538-X-4 for transfer / change of ownership, e.g. processors under Rule 538-X-6-.21 and testing laboratories under Rule 538-X-10-.24 (rule numbers from Run 1; substantive transfer text is in Chapter 538-X-4 above). No general medical ownership cap beyond the one-category application rule and the 35% transfer rule above was confirmed in this research. [UNAVAILABLE] for any broader cap — do not invent one.

Material change and relocation. A material change includes: a change in licensee management, including any director, officer, or other person responsible for day-to-day operations, but not resulting in a change of ownership; a change in location of any facility used under the licence; or any other change that would render the applicant / licensee ineligible under Rule 538-X-3-.14 or other law. Licensees must seek prior approval for a material change, except where prior approval is not feasible because of death or circumstances beyond the licensee's control, in which case written notice must be given as soon as practicable and in no event more than 30 days after the material change. A relocation request must provide: current facility address and proposed relocation site; photographs from all sides of the proposed location, including aerial and street views; reasons for relocation; proof of authorisation to occupy the proposed facility; verification that the proposed site will comply with all local laws, the Act, and the rules; and a detailed explanation of expected impact on patients, the community, and the general public. Self-reporting is mandatory for "injury," "loss," or "material breach" of policies / procedures affirmed in the application or amendments; reports must be made promptly to the Commission and, as applicable, law enforcement, in no event more than 24 hours after occurrence or discovery.

Renewal — Rules 538-X-4-.10 and .12 (confirmed against official text). Renewal by filing an Application for Renewal of License (forms on the Commission website) and paying the appropriate application fee at the time of filing, or the Commission will not process the application. Applications must be filed not more than 60 days before licence expiration to ensure timely renewal, and are delinquent if not filed on or before the expiration date (r. 538-X-4-.10). Licences expire one year from issuance (Rule 538-X-4-.12(1)). A delinquent licensee may continue operating for not more than 60 days. A licensee filing an untimely renewal during those 60 days is assessed an application fee, a renewal licence fee, and a per-day penalty equal to 10 times the daily cost of the licence fee. If the licence is not renewed on or before 60 days after expiration, the licensee must cease operations pending renewal; the Commission is not responsible for loss from inability to operate beyond 60 days. If renewed after the 60th day, the licensee may then resume operations. An untimely renewal does not change the next expiration date; the licensee must file and pay one year from the date the previous year's licence expired. If a licensee fails to file on or before the 60th day after expiration, its licence is revoked, and it must pay a per-day penalty equal to 10 times the daily cost of the licence fee for each day it continued to operate. Reinstatement requires reapplying and competing for licensing like any other prospective licensee (r. 538-X-4-.12 (official); r. 538-X-4-.12 (Justia)).

Surrender — Rule 538-X-4-.21. At any time after issuance, a licensee may voluntarily surrender its licence and cease operations. If not subject to sanctions, it must give 60 days' notice of intent to surrender and cease operations; otherwise it must seek written Commission permission based on a demonstration of extraordinary circumstances. Failure to provide such notice subjects the licensee to a per-day penalty for noncompliance. Surrender does not excuse sanctions or other disciplinary action. A licensee intending to cease operations within 60 days prior to licence expiration must instead comply with the voluntary non-renewal provisions of Rule 538-X-4-.15 (r. 538-X-4-.21). Non-renewal (category cross-reference): Processor non-renewal is governed by Rule 538-X-4-.15 (Rule 538-X-6-.20). The substantive text of Rule 538-X-4-.15 was not opened in full in this research. [VERIFY] for its detail.

Revocation / discipline — Rule 538-X-4-.22. Suspension is a temporary restriction where the licensee is / will be ineligible to operate or where operation poses a risk to patients, caregivers, employees or the public. A notice of suspension may issue peremptorily before a full investigation where ongoing operation poses such a risk; a full investigation and determination should follow as soon as practicable and not more than 30 days from the peremptory notice. A suspension may not exceed one year, will in most cases include a penalty / fine, and may involve probation following suspension. Revocation is the most serious measure the Commission may impose on its own; it should not be imposed arbitrarily / capriciously, but only for grave misconduct in contradiction of §20-2A-57(a), usually only on repeated instances of serious misconduct, posing a serious risk of loss to property, injury, or death, or overtly intentional disregard of Commission authority, the Act, or the rules. In most instances revocation is not imposed until other discipline has been unsuccessful, after a fair opportunity to correct, and / or a clear pattern of misconduct is apparent. Civil penalties, restitution and damages may also apply, and the Commission may notify appropriate civil authorities (r. 538-X-4-.22). Temporary licences are cross-referenced to Rule 538-X-4-.20 (Run 1); substantive text not re-opened. [VERIFY].

Insurance / bonding — medical. Integrated-facility finance tests from Run 1 retained: $2,000,000 performance bond, at least $250,000 liquid assets, and financial ability to maintain operations for at least 2 years. No other general medical insurance minimum was located in Chapter 538-X-4 or the category chapters opened in this research. [UNAVAILABLE] — do not present a general liability-insurance minimum for medical licensees. Caution added by this audit: a dispensary application extract cites $2,000,000 liability and casualty insurance as required by §20-2A-53(a)(2) — that is an application attestation, not a confirmed general insurance minimum; [VERIFY] before generalising it. Secondary (not official) application-guide figures that must not be presented as confirmed: cultivation applicants at least $500,000 liquid assets; dispensary applicants at least $200,000; $50,000 non-refundable application fee per licence type. These conflict in detail with the integrated-facility figures above and were not confirmed on an AMCC page in this research. [VERIFY].

A.11.3 Cultivation — medical

Governing chapters: Ala. Admin. Code ch. 538-X-5 (amended, published 30 September 2024, effective 14 November 2024, for the construction rule) read with ADAI cultivation rules at ch. 80-14-1 (Chapter 538-X-5). Indoor / outdoor / greenhouse — resolved from official rule: All cannabis must be cultivated in an enclosed facility. Rule 538-X-5-.05(1)(a). "Enclosed Facility" (Chapter 538-X-1 definitions) = a fully floored, walled, roofed, locked and secured building, room, greenhouse, or warehouse facility for cultivating, storing, processing, or dispensing cannabis / medical cannabis, at which security is maintained and accessible only to persons employed / contracted by a licensee or given permission and providing state / federally issued photo identification (Chapter 538-X-1, revised 6/14/26). A greenhouse therefore qualifies only as an enclosed facility. No cultivation is allowed outdoors or directly in the ground. Rule 538-X-5-.05(1)(e). Cultivators must limit visibility of cannabis, in any form, from outside the perimeter barrier. Each cannabis plant or batch must be cultivated in an individual receptacle containing soil / growing media, to foster portability, limit cross-contamination, and facilitate monitoring. Containers may be for individual plants or batches as long as each plant is clearly identified and traceable. Canopy limit / plant-count cap: none confirmed. No medical canopy limit, plant-count cap, or per-facility plant number was found in Chapter 538-X-5 or in the searches of Chapter 80-14-1 in this research. Secondary web pages claiming 100, 150, 1,500, 5,000, or 12,500 plants are mutually contradictory and unreliable and must not be used. The control mechanism found instead is the grow plan (below). [UNAVAILABLE] for a numeric cap. Cultivar approval: cultivators may only cultivate cultivars approved by the Commission prior to acquisition of plant material. Cultivars cannot be derived from hemp / industrial hemp as defined by Rule 80-10-21-.02(19); they must be derived from cannabis plants with a high likelihood of producing medical cannabis. Grow plan: the cultivator / integrated facility must provide ADAI and AMCC with engineering plans / specifications for the entire cultivation facility, and an operations plan including a grow plan showing the number of cannabis plants and methods of cultivation intended. Plant numbers are therefore approved through the plan, not stated as a rule cap in the material opened.

Security and premises (cultivation). Strict access controls must protect areas where cannabis / medical cannabis is handled / stored, in a secured, locked room or vault. Records of all persons on the premises (employees, vendors, transporters, other licensees, others) must record name and ingress / egress date / time, plus reason for presence for non-employees, and be kept at least 2 years, longer on Commission / law-enforcement request. Audio / video surveillance records kept at least 60 days, longer on Commission / inspector / law-enforcement request. Recordings potentially reflecting actual / attempted diversion kept for the longer of 2 years or until resolution and apprehension / discipline / prosecution. Employees on duty must wear identification badges identifying them as employees. Visitors, vendors, other licensees, Commission members, inspection personnel must wear a visitor pass or "AMCC Official" pass at all times. Theft, diversion, or other loss reported to the Commission and law enforcement as early as practicable and not more than 24 hours from event / discovery. On request, a cultivator must make available its full security plan, including alarm systems, monitoring, alarm activity, camera-location maps and coverage, audio / video footage, surveillance-equipment maintenance logs, authorised-use lists, operation instructions, and other relevant security information. Cultivation facilities must be protected by a 24-hour monitored security alarm system. Video monitoring inside a cultivation facility must cover all entry / exit points and all areas where cannabis is present, with numbers, scope, and clarity sufficient to determine facial features at all times of day. Vehicle entry / exit cameras must be sufficient to record licence-plate information and vehicle descriptions.

Pesticides (cultivation). Cultivators must fully comply with all Alabama laws / rules on pesticide usage; the Commission or its representative / agent may perform pesticide testing on a random basis or if it has reason to believe a pesticide was applied in violation of the product label. See A.11.1 for the testing consequence (failure + recall). No Alabama medical-cannabis pesticide product list with numeric tolerances was located. [VERIFY].

A.11.4 Security and transport — medical

Governing chapter: Ala. Admin. Code ch. 538-X-7, as amended, published 30 April 2026, effective 14 June 2026 (Chapter 538-X-7 — pre-amendment PDF URL; amendment date from Run 1 research — confirm the amended text on the Commission site before quoting the 2026 amendment [VERIFY]). Vehicles, GPS, manifest, crew: Secure transport vehicles must be equipped with GPS tracking and monitored throughout transit by the transporter's security centre through Wi-Fi or hardwire networking technology. Before transport, secure transporters must enter route plans and manifests into the Statewide Seed-to-Sale Tracking System. A manifest is a document listing cargo and crew for review / use by state officials and licensee personnel. Before transport, the transporter must complete a Commission-approved manifest form and input it to seed-to-sale. Minimum manifest contents: driver, crewmember, and any other individuals onboard; destination name and address; weight and description of each individual package and total number of packages; date / time the shipment is placed into the transport vehicle; date / time accepted at the delivery destination; identity of the employee having custody and circumstances, duration, and disposition of any other person who had custody / control; and handling / storage instructions. The manifest must be signed. Secure transport vehicles must have no fewer than two personnel — a driver and one other — in the vehicle at all times when carrying cannabis / medical cannabis and either making more than a single stop or travelling more than 10 miles while carrying product. A single employee may transport cannabis / medical cannabis to / from a State Testing Laboratory. Secure transport vehicles must not be left unattended at any time when containing cannabis / medical cannabis; at least one employee must remain with the vehicle at all times. Only designated personnel may occupy a secure transport vehicle during transport; non-employee passengers are prohibited. Vehicles must adhere to the designated route at all times. If an alternate route is necessary, the driver must contact the security office and note the change on the route plan. All stops in transit for refuelling or otherwise must be documented, including reason, duration, location, and activities of employees exiting the vehicle. Route plans, manifests, transport logs, freight bills, bills of lading, FOB terms documents, maintenance / repair records, and insurance documentation must be kept, manually or electronically including in seed-to-sale, for at least 2 years, longer on Commission / law-enforcement request, and made available during inspections / official visits. Vehicle locks and alarm systems must be installed on all vehicles, including the storage area. Vehicle dashboard and storage-area audio / video recording devices must be installed and operational at all times in transit, self-recording and, where possible, viewable from and saved directly to the security centre, with lighting / resolution sufficient to readily identify persons. Fleet summaries must show make, model, VIN, licence-plate number, and specifications of all proposed secure-transport vehicles, including design / specification of storage areas. Transport personnel (drivers and other employees accompanying drivers) must annually complete and receive certification for at least 5 hours of training specifically tailored to driver safety and proper procedures for transporting cannabis / medical cannabis. This rule does not apply to a State Testing Laboratory transporting samples to / from the laboratory. Processor security plans (Rule 538-X-6-.06) likewise require: 24-hour alarm systems installed by experts in industry-standard commercial-grade alarm systems, fully operational, securing all entry points and perimeter windows, equipped with motion detectors and pressure switches, covering all areas where cannabis / medical cannabis products are delivered, received, handled, stored, prepared, processed, tested, packaged, labelled, or readied for transport; and reception areas / personnel adjacent to ingress / egress points with ready access to duress panic and holdup alarms (r. 538-X-6-.06). Dispensing-site security (Chapter 538-X-8, official: Chapter 538-X-8): a dispensing site is defined as a standalone building rather than a multiuse structure / strip mall / shared-parking facility that may attract public attention, and must not share space with another retail / professional business including a physician's office or another licensee; it must maintain an exclusive-use parking area for patients / caregivers designed for privacy on ingress / egress (or a designated, monitored portion if exclusive parking is not feasible) — and the parking paragraph also provides a designated-portion rule "to the extent that a dispensing site is housed in a multiuse structure, strip mall or other such retail facility," a tension that is preserved here rather than smoothed over; it must be at least 1,000 feet in a straight line, property line to property line at the nearest point, from any school, daycare, or childcare facility (K-12 school or licensed daycare / childcare actively operated within the last 6 months; a homeschool residence is excluded); and it may not operate in an unincorporated county area or municipality that has not adopted a resolution / ordinance authorising dispensing sites under §20-2A-51.

A.11.5 Waste disposal — medical

Every licensee must maintain at all times, and review at least annually, a Cannabis / Medical Cannabis Waste and Disposal Plan for tracking and proper disposal of waste cannabis / medical cannabis, including all parts thereof. The plan must, at a minimum, leave no part of the disposed / waste cannabis or medical cannabis either usable or recognisable as such. Failed-batch destruction (see A.11.1): after a failed retest, destroy / dispose of the entire batch, document in seed-to-sale, ensure it is not recognisable or usable for any legal / illegal purpose. Licensees must also maintain and review at least annually: an Emergency Procedures and Disaster Plan (employee / public safety, preservation of product, reasonable efforts to maintain patient access); an Alcohol, Smoke, and Drug-Free Workplace Policy and a Non-Discrimination Policy (in the Employee Handbook and / or Policies and Procedures Manual); an Employee Safety Plan complying with parallel OSHA standards to the extent extrapolable; and a Confidential Information and Cybersecurity Plan. General waste timelines, rendering methods beyond "not usable or recognisable," and any requirement for Commission or law-enforcement witnessing of routine (non-failed-batch) waste disposal were not located in the chapters opened. [UNAVAILABLE] — do not import another state's witnessing rule.

A.11.6 Environmental — medical

Water: no medical-cannabis-specific water-use, discharge, or irrigation rule was located in Chapters 538-X-4 / 5 / 6 / 8 / 10 or Chapter 80-14-1 extracts opened. [UNAVAILABLE]. Pesticides: see A.11.1 and A.11.3 — compliance with all Alabama pesticide laws / rules, Commission random / label-violation testing, prohibited-list ban, failure + recall consequence. No numeric tolerance list located. [VERIFY] for any numeric list. Energy: no medical-cannabis-specific energy-efficiency, lighting, or carbon rule was located. [UNAVAILABLE]. Processors must use documented good quality practices and meet current Good Manufacturing Practices; products must be shown to meet intended purity, be reliably free of toxins / contaminants (Appendix A to Chapter 10), contain no additives other than pharmaceutical-grade excipients, not be processed into a form attractive to / targeting children, and, for gelatinous cube / cuboid / lozenge products, conform to the Commission's universal flavour, which is peach (§20-2A-63(f)) — confirmed on the official rule text (r. 538-X-6-.04(2)(e), revised 6/14/26).

A.11.7 Sampling, giveaways, discounts and promotions — medical

Patient / caregiver sampling is prohibited: "No patient or caregiver shall provide or accept samples of medical cannabis." (Rule 538-X-2-.08(3), official: r. 538-X-2-.08 — confirmed in the official rule, not a proposal extract.) Patients / caregivers must purchase only from a certified dispensing site operated by a licensed dispensary / integrated facility; must store in a secure location preventing theft / loss / access by unauthorised persons; must carry their medical cannabis cards whenever in possession; and must keep medical cannabis in the original dispensing package with unaltered dispensary label, or in a dispensary / integrated-facility-provided storage container, until administered. At dispensing, the certified dispenser (or a dispensary employee under the dispenser's supervision) must enter into the patient registry and seed-to-sale, and attach to the package: patient name and card number; caregiver name / card number if applicable; registered certifying physician name / contact; amount / type dispensed; physician dosing comments and maximum daily dosage recommendation; and date / time dispensed. The dispenser may, at patient / caregiver request, give administration instructions, side-effect / drug-interaction education, or other aspects — but may not advise on safety / effectiveness, recommended daily dosage, or type recommended by the physician, except to direct the patient / caregiver back to the physician (r. 538-X-8-.03). No licensee discount, coupon, BOGO, loyalty, or giveaway rule specific to medical cannabis was located in Chapters 538-X-4 / 8 opened in this research, beyond the patient-sampling ban above and the Run 1 advertising bans. Third-party deal-listing pages (e.g. Weedmaps "Pell City deals") are not Alabama law and must not be cited as authorised promotions. [UNAVAILABLE] for a medical discount / giveaway permission — the safe statement is that patient sampling is banned and no discount rule was found.

A.11.8 Drug testing and background checks — medical licensees and staff

Registered Agents (all facility staff with access): Rule 538-X-4 — an agent seeking Registered Agent status must submit a completed agent registration application electronically through the AMCC Application & Licensing Portal plus the licensee's verification of association. The agent must, as required by §20-2A-59(a), submit to state and national criminal background checks performed respectively by ALEA and the FBI. The licensee must verify the agent has no disqualifying pending charge or conviction as provided in §20-2A-59(b). All Registered Agent records, including criminal background checks, must be maintained by the licensee and made available on request to the Commission, its employees, investigators, agents, or auditors. Registered Agent status expires one year from issuance and must be renewed on or before expiration. Owners / applicants — CORRECTED against §20-2A-59: Ala. Code §20-2A-59(b) provides that if a criminal background check of a prospective officer, employee, or contractor indicates a pending charge or conviction within the past five years for a controlled-substance-related felony or misdemeanor, the licensee may not appoint, hire, or contract with that person without written permission of the Commission (overturned-on-appeal convictions and Chapter 27-expunged charges excluded) (§20-2A-59 (2025)). It is therefore neither a 10-year absolute bar (Run 1) nor a felony-only bar (JD Supra secondary summary); both earlier wordings are superseded. A separate secondary claim — that a majority of ownership must be attributable to individuals with proof of Alabama residence for a continuous period of no less than 15 years preceding application — remains [VERIFY]: its statute section was not pinned in this audit. Commission investigations: during the licence term, the Commission, on information received or other reasonable cause / suspicion, may investigate any alleged violation by the licensee, its owners, officers, directors, interest holders, administration, management, or employees, through its employees, an independent third party, a state agency, or a combination. The fact of an investigation may or may not be disclosed while ongoing; results revelatory of concern must be made known to the licensee, who must be given an opportunity to respond if it has not already had one (r. 538-X-4-.03). Employee drug testing / drug-free workplace: licensees must maintain and review at least annually a clear written Alcohol, Smoke and Drug-Free Workplace Policy (see A.11.5). No rule was located requiring a medical licensee to drug-test its own staff as a licence condition (as opposed to the employer's general right to maintain a drug-testing / drug-free workplace programme). [UNAVAILABLE] for a licensee-staff drug-testing mandate. General employment (secondary, for context only): Alabama's Act does not require employers to permit marijuana use or accommodate medical use (including altering duties); does not require health coverage to pay for it; permits adverse action (refusal to hire, firing, discipline) regardless of on-the-job impairment; does not prohibit drug-testing or drug-free workplace / DOT programmes; permits requiring employees to notify the employer of cardholder status; does not alter workers'-compensation premium discounts or the right to deny benefits on a positive test; an employee discharged for medical cannabis use or refusal to submit to / cooperate with a drug test is conclusively presumed discharged for misconduct and disqualified from unemployment benefits; and the Act creates no lawsuit basis over an employer's adverse action for physician-prescribed marijuana use (secondary).

A.11.9 Research and university work — medical

Medical Cannabis Research Fund — §20-2A-10 (partially verified). The Medical Cannabis Commission Fund receives (1) tax proceeds under Section 2 of the adding act, less administration costs retained by the Department of Revenue; (2) licence fees, civil penalties, and other fees / charges under Article 4; and (3) legislative appropriations for initial Commission operation. Amounts are budgeted / allotted under §§41-4-80–41-4-96 and 41-19-1–41-19-12, not limited by the fiscal-year appropriation cap.
