Beginning 1 October 2025, any funds in the Medical Cannabis Commission Fund in excess of actual expenses from the previous fiscal year shall be distributed, less 10 percent, as follows: (1) 60 percent to the General Fund; (2) 30 percent to the Medical Cannabis Research Fund established pursuant to subsection (f) of Section 4. The remaining distribution percentage and the full subsection (f) text were truncated in the source opened and were not verified. [VERIFY] the balance of §20-2A-10(c) / (f) before quoting a complete split. Carly's Law / UAB study (historical, pre-Compassion Act; secondary). Carly's Law (SB 174, 2014, signed 1 April 2014, effective 1 June 2014), named for Carly Chandler of Birmingham, a 3-year-old with CDKL5-related uncontrollable seizures, funded a UAB Department of Neurology study of cannabidiol (CBD) oil for severe seizures with $1 million (Education Trust Fund in secondary accounts), contingent on DEA and FDA approval. UAB launched two studies (adult at UAB, paediatric at Children's of Alabama) authorised by the 2014 legislation; the design was to test safety / tolerability of CBD oil in intractable seizures, enrolling 100 subjects (50 adult, 50 paediatric), each application requiring referral from the patient's primary treating neurologist and review by a UAB neurology panel; all enrolled patients received CBD oil. A clinical-trials registry entry for the adult dose-finding study (NCT02700412) records actual enrolment 80, doses 5–25 mg / kg / day with titration to 50 mg / kg / day, status completed, and states its goal was to fulfil the mandate of "Carly's Law." Leni's Law (2016) subsequently expanded CBD-oil access beyond the UAB study on a physician's recommendation for debilitating conditions, with oil not to exceed 3% THC in secondary accounts — that 3% figure is secondary and must not be confused with the 0.3% hemp threshold. Auburn University, Alabama A&M, Tuskegee — medical cannabis research: no Alabama medical-cannabis (as opposed to hemp) university research programme, licence, or study specific to Auburn, Alabama A&M, or Tuskegee was located in this research. For hemp university licences, see B.11.9. Auburn appears in this research only as the affiliation of a veterinary pharmacology professor commenting on CBD (see Part 12 pets). [UNAVAILABLE] for a current medical-cannabis university research programme at those institutions. Physician certification guardrails relevant to research / patients (Chapter 540-X-25): a registered certifying physician must not certify / recommend unless both physician and patient are physically located in Alabama and any examination / visit / consultation occurs while both are in Alabama; must only evaluate / diagnose / certify qualifying conditions within their education / training / experience / specialty; must not certify a patient who is pregnant, breastfeeding, or attempting to conceive; must not certify a condition for which cannabis is contraindicated under the current standard of care or evidence-based research; and is strictly prohibited from using telemedicine for certification / recommendation or associated examinations (Chapter 540-X-25).

B. HEMP / HEMP-DERIVED BUSINESSES

B.11.1 Testing and labelling — consumable hemp

Governing chapters: Ala. Admin. Code ch. 20-X-33 (Licensure of Consumable Hemp Products; published 31 October 2025, effective 15 December 2025, operative 1 January 2026) and ch. 20-X-34 (Labelling, Promotions and Advertising) (Chapter 20-X-33 filing; Chapter 20-X-34 filing). Records and COAs: All records and receipts for consumable hemp purchases by a licensee, including certificates of analysis, must be retained for 3 years from purchase date, under §28-12-43. Records may be electronic if immediately transferable on ABC request, and all records, electronic or physical, on the premises must be immediately available on ABC request. No person licensed / permitted under the title may refuse entry to licensed premises, including locked areas, to ABC personnel or law enforcement, nor refuse an audit / inspection or fail to provide required records. No licensee, employee, or agent may consume consumable hemp products on licensed premises. No licensee, employee, or agent may have consumable hemp products on licensed premises that are not for sale. No licensee, employee, or agent may sell / provide consumable hemp products to a person who appears, considering the totality of the circumstances, to be under the influence of alcohol or any substance impairing mental / physical faculties.

Label registration — ABC Form LCD-55, January 2026 (Consumable Hemp Brand Label Registration Form) (ABC Form LCD-55, Jan 2026): The form requires checking that the label contains: ingredients in descending order of predominance; a scannable barcode or QR code linked to the certificate of analysis; batch number corresponding to the certificate of analysis; manufacture date and expiration date; total milligrams of THC in the container; serving size and total milligrams of THC per serving; warning: keep product out of reach of children; warning: consumption may cause a person to fail a drug test due to THC; warning: product is not safe nor intended for any person under 21; warning: product is not safe for any person who is pregnant or breastfeeding; warning: product may impair a person's ability to drive and operate machinery; each edible individually wrapped as a single serving; child-resistant packaging; no likeness or cartoon-like characters of a real / fictional person, animal, or fruit appealing to children; product not modelled after a brand primarily consumed by / marketed to children; no statement / artwork / design reasonably misleading a person to believe the package contains anything other than a consumable hemp product; no intoxicating substance other than cannabinoids; laboratory has no direct / indirect interest in the producer whose product is being tested; laboratory has no direct / indirect interest in a facility that cultivates, processes, distributes, or sells hemp / consumable hemp products in Alabama or another jurisdiction. The same form states: "The ABC Board does not certify that these products are safe for human consumption. The ABC Board is strictly reviewing imaging, marketing, and flavors to ensure compliance with state laws." Secondary Burr summary of HB 445 is consistent on the label list (ingredients, scannable barcode linked to COA, manufacture / expiration dates, batch number, total THC mg in container, serving size and mg per serving, consumer warnings) and describes a COA as a document issued by an independent testing laboratory providing chemical composition for a particular batch (secondary). Secondary Nothing But Canna summary states consumable hemp testing requires COAs from independent ISO 17025-accredited labs testing THC / CBD potency, terpenes, pesticides, heavy metals, solvents, mycotoxins, and microbials, and that COAs must match label claims exactly. That panel and ISO claim are secondary and remain [VERIFY] against the ABC rule and Title 28 Chapter 12 text — the ABC form opened requires laboratory independence (above) but does not, in the extract opened, state an ISO 17025 mandate or the full analyte panel.

Label approval (Chapter 20-X-34, secondary summary of official rule): manufacturers may seek pre-approval of product labels before selling / distributing in Alabama; applications include a completed form, a copy of the label, and a $50 fee; approved labels are listed on the ABC Board website. If a product is confiscated / removed by the ABC Board, the retailer or manufacturer listed on the label may appeal within 15 days of written notification under Chapter 20-X-3 procedures. The $50 fee and 15-day appeal are from a secondary summary of the official chapter — [VERIFY] against the full Chapter 20-X-34 text before quoting as official.

Promotions / advertising bans — Chapter 20-X-34-.01 (official filing): consumable hemp products must not advertise, market, or offer for sale, in labelling / design, packaging, or advertising / marketing materials, using: (a) Trade dress, trademarks, branding, or related imagery depicting / signifying characters / symbols known to appeal primarily to minors, including superheroes, comic book characters, video game characters, television show characters, movie characters, celebrities, mythical creatures, unicorns, or related imagery / scenery; (b) Trade dress / trademarks / branding imitating / replicating food brands or related products marketed to minors, including breakfast cereal, cookies, juice drinks, soft drinks, frozen drinks, ice cream, sorbets, sherbets, frozen pops; (c) Trade dress / trademarks / branding using the terms candy, candies, cake, cakes, cupcake, cupcakes, pie or pies, any variant, or any other term referencing a type / brand of these items; Plus, per secondary summary: no resemblance to school / office supplies (backpacks, pens, markers) and no depiction of personal items (phones, toys, cosmetics, clothing). Those two items are secondary-summary only — [VERIFY] against the full rule text. Whether a distinct ABC manufacturer / distributor licence exists and its fee: already flagged in Run 1 as [VERIFY] against Title 28 Chapter 12 full text. It remains open — the three licence types confirmed in Chapter 20-X-33 are retailer types (Specialty Retailer, Pharmacy, Retail Food Store), not a manufacturer / distributor licence. See B.11.2.

B.11.2 Hemp licence rules

ABC consumable hemp retailer licences — Chapter 20-X-33: Three separate and distinct licence types: (1) Specialty Retailer of Consumable Hemp Products License; (2) Pharmacy Consumable Hemp Products License; (3) Retail Food Store Consumable Hemp Products License. ABC Board confirms: effective 1 January 2026, consumable hemp products may only be sold in Alabama by ABC-licensed consumable hemp product retailers, per Title 28 Chapter 12; questions to consumablehemp@abc.alabama.gov (ABC Board — Hemp). Application requirements — Rule 20-X-33-.02 (official): every applicant, in addition to Title 28 requirements, must give the ABC Board: (a) an approval letter from the local governing body of the county / municipality where the facility will be located; (b) name, date of birth, place of birth, address, telephone number, driver's licence number, and Social Security number of every person with a 10% or greater proprietary / profit interest (except public corporations traded on a recognised stock exchange); (c) proof under §§28-12-40(d)(2) and 31-13-7 that every 10%+ interest holder (except public corporations) is lawfully present in the United States and otherwise qualified; (d) the true, correct, and complete criminal court record of all arrests and subsequent dispositions for the past 10 years for the applicant and any 10%+ interest holder, and for corporations / clubs / associations, each officer and / or board member — minor vehicular offences may be omitted, but DUI and reckless driving must be disclosed, with court name(s) and disposition; ABC may require additional information on offences over 10 years old as it deems necessary; (e) proof of a surety bond in the amount of $25,000, provided each year at renewal; (f) certification of correctness / truthfulness / completeness (individual applicant, or authorised corporate / club / association representative with authority); (g) consent, as a privilege of holding the licence, to allow ABC authorised personnel or commissioned state / county / municipal law enforcement to enter and search without a warrant the licensed premises or any building owned / occupied by the licensee in connection therewith, adjoining, adjacent to, or part of the curtilage, whether used as a private dwelling or not, at any time; (h) on request, evidence of primary source of funds, owned or borrowed, to be applied to establishment / acquisition of the business. Secondary summary adds proof of property ownership, lease, or use agreement for the location (r. 20-X-33-.02). Fees — CORRECTED: retailer fees are confirmed from primary statute §28-12-40 (see Part 7.3): $50 application fee and $1,000 annual licence fee, plus the $25,000 bond. The Part 11 [VERIFY] flag for retailer fees is superseded by Part 7.3 and is removed. Manufacturer / wholesaler $5,000 is confirmed from HB 445 engrossed text, but its current-Code section number remains [VERIFY]. Transfer, renewal timelines beyond annual bond proof, surrender, revocation, ownership caps, relocation, and hemp-specific insurance beyond the $25,000 bond: no ABC / Title 28 transfer, surrender, revocation, ownership-cap, or relocation rule was located in the chapters opened in this research. [UNAVAILABLE] — do not import the medical 35% / 60-day transfer rule into hemp. The only renewal point confirmed is annual re-proof of the $25,000 bond. Secondary summary notes false / incorrect / incomplete application information may result in denial, revocation, or disciplinary action, and that ABC may verify through interviews, community input, and background checks (valid if within 2 years) — secondary only, [VERIFY]. 2026 amendment note (secondary / official-enrolment extract, flag for audit): SB 287 (enrolled, 2026) amends §28-12-45 to authorise persons permitted as a specialty retailer of electronic nicotine delivery systems to obtain a consumable hemp product retailer licence, and makes nonsubstantive conforming revisions. The enrolled-bill extraction is garbled; the operative effect on ENDS retailers should be [VERIFY] against the enrolled Act text (Act 2026-504) before relying on it.

ADAI hemp grower / processor licences: see B.11.3 (agreement terms) and B.11.5 (destruction). Grower / handler and processor / handler licence applications for 2026 are listed on ADAI's programme overview page, with application windows noted as active 1 November 2027 for the next cycle in the page extract — that future-window wording is as extracted and should be [VERIFY] against the live ADAI page at republication, as it may reflect a rollover notice (ADAI Hemp Program Overview).

B.11.3 Hemp cultivation, plot registration, and pre-harvest sampling

ADAI Chapter 80-10-21. Grower Licensing Agreements, Rule 80-10-21-.06: an applicant is not a programme participant until the conditionally approved applicant and ADAI have executed a grower licensing agreement after the applicant's mandatory orientation session. Each licensed grower / producer is assigned a department licence number in the form prescribed by USDA (r. 80-10-21-.06). Grower agreement minimum terms include: growers act as agents of ADAI and must comply with instructions from ADAI and law-enforcement representatives; pay the licensing fee established by the rules; consent to entry and inspection of all premises where hemp or other cannabis plants / materials are or are licensed to be located, by ADAI and law-enforcement representatives, with or without cause and with or without advance notice; and consent to forfeiture and destruction, without compensation, of material with measured total delta-9-THC over 0.3% on a dry-weight basis, plants in an unlicensed area, and plants not accounted for in required reporting. Processor / handler agreements, Rule 80-10-21-.19: parallel terms — agent status, fee payment, inspection consent with or without cause or notice, and forfeiture / destruction without compensation for material over 0.3% total delta-9-THC, material in an unlicensed area, or material not accounted for in required reporting (r. 80-10-21-.19, Cornell mirror). Inspections and sampling, Rule 80-10-21-.09: all licensees are subject to sampling to verify THC does not exceed 0.3% on a dry-mass basis. During inspection, the licensee or authorised representative must be present at the growing area, research site, storage area, or other building facility, and must give the inspector complete and unrestricted access to all industrial hemp plants and seeds (growing or harvested), all land, buildings, and other structures used for cultivation and storage, and all documents / records for the hemp business. Samples of each variety may be sampled from the growing area, research site, storage area, or building facility at the Commissioner's discretion. Quantitative laboratory THC determination on a dry-mass basis is performed according to Commissioner-approved protocols. ADAI 2019 kick-off material (garbled extraction — re-verify before use): indicates growers must notify ADAI 14 days in advance to allow inspectors time to schedule sampling; a 14-day window to harvest after sampling; growers must not sell / move harvested material to a processor until after receiving a Release / Movement form and laboratory certificate of analysis from ADAI; ADAI must witness destruction; samples are taken of each plot and variety / strain; THC results may take up to 6 weeks, with ADAI trying to keep results within 5 days; the grower or knowledgeable representative must be present for inspections, site visits, and sampling; additional pre-harvest sampling fees are assessed per sample and variety, invoiced with 30 days to pay. Because the extraction is garbled, the 14-day notice and 14-day harvest-window points must be re-verified against a clean ADAI source before use. [VERIFY] (Note: Part 7.6, from cleaner ADAI procedure documents, states a 30-day harvest window beginning the day ADAI samples — the 14-day vs 30-day window is itself a conflict to resolve; do not quote either as settled without a current ADAI protocol.) USDA final-rule context (federal-plan context, not Alabama-specific confirmation): sample collection up to 30 days before anticipated harvest (extended from 15 days in the interim rule); sampling must demonstrate with 95% confidence that no more than 1% of plants in the lot would exceed the acceptable hemp THC level; laboratories must report measurement uncertainty; if the test-result range including measurement uncertainty includes 0.3% or less, the sample is considered hemp — e.g. reported 0.35% with ±0.06% uncertainty gives 0.29%–0.41% and is compliant, while 0.35% with ±0.02% gives 0.33%–0.37% and is not compliant. Whether Alabama's ADAI plan implements the 30-day window and measurement-uncertainty rule in exactly this form was not confirmed on an ADAI page in this research. [VERIFY]. DEA-registered lab delay: USDA enforcement of DEA-registered lab testing for hemp is delayed to 31 December 2026 under the fixed federal baseline given in the original commission, confirmed on the USDA AMS hemp page (USDA AMS — Hemp Production: "delaying until December 31, 2026, the enforcement of a requirement that all hemp must be tested by a Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA)-registered laboratory"). Whether Alabama has separately confirmed that delay through ADAI plan implementation remains [VERIFY]. Plot registration detail beyond the agreement / inspection rules above: no separate ADAI plot-registration form, GPS-coordinate, or lot-number rule text was opened in this research. [UNAVAILABLE] for plot-registration mechanics beyond "plants in an unlicensed area" forfeiture and the inspection-access rules above.

B.11.4 Security, storage, and transport — hemp

Consumable hemp retail premises (Chapter 20-X-33-.03, official + secondary detail). Specialty Retailer: per secondary summary of the official rule — may sell all consumable hemp products; must either hold a Lounge Retail Liquor (Class II) licence or sell only hemp products; must restrict access to individuals 21+ including employees; must post a visible 8½" × 11" sign stating "It is illegal for anyone under 21 years of age to enter this licensed location"; sales for off-premises consumption only; must maintain at least 500 sq. ft. of customer-accessible sales / service area (excluding storage / offices). The 500 sq. ft. and sign-wording details are secondary-summary — [VERIFY] against the full Rule 20-X-33-.03 text. Retail Food Store: may sell consumable hemp beverages only; must place all beverages behind glass or clear plastic / acrylic material similar in function to glass, in an area dedicated only to consumable hemp beverages; beverages must not be visible from an area containing products intended for children, and must be locked, requiring an employee to obtain them for the consumer. The beverage-area sign must be 8½ × 11 inches, font no smaller than 2 inches, stating: "These products contain hemp derived compounds. Must be 21 years of age or older to purchase." A licensee certified in the Responsible Vendor Program may employ a person under 21 to obtain hemp beverages from the locked area and sell them under supervision of a person 21 or over. Note a conflicting secondary account: a December 2025 LexBlog summary states ABC modified the rule to allow unlocked plexiglass without employee assistance, in a self-service manner like beer, while keeping 21+ restriction. That conflicts with the locked / employee-retrieved text in the official filing extract. [VERIFY] — the final report must state which version is operative and not present both as current. Pharmacy: limited to topical / sublingual products (Run 1 baseline; confirmed in secondary LexBlog summary: "hemp dispensaries may sell all forms… retail grocers may only sell beverages… pharmacies are limited to topical or sublingual"). [VERIFY] against §28-12-45 full text for the pharmacy scope. No vending machines, tastings, or self-service (secondary Nothing But Canna summary) — [VERIFY] against Chapter 20-X-33 full text; the self-service point is directly in tension with the LexBlog unlocked-plexiglass account above. Sales must be reported monthly to the state (secondary Nothing But Canna) — [VERIFY].

ADAI grower / processor storage and transport. No ADAI hemp storage-security (camera / alarm) rule, no hemp transport manifest / GPS rule, and no hemp secure-transporter licence equivalent to the medical Chapter 538-X-7 regime was located. The controls found are inspection consent (with / without cause / notice), unrestricted inspector access, and the post-sample movement ban (see B.11.5). [UNAVAILABLE] for hemp-specific security-camera, alarm, storage, and transport rules — do not import medical transport rules into hemp. General retail controls (official): no refusal of entry to licensed premises including locked areas; no consumption on premises; no non-for-sale product on premises; no sale to a person appearing impaired (see B.11.1). Records / COAs retained 3 years, immediately available.

B.11.5 Hemp waste and non-compliant plant destruction

ADAI destruction rule (Chapter 80-10-21). Cannabis plants found in violation of the Act or Chapter 80-10-21 must be destroyed in accordance with a departmental directive or destruction order. Destruction must be performed in accordance with a Commissioner directive, which may include destruction by any means necessary and reasonable to ensure all plants exceeding allowable THC limits are destroyed, e.g. removal and incineration, field burning, deep burial, or other ADAI-authorised means. After ADAI obtains a sample, licensees must not move any cannabis plant or plant product from the area represented by the sample until ADAI determines it tests no higher than 0.3% THC on a dry-mass basis. The Commissioner must furnish the licensee a portion of the violative sample if the licensee requests it within 30 days of notification. Inspection fees in the same rule extract: $250 per inspection for each growing area, research site, storage area, or building facility. Administrative appeal: a licensee aggrieved by an order under the chapter may submit a written hearing request within 15 days of the destruction order being issued. If no petition is filed within 15 days, the order becomes final and is not subject to review. The pilot-programme sentence treating hemp plants as department property for hearing purposes appears in the older rule extract and must be checked against the current rule before use. [VERIFY]. Grower / processor agreement forfeiture (see B.11.3): forfeiture and destruction without compensation for material over 0.3% total delta-9-THC, plants in an unlicensed area, and plants not accounted for in required reporting. USDA final-rule disposal context (federal, not Alabama-confirmed procedure): plants testing above 0.3% but below 1% are not a negligent violation but still need disposal or remediation; negligent-violation threshold raised from 0.5% to 1%, with a maximum of one negligent violation per growing season / calendar year in secondary summaries; disposal / remediation options include plowing under, composting into green manure for use on the same land, tilling, disking, burial, or burning; producers bear associated costs. These USDA points are federal-plan context, not confirmed as Alabama-specific ADAI procedures except for the ADAI destruction methods above. "Render unusable" for hemp: no Alabama rule text was located stating a hemp-specific "render unusable / unrecognisable" method equivalent to the medical waste-plan standard, and no DEA notification rule for hemp destruction was located. [UNAVAILABLE] — the medical "not usable or recognisable" standard must not be copied into hemp. Consumable hemp product waste, failed-COA product disposition, and ABC seizure / destruction procedures: not located in Chapters 20-X-33 / 34 extracts opened. [UNAVAILABLE]. Beyond the label-appeal rule (15 days, Chapter 20-X-3 procedures, secondary) and the ban on non-for-sale product on premises, no ABC destruction timeline was found.

B.11.6 Environmental — hemp

No hemp-specific Alabama water-use, pesticide, or energy rule was located in Chapter 80-10-21 extracts or Chapter 20-X-33 / 34 extracts opened, beyond the general requirement to comply with Alabama pesticide laws (medical rule, not hemp) and the COA pesticide-panel claim (secondary, [VERIFY] in B.11.1). [UNAVAILABLE] for hemp water / pesticide / energy rules — do not state "none exist," only that none were located.

B.11.7 Sampling, giveaways, discounts and promotions — hemp

Promotions / advertising bans: see B.11.1, Chapter 20-X-34-.01 (child-appealing imagery, child-marketed food-brand imitation, candy / cake / cupcake / pie terms; secondary additions: school / office-supply resemblance, personal-item depiction). Sampling / giveaways / discounts: no ABC rule was located expressly permitting or banning free samples, tastings, coupons, or discounts for consumable hemp products, except: (a) no consumption of consumable hemp products on licensed premises by licensee / employee / agent; (b) no non-for-sale product on licensed premises — which together strongly constrain on-premises sampling, but do not by themselves state an off-premises giveaway rule; and (c) secondary summary stating no vending machines, tastings, or self-service. [VERIFY] / [UNAVAILABLE] for a free-sample / discount rule — do not state that hemp discounts are banned or permitted on this record. Sales to impaired persons banned (see B.11.1) — this is a promotion-adjacent sales restriction, not a discount rule.

B.11.8 Drug testing and background checks — hemp

ABC retailers (official, Rule 20-X-33-.02): 10-year criminal court record (arrests + dispositions) for the applicant and every 10%+ interest holder, and for corporations / clubs / associations each officer / board member; minor vehicular offences may be omitted, DUI and reckless driving must be disclosed; ABC may require information on offences over 10 years old as it deems necessary; proof of lawful U.S. presence for 10%+ holders; local governing-body approval letter. Fingerprinting — CORRECTED: fingerprinting is not stated in the Rule 20-X-33-.02 extract opened, but Part 7.3, from §28-12-40 primary text, confirms two fingerprint sets for retailer applicants — the Part 11 flag is superseded by Part 7.3 for retailers, and the fingerprinting requirement is adopted as confirmed for retailers. ADAI growers / processors: no separate ADAI hemp background-check or drug-testing rule text was opened in this research beyond the licensing-agreement terms (agent status, inspection consent, forfeiture). [UNAVAILABLE] for an ADAI hemp staff background-check / drug-testing mandate. General hemp-employee drug testing: no hemp-specific employee drug-testing mandate was located. [UNAVAILABLE].

B.11.9 Research and university work — hemp

ADAI university licences — current programme: ADAI's Hemp Program overview lists a 2026 Hemp University License Application (with the next application window noted as active 1 November 2027 in the page extract — [VERIFY] at republication) (ADAI Hemp Program Overview). University affiliation rule — Rule 80-10-21-.25: an authorised representative of an eligible institution of higher education with faculty / administration / staff wishing to conduct academic research projects involving hemp under the department's programme must complete and submit a University / College Affiliation Application annually. An institution must not authorise faculty / administration / staff or any sponsored student to conduct academic hemp research without first completing / submitting that application. The department accepts annual applications at any time during a programme year. On request, a letter from a faculty department chair or other appropriate academic authority must be submitted in support. Following receipt, the department issues a university / college affiliation confirmation letter to grow, cultivate, and process hemp in accordance with: (a) the institution's research plan; (b) state and federal law; and (c) the regulation (r. 80-10-21-.25). 2019 pilot universities (historical, not current licence proof): ADAI licensed 157 growers, 59 processors (per Alabama Farmers Federation account: 59 licensed to process through the Industrial Hemp Research Pilot Program), and five universities to research hemp: Alabama A&M University, Alabama State University, Troy University, Tuskegee University, and the University of Alabama. A separate Journal of Blacks in Higher Education account names the same five (three HBCUs: Tuskegee, Alabama State, Alabama A&M, plus Troy and UA). Tuskegee's work (Dr. Desmond Mortley, College of Agriculture, Environment, and Nutrition Sciences) focused on best varieties / techniques, planting dates, varieties, adaptability, productivity, days to maturity, and proportions of CBD oil vs fibre; in June (2019) the team planted more than 900 "Cherry Wine" female plants in greenhouses / growth chambers for 75 days before harvest / examination. Alabama A&M's work (Research Associate Professor Ernst Cebert, Winfred Thomas Agricultural Research Station, "The Farm," 972 acres) covered industrial, CBD, and medical cannabis topics in field-day presentations, with interests including organic production, CO2 monitoring, soil physics, soil health, and forestry, and potential applications in homes, clothes, and oil extraction. Auburn University: Auburn does not appear in the 2019 five-university list above. No current ADAI university hemp licence for Auburn was located in this research. [UNAVAILABLE] — do not list Auburn as a licensed hemp university on this record. Auburn does appear in hemp-adjacent research: Tuskegee's hempseed-meal goat-feed project (USDA-NIFA) notes Tuskegee is among five Alabama universities licensed to grow / study industrial hemp, with the goal of feeding trials to support AAFCO / USDA / FDA approval of hempseed meal as a novel feed — hempseed meal has not been approved for use as animal feed by USDA / FDA / CVM to date in that project summary. Medical cannabis research fund: see A.11.9 (§20-2A-10). No separate hemp research fund was located. [UNAVAILABLE].

PART 12 — CONSUMER AND SOCIAL

12.1 Paraphernalia and smoke / vape shops

Ala. Code §13A-12-260 (2025 Justia text) (§13A-12-260 via Justia — mirror; re-check on the Legislature's official Code viewer at republication): Use, or possession with intent to use, drug paraphernalia to plant, propagate, cultivate, grow, harvest, compound, convert, produce, process, prepare, test, analyse, pack, repack, store, contain, conceal, inject, ingest, inhale, or otherwise introduce a controlled substance into the body in violation of Alabama controlled-substances law is a Class A misdemeanor. Delivery / sale, or possession with intent to deliver / sell, or manufacture with intent to deliver / sell, drug paraphernalia to manufacture a controlled substance in violation of Alabama law is a Class C felony; if the person is in possession of a firearm at the time, it is a Class B felony. Delivery / sale of drug paraphernalia knowing it will be used for a controlled-substance violation is generally a Class A misdemeanor; a subsequent violation is a Class C felony. Delivery by a person 18 or older to a person under 18 who is at least three years younger is a Class B felony. All drug paraphernalia used in violation of the section is contraband and subject to Alabama forfeiture law, including §20-2-93. Factors for determining whether an object is drug paraphernalia include: owner / control-person statements; prior controlled-substance convictions; proximity in time / space to a direct violation or controlled substance; residue; instructions (oral / written); descriptive materials explaining / depicting use; national / local advertising; manner of display for sale; whether the owner is a legitimate supplier of like / related items, such as a licensed tobacco distributor / dealer; ratio of object sales to total business sales; legitimate uses in the community; and expert testimony. Fentanyl-testing-equipment exception — RESOLVED: §13A-12-260(f), as amended by Act 2022-154 (SB 168), effective 1 June 2022, provides that "a person may possess, deliver, or sell testing equipment designed to detect the presence of fentanyl or any synthetic controlled substance fentanyl analogue." The subsection letter is (f); the original's [VERIFY] on the letter is removed. No Alabama-specific smoke / vape-shop licensing statute separate from the general paraphernalia law and the ABC consumable-hemp licensing regime was located. Local hemp-shop ordinances from Run 1 were not re-researched in this run. A 2026 enrolled bill (SB 287) authorising ENDS specialty retailers to obtain a consumable hemp retailer licence (see B.11.2) is the only vape-shop / hemp-shop crossover found, and its operative text is [VERIFY]. Expungement note for paraphernalia (secondary, see 12.4): a standard (non-violent, non-sex, non-moral-turpitude) misdemeanor paraphernalia conviction is described in secondary law-firm material as expungeable after 3 years with all probation / parole / fines / costs / restitution completed, filed in the circuit court of the county of conviction; felony paraphernalia convictions have a much narrower path. [VERIFY] against §§15-27-1(b) / 15-27-2.

12.2 Minimum age for hemp-derived THC products

Confirmed: 21+ to purchase consumable hemp products. ABC materials (see B.11.1 / B.11.4): specialty retailers are 21+-only premises; retail food store beverages require the 8½ × 11-inch, ≥2-inch-font 21+ sign and locked, employee-retrieved storage (subject to the LexBlog unlocked-plexiglass conflict flagged in B.11.4 — the age itself is not in conflict, only the storage mechanism). Pharmacy / grocery exceptions (scope, not age, exceptions): pharmacies limited to topical / sublingual products; qualifying retail food stores may sell beverages only; specialty retailers may sell all consumable hemp products. The purchaser age remains 21+ in all three types. No pharmacy / grocery age exception below 21 was found. Employee-age distinction (do not confuse with purchaser age): a Responsible Vendor Program-certified licensee may employ a person under 21 to obtain hemp beverages from the locked area and sell them under supervision of a person 21 or over (Rule 20-X-33-.03). That is an employment exception, not a purchaser exception. Non-consumable CBD sold outside Title 28 Chapter 12: whether a non-consumable CBD product (e.g. non-ingestible, non-topical hemp product outside the consumable-hemp definition) has a different age rule was not confirmed. [VERIFY]. Secondary LegalClarity summary is consistent: as of 1 January 2026, a person must be at least 21 to buy any consumable hemp product in Alabama, sold only by ABC-licensed retailers; the gas-station / vape-shop no-age-verification era is over (secondary).

12.3 Driving, THC limits, and impairment testing

Ala. Code §32-5A-191 (2025 Justia text) (§32-5A-191 via Justia): A person must not drive or be in actual physical control of a vehicle while: there is 0.08% or more alcohol by weight in blood; under the influence of alcohol; under the influence of a controlled substance to a degree rendering the person incapable of safely driving; under the combined influence of alcohol and a controlled substance to that degree; or under the influence of any substance impairing mental / physical faculties to that degree. Under-21 alcohol threshold: 0.02% or more alcohol by weight. No per se numeric THC limit appears in the current §32-5A-191 text found. A secondary Marijuana Herald table updated 15 September 2026 likewise lists Alabama as impairment-based with no specific THC concentration establishing a marijuana DUI (secondary). A 5 ng/mL proposal — CORRECTED citation: a proposal to add a "greater than five nanograms Delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) per milliliter of blood" prong to §32-5A-191 is documented as SB 255 (2016) (SB 255, 2016, Alison), not SB 180 (2017) as stated in the original. That was a proposal only and must not be cited as current law; [VERIFY] whether a separate SB 180 (2017) proposal also existed before citing SB 180. Drug Recognition Expert (DRE) / impairment testing: secondary LegalClarity material states Alabama uses an impairment-based standard, prosecutors must show cannabis actually impaired driving ability, and law enforcement relies on field sobriety tests and DRE evaluations. No Alabama statute or ALEA rule text establishing a DRE programme or a THC blood / urine testing protocol for DUI was opened in this research. [VERIFY] for any ALEA DRE protocol before stating it as official procedure. Medical-patient driving rules: a patient must not operate a motor vehicle, watercraft, heavy machinery, or aircraft while under the influence of medical cannabis. Rule 538-X-2-.08(12) repeats this for patients (r. 538-X-2-.08). Possession / use in a vehicle is permitted only if the medical cannabis is in its original package, sealed, and reasonably inaccessible while the vehicle is moving (see 12.6). Above-75 mg terminal-illness dose — driver's licence suspension mechanism: still [VERIFY]. The physician must notify the patient that the patient's driver's licence will be suspended. Which agency acts, whether automatic or court-ordered, and what triggers it were not resolved in this research. Do not state a mechanism. Old automatic suspension history (secondary, [VERIFY]): secondary law-firm material states the old §13A-12-291 automatic licence suspension for marijuana possession, first or second degree, was removed effective 30 January 2016, leaving DUI-related suspensions governed by §32-5A-191. That history was not verified against current §13A-12-291 text in this research.

12.4 Expungement and record clearing

Ala. Code §15-27-1 (2025 Justia text) — non-conviction misdemeanor / violation records (§15-27-1 via Justia): For a misdemeanor offence, violation, traffic violation, or municipal ordinance violation, a person charged may petition the criminal division of the circuit court in the county where charges were filed to expunge records where: Charge dismissed with prejudice and more than 90 days have passed; Charge no-billed by a grand jury and more than 90 days have passed; Person found not guilty and more than 90 days have passed; Charge nolle prossed without conditions, more than 90 days have passed, and charges have not been refiled; Indictment quashed and the statute of limitations for refiling has expired, or the prosecuting agency confirms charges will not be refiled; Charge dismissed after successful completion of a drug court, mental health court, diversion, veterans court, or other court-approved deferred prosecution programme; petition may be filed one year from successful completion; expungement may also be a court-ordered condition of such a programme; Charge dismissed without prejudice more than one year ago, not refiled, and the person has not been convicted of any other felony or misdemeanor crime, violation, or traffic violation, excluding minor traffic violations, during the previous two years. Secondary Collateral Consequences Resource Center material adds: for charges dismissed without prejudice, the waiting period is one year for misdemeanors (reduced from two years in 2021) and five years for felonies, if during the waiting period the person has not been convicted of any other felony, misdemeanor, violation, or traffic violation, excluding minor traffic violations (secondary).

Conviction expungement — substantially corroborated by secondary sources, pinpoint official text still [VERIFY]. Until 2021, Alabama courts had no statutory authority to expunge / seal adult conviction records except a narrow human-trafficking exception. The REDEEMER Act, Act No. 2021-286 (SB 117), first authorised expungement of non-violent misdemeanors and violations, and pardoned felonies (§§15-27-1(b), 15-27-2(c)(1)). Only two misdemeanor convictions / violations may be expunged, and only one pardoned felony conviction (§15-27-2.1). In 2024, juvenile adjudications were added (SB 153) under §15-27-1(b), subject to all other aspects of law. Eligible misdemeanors / violations may be applied for three years after conviction if "all probation or parole requirements have been completed, including payment of all fines, costs, restitution, and other court-ordered amounts, and are evidenced by the applicable court or agency" (§15-27-1(b)). Felonies that have been pardoned are eligible 180 days after the pardon (§15-27-2(c)). Secondary law-firm examples of qualifying misdemeanor convictions expressly include low-level drug offences (excluding trafficking), such as unlawful possession of a controlled substance, unlawful possession of marijuana (1st or 2nd degree), and unlawful possession of drug paraphernalia; plus low-level property offences and low-level violations / traffic / municipal offences such as public intoxication. Exclusions: violent and / or sex offences, serious traffic offences, and crimes of moral turpitude. The pinpoint official text (§§15-27-1(b), 15-27-2, 15-27-2.1) was not opened as official text in this research — keep the pinpoint as [VERIFY], and do not present the secondary examples as a statutory list. Fees and procedure — RESOLVED as to the fee figure: Ala. Code §15-27-4(a) (2024 Code text) provides: "In addition to any cost of court or docket fee for filing the petition in circuit court, an administrative filing fee of five hundred dollars ($500) shall be paid at the time the petition is filed and is a condition precedent to any ruling of the court pursuant to this chapter," distributed $75 to the State Judicial Administrative Fund, $25 to the Alabama Department of Forensic Sciences, $50 to the district attorney's office, $50 to the circuit court clerk, $50 to the Public Safety Fund, $50 to the general fund of the county where the arresting law enforcement agency is located (or the funding municipality/entity/agency), $100 to the state General Fund, $50 to the Education Trust Fund, and $50 to the Fair Trial Tax Fund; §15-27-4(b) requires one fee for multiple charges arising from one arrest and a fee for each arrest where multiple arrests are involved (§15-27-4 (2024)). The $300 figure is the superseded 2014 version of §15-27-4 and is removed as a current figure everywhere. Indigency: §15-27-4(c) provides an Affidavit of Substantial Hardship route; the National Reentry Resource Center states a petitioner may apply for indigent status and, if the court finds the petitioner indigent, the court shall waive the filing fee — [VERIFY] the current §15-27-4(c) wording on the official Code viewer, as the same NRRC page also labels the fee "non-waivable" in apparent tension with its own waiver sentence. If the prosecutor or victim objects, a hearing must be held; without objection, the court grants the petition if reasonably satisfied the petitioner complied with the chapter. The court has discretion over the number of cases that may be expunged after the first case, §15-27-5(c) (secondary). No expungement order may issue until outstanding restitution or fines are paid, absent a finding of indigency, §15-27-12 (secondary). Effect — §§15-27-6 and 15-27-7 (secondary summaries): proceedings are deemed never to have occurred; courts / agencies reply that no record exists. The petitioner need not disclose the record on employment, credit, or other applications, but must disclose it to any government regulatory / licensing agency, any utility and its agents / affiliates, or any bank / financial institution, which may inspect the expunged record after filing notice with the court. Expunged records are not transmitted to the FBI, and the state criminal justice information centre requests withdrawal of records previously transmitted to the FBI and later expunged. Unauthorised, intentional, and malicious release of expunged records is a Class B misdemeanor, §15-27-16 (secondary). No general automatic marijuana expungement was found. Secondary LegalClarity material states a felony dismissed after successful drug-court or other court-approved diversion becomes eligible one year after programme completion, while a felony conviction through conventional sentencing is far more limited. SB 285 (2026), which would have decriminalised up to 1 ounce and created an expungement-petition mechanism after 5 years without further conviction, is dead from Run 1 and creates no current expungement right (re-check on Alison at republication).

12.5 Guns — Alabama state law vs federal law (kept separate)

Alabama state law. Secondary alabamacannabis.org material states the Alabama Medical Cannabis Act is silent about gun ownership by cannabis patients and, as of 2025, there were no state-level laws on firearm possession / ownership by medical marijuana patients. That remains secondary and [VERIFY] against a current Alabama firearms-code search — no Alabama firearms statute mentioning medical cannabis patients was located in this research. General Alabama firearms framework (secondary summaries, not patient-specific): no state permit required to purchase (long guns or handguns); no firearm registration; no assault-weapon law; no magazine-capacity restriction; no owner licence required; permitless concealed carry for residents 18+ took effect 1 January 2023 (HB 272, approved 10 March 2022); open carry without a permit (handgun must be secured in a holster); Alabama is "shall issue" for carry permits (§13A-11-75, sheriff of county of residence, minimum age 19, or 18 for service members / veterans); state preemption of local firearms regulation (§13A-11-61.3) (secondary). State pistol prohibitions that are not patient-specific but are relevant context (secondary NRA-ILA summary): a handgun-specific prohibition bars anyone who is a "habitual drunkard" or has a drug addiction from owning / possessing / having control of a pistol (§13A-11-72(b)(1)); "unsound mind" (§13A-11-72(h)) generally requires involuntary commitment or similar adjudication. Whether "drug addiction" in §13A-11-72(b)(1) has ever been applied to a medical cannabis patient was not located. [VERIFY] — do not state that it does or does not apply to patients. Permitless carry is limited to persons not prohibited by state or federal law from possessing a firearm (§§13A-11-74.1, 13A-11-85(a)) — so the federal prohibition below, if it applies to a given person, also limits the state permitless-carry privilege on its own terms (secondary summary).

Federal law (NOT Alabama law — flag separately). 18 U.S.C. §922(g)(3) prohibits possession of firearms / ammunition by a person who is an unlawful user of or addicted to any controlled substance. ATF's 2011 open letter to federal firearms licensees stated that possession of a state-issued medical cannabis card is reasonable cause to believe the person is an unlawful drug user; the letter's existence and dealer-sale effect are confirmed by Wilson v. Lynch (below). Answering falsely on ATF Form 4473 about controlled-substance use is itself a federal offence; secondary sources state up to 10 years' federal imprisonment for a false statement — [VERIFY] against 18 U.S.C. §924 before quoting a maximum. Wilson v. Lynch, 835 F.3d 1083 (9th Cir. 31 Aug 2016), No. 14-15700 — CORRECTED: plaintiff S. Rowan Wilson was a Nevada resident holding a Nevada medical marijuana registry card, who alleged she chose not to use medical marijuana. The court held she lacked standing to challenge 18 U.S.C. §922(g)(3) (she had not alleged unlawful drug use or firearm possession), but upheld dismissal of her challenge to 18 U.S.C. §922(d)(3), 27 C.F.R. §478.11 and the ATF Open Letter under intermediate scrutiny, finding a reasonable fit with the government's substantial interest in violence prevention (Wilson v. Lynch (9th Cir. 2016)). Do NOT repeat the secondary claim that the plaintiff was "an Alabama medical marijuana cardholder." That description is wrong and is removed. Schedule III alone does not remove a person from §922(g)(3) text, because the statute applies to users of any controlled substance, not only Schedule I drugs. Secondary LegalClarity and Congressional Research Service summaries make that point, and note that only Congress removing marijuana from the schedules or amending §922(g)(3) would eliminate the conflict. ATF interim final rule, effective 22 January 2026 (federal baseline, corrected wording): rewrote 27 CFR 478.11 to require regular use continuing into the present for "unlawful user" status. The original's paraphrase ("regular, recent use over an extended period") is superseded by the baseline wording. The rule clarifies that someone using a lawfully prescribed controlled substance is not an "unlawful user" — but because marijuana cannot be legally prescribed under federal law, regular medical marijuana users still face potential federal liability. [VERIFY] against the Federal Register text before stating the rule's scope further. Draft ATF Form 4473 — flagged, not adopted as final law: a draft revised Form 4473 reportedly says only use / possession of marijuana for recreational purposes is federally prohibited, omitting prior medical-cannabis language, tied to the state-licensed medical Schedule III order. One source gives a public-comment deadline of 7 July 2026; another gives 6 August 2026. That date conflict remains [VERIFY]. A revised form is not a statutory change; §922(g)(3) remains on the books, and the draft was not final in the sources found. Patients must not be advised to answer the current form differently based on draft coverage. United States v. Hemani, No. 24-1234, decided 18 June 2026, Justice Gorsuch — FEDERAL case law, NOT Alabama law (given baseline): held a status-only §922(g)(3) prosecution of a regular marijuana user for in-home possession, with no danger showing, inconsistent with the Second Amendment, as applied and narrow. No ATF safe harbour for Alabama medical patients was located in the federal research baseline. Secondary Homestead Health summary is consistent: Hemani narrowed the prohibition — barring punishment based on cannabis use alone without a showing of dangerousness — but did not strike down §922(g)(3); Alabama's authorisation has no effect on the federal firearms statute, and patients should consult a qualified attorney on their specific situation (secondary).

12.6 Consumption rules

Official patient / caregiver restrictions — Rule 538-X-2-.08 (r. 538-X-2-.08 (official)): (1) Registrations non-transferrable. (2) No cultivation or manufacture of extract; registration is not a licence to cultivate, produce, transport or dispense. (3) No patient or caregiver shall provide or accept samples of medical cannabis (see A.11.7). (4) Purchase only from a certified dispensing site operated by a licensed dispensary / integrated facility. (5) Secure storage preventing theft / loss / unauthorised access. (6) Carry the card whenever in possession; no more than a 70-day supply per patient at any time. (7) Maintain in the original dispensing package with unaltered label, or a dispensary / integrated-facility-provided storage container, until administered. (8) Medical cannabis shall not be possessed or administered on federal property or in federal buildings. (9) Medical cannabis shall not be possessed or administered at state or federal correctional detention facilities, including prisons and juvenile detention centers. (10) Medical cannabis shall not be possessed or administered in any public or private place where medical cannabis is prohibited. (11) Medical cannabis shall not be administered or possessed outside of its packaging on the premises of a dispensing site or any other licensed facility. (12) No patient shall operate a motor vehicle, watercraft, heavy machinery, or aircraft while under the influence of medical cannabis. (13) A caregiver may receive compensation for services plus reimbursement for reasonable expenses. (14) On expiration of registration or suspension / revocation, or on a patient's death, patients / caregivers (or personal representatives on death) must dispose of all medical cannabis within seven calendar days after death or expiration; acceptable disposal methods are to be available on the Commission's website. The Commission's disposal-methods list itself was not opened. [VERIFY] on amcc.alabama.gov. (15)–(16) Reciprocity bar in rule form: an Alabama Medical Cannabis Card is valid only within Alabama and may only be issued to and used by Alabama residents as defined in the rules. Cards may not be obtained or used by nonresidents, even though the nonresident is present in Alabama or is eligible to receive cannabis in any form under another jurisdiction's laws.

Statutory consumption bars — §20-2A-8 (as introduced / enrolled SB 46 text, secondary republication — verify against current official Code before quoting as current). Diverted medical cannabis: an individual may not distribute, possess, manufacture, or use medical cannabis / medical cannabis product diverted from a registered patient, registered caregiver, or licensed cultivator, processor, secure transporter, dispensary, or state testing laboratory; violation is a Class B felony, in addition to any Title 13A marijuana penalties. The chapter does not permit, and does not prevent civil / criminal / other penalty for: undertaking any task under the influence of cannabis when doing so would constitute negligence, professional malpractice, or professional misconduct, or violation of law; possessing / using medical cannabis on any K-12 school property (enrolled text adds daycare / childcare facility), in any correctional facility, or in a vehicle unless the medical cannabis is in its original package, sealed, and reasonably inaccessible while the vehicle is moving. Secondary alabamacannabis.org summary adds: marijuana consumption in public places is prohibited for both AMCC-approved persons and adult consumers; transporting cannabis across Alabama state lines is unlawful; gifting marijuana is illegal in Alabama. Those three points are secondary — [VERIFY] against statute / rule text (the gifting point is consistent with the diversion felony above only if the gifted product is diverted medical cannabis; a general "gifting" ban for non-medical marijuana follows from Title 13A distribution law, not from a standalone gifting statute located here).

Hemp consumption. Consumable hemp products may not be consumed on ABC-licensed premises by licensee / employee / agent (Chapter 20-X-33-.03); specialty retailer sales are for off-premises consumption only (secondary summary of Rule 20-X-33-.03). No Alabama public-consumption rule specific to hemp products (as opposed to medical cannabis) was located beyond the medical rules above and the general 21+ retail regime. [UNAVAILABLE] for a hemp-specific public-consumption statute.

12.7 Visitor and out-of-state patient rules

No reciprocity — confirmed from multiple sources, including official rule text. Alabama does not recognise medical cannabis cards issued by other states. A visitor from a medical-legal state cannot legally purchase or possess (medical) cannabis in Alabama on the strength of a home-state card. Rule 538-X-2-.08(15)–(16) (above) is the official-rule basis: Alabama cards are Alabama-resident-only and valid only within Alabama. Physician-certification residency guardrail: a registered certifying physician must not certify / recommend unless both physician and patient are physically located in Alabama (Chapter 540-X-25, see A.11.9) — a visitor cannot obtain Alabama certification by telemedicine from out of state. What a visitor CAN lawfully do with hemp products: a visitor who is 21+ may purchase consumable hemp products from an ABC-licensed retailer on the same terms as an Alabama resident (21+ purchase, in-person only, licensed retailer only, 10 mg / serving / 40 mg / package limits) — no residency requirement for hemp purchase was located in Chapter 20-X-33 or Title 28 Chapter 12 extracts. Non-consumable hemp-derived CBD at ≤0.3% delta-9-THC by dry weight is described in secondary sources as legal in Alabama on the federal standard; the visitor's home-state medical card confers no additional hemp right and no medical right. A visitor may NOT: purchase / possess medical cannabis in Alabama; use a home-state card at an Alabama dispensary; bring medical cannabis into Alabama from another state (interstate transport is unlawful under federal law and Alabama has no import / reciprocity provision — secondary summary, consistent with the rule text); or obtain Alabama certification without being physically in Alabama before a registered certifying physician and completing Alabama registration. Whether a nonresident can ever become an Alabama resident for card purposes (e.g. by relocating) is a residency-definition question — the rule defines "Alabama Residents" but the definition text was not opened. [VERIFY] for the residency definition. Alabama card outside Alabama: secondary LeafWell material lists states / territories with visitor / reciprocity regimes where an Alabama card may be recognised (Arizona, Arkansas*, Hawaii*, Louisiana, Maine, Michigan at dispensary discretion, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey*, New Mexico, Oklahoma*, Puerto Rico, Rhode Island, U.S. Virgin Islands*, Utah* up to two 21-day periods per calendar year, Washington, D.C.; * = visiting-patient application required). That list is secondary, dated, and must not be presented as current law for those states without re-checking each state's programme. It is included only to show the direction of travel: Alabama's card has no force in states without reciprocity, and Alabama itself offers none.

12.8 Landlord and tenant rules

No Alabama statute specific to medical cannabis and housing was located. SB 46 (the Compassion Act) does not address housing specifically in the material opened (secondary Alabama Marijuana Card summary: "SB 46 doesn't address housing specifically"). Private landlords — secondary analysis, not Alabama statute: the law gives landlords leeway in rental agreements; if a term is not explicitly legally forbidden, it is probably fair game for a landlord to include. It therefore "seems likely" a landlord could enforce an eviction based on a tenant's legal medical marijuana use if the rental agreement forbade it — but the same source stresses there is no certainty. A separate general (non-Alabama-specific) landlord guide states private, non-federally-assisted landlords have significant freedom to ban cannabis use regardless of state legalisation, often treating cannabis identically to tobacco in smoking policies, and that state law typically does not prevent a private landlord from prohibiting it on their property. Neither is Alabama law. [VERIFY] / [UNAVAILABLE] for an Alabama landlord-ban statute. Smoking vs non-smoking medical forms — material distinction for Alabama: because Alabama medical forms are non-smokable only (tablets, capsules, tinctures, gels / oils / creams, suppositories, patches, nebulizers, inhaler liquids — raw plant material and smokable / vapeable products prohibited), a "no smoking" lease clause does not on its face ban all Alabama medical cannabis use. But a broader "no drugs" / "no marijuana" / "illegal drug activity" clause, and any clause banning cannabis possession / use generally, could still be invoked — that application has not been tested in an Alabama case located here. [UNAVAILABLE] for Alabama case law. Illegal-activity eviction generally: secondary US Legal Forms material states illegal drug activity on rental property can be grounds for termination under Alabama law, with evidence (police reports, witness statements, inspection photos) and court process required if the tenant does not vacate. Without a card, all marijuana use is illegal in Alabama, so uncarded use is illegal-activity grounds; with a card and lease compliance, the secondary Alabama Marijuana Card summary says the tenant is "probably fine" — that is advice-column language, not law. Public / federally assisted housing — federal law controls: under federal statute, housing authorities and owners of federally assisted housing must establish lease provisions allowing termination of tenancy for any household with a member illegally using a controlled substance (42 U.S.C. §13662). Because marijuana remains federally illegal regardless of state law, HUD prohibits admission of marijuana users — including medical marijuana patients — to assisted housing programmes, and housing authorities cannot grant a reasonable accommodation for medical marijuana use (HUD Exchange position as cited in secondary summary — [VERIFY] the HUD Exchange wording before quoting it as HUD's current position; the baseline does not state that HUD's position changed with Schedule III). This is federal, not Alabama, law and must be flagged as such. Reasonable accommodation / disability: no Alabama rule was located requiring a landlord to accommodate medical cannabis use as a disability accommodation, and the federal HUD position above points the other way for assisted housing. For private housing, [UNAVAILABLE].

12.9 Pet and veterinary products

No Alabama-specific statute, ADAI rule, or Alabama Board of Veterinary Medical Examiners rule on CBD for animals was located in this research. [UNAVAILABLE] for an Alabama pet-CBD rule — do not state that Alabama "allows" or "bans" pet CBD on this record. Federal / FDA position (secondary, but consistent across sources): CBD and hemp-derived products have not been approved by FDA for use in animals as drugs or food / feed supplements — the only two legal marketing routes for animal products, as there is no dietary-supplement category for animals (DSHEA 1994 does not apply to animal products). Because FDA has approved CBD as a human drug (Epidiolex), CBD in any animal product would make it an Unapproved New Drug / Unapproved New Animal Drug; new animal drugs and new animal foods require pre-market approval for specific species. FDA's position is that pet food / treats containing hemp-derived CBD are adulterated and illegal for sale in interstate commerce; FDA has stated it will not undertake rulemaking to permit CBD products including for animals, and any path forward must come from Congress. FDA is particularly concerned about risks to animals consuming CBD and unintentional human exposure through meat, milk, and eggs. AAFCO guidance (model policy, adopted / binding in many states, referenced in others) states hemp ingredients including CBD and other cannabinoids cannot be used in pet food — that guidance was recently removed from the AAFCO website with no indication it was rescinded, and many states still reference it (secondary). Alabama-specific historical note (secondary, dated, do not present as current): a letter from Auburn University College of Veterinary Medicine professor Dawn Merton Boothe, DVM, PhD, DACVIM, DACVCP, in dvm360, summarising state guidance, stated that in Alabama, while persons might be able to possess the products, they cannot legally sell the products (referring to the state's industrial hemp programme directive at the time of writing). That is a dated secondary characterisation of older ADAI guidance, not a current Alabama pet-CBD rule. [VERIFY] against current ADAI / Board guidance before any use. Veterinarian practice (secondary): veterinarians may prescribe FDA-approved human medications such as Epidiolex for extra-label use in animals when medically appropriate, but generally cannot recommend or sell unapproved hemp / cannabis products marketed for pets; there are currently no FDA-approved cannabis drugs specifically for animals. Veterinarians have no DEA Schedule I authority to prescribe / recommend cannabis products. THC (marijuana) can be toxic to animals — pet owners should avoid human-use cannabis products, especially edibles. These are general U.S. practice points, not Alabama rules. Tuskegee hempseed-meal research (see B.11.9): hempseed meal has not been approved as animal feed by USDA / FDA / CVM to date — consistent with the FDA position above.

12.10 Medical cannabis in schools

Possession / use on school property is prohibited — statutory (enrolled text) + general rule. §20-2A-8 (enrolled SB 46 text; current-Code wording [VERIFY]) does not permit possessing or using medical cannabis on any K-12 school property (enrolled text adds daycare / childcare facility), in any correctional facility, or in a vehicle unless in its original package, sealed, and reasonably inaccessible while moving. Rule 538-X-2-.08(10) adds the general bar on possession / administration in any public or private place where medical cannabis is prohibited (r. 538-X-2-.08); the rule itself does not name schools, so the school bar must be cited to the statute, not to the rule alone. Dispensing sites must be ≥1,000 feet from any school / daycare / childcare facility (Chapter 538-X-8, see A.11.4; Chapter 538-X-8). Student patient possession / use at school / caregiver administration at school: no Alabama school-administration rule, ALSDE guidance, or Alabama school-district policy was located in this research. The searches returned New Jersey and other states' caregiver-administration policies (principal approval, private location, caregiver retains possession, escort / observation procedures) — those are not Alabama law and must not be imported. On the Alabama record, the position is: possession / use on K-12 school property is prohibited by the Act / rules as written, with no school-administration exception found. Whether an individual school district has adopted a private accommodation, and whether a student patient may leave school grounds for caregiver administration off property, are [UNAVAILABLE] on this record. Minors generally (for context, official AMCC FAQ): patients 19 or older with a qualifying condition may receive a medical cannabis card; parents / others may register as caregivers to obtain products for minors. A qualified patient under 19 must have a registered caregiver who is the patient's parent or legal guardian; a patient 19+ may designate a parent, legal guardian, grandparent, spouse, or individual with valid healthcare power of attorney. That caregiver framework does not override the school-property prohibition above (AMCC FAQ — Age restrictions; AMCC — Patients). Note: the minor-caregiver scope conflict (statute parent/legal guardian vs broader rule list) is a Part 1.4 / R1-16 issue and is NOT resolved by this FAQ. Correctional facilities: possession / administration at state / federal correctional detention facilities, including prisons and juvenile detention centers, is prohibited (Rule 538-X-2-.08(9)) — relevant to juvenile-justice school settings, but again no administration exception was found.
